title: English, Class 3
subject: English
description: NCERT Grade 3 English, chapter by chapter.

chapters.title: Fun with Friends
chapters.summary: In this chapter: a trip to the village fair; sharing crayons; finding colours and action words; action grid and new alphabet examples.

lessons.title: A Trip to the Village Fair

activities.prompt: How will the duck and her friends get across the stream together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Setting Off for the Fair
activities.body: A hen is invited to go to the village fair. She says that she will bring her chicks. A duck invites the ducklings to go along. The group reaches the stream. The duck cannot swim, so she wonders how they will cross. She says there is a plan. A duckling is a duck's young one. A chick is a hen's young one.
keyPoints: The hen and duck invite their young ones.
The group reaches a stream.
The duck cannot swim, but she has a plan.
activities.explanation: This story begins a journey to the fair and sets up a problem at the stream.

activities.prompt: The duck cannot swim, and the group is at a stream. How can they cross?
steps: The stream is a problem because the group has reached it.
Swimming cannot help the duck because the duck cannot swim.
The duck wonders how to cross because the group needs a way.
The group should listen because the duck says there is a plan.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Hen's Plan
activities.prompt: The hen says that she will bring her chicks.
activities.explanation: Yes. The hen tells everyone that her chicks will come too.

activities.title: The Duck's Guests
activities.prompt: Who does the duck invite to go along?
options: The ducklings
The chicks
The hen
The chicks and hen
activities.explanation: The duck invites the ducklings to join the group.

activities.title: Parents and Young Ones
activities.prompt: Match each bird or young one with the correct description.
activities.explanation: The hen brings her chicks, and the duck invites the ducklings.

activities.title: What Happens at the Stream?
activities.prompt: Put these events in the correct order.
items: The duck says that she cannot swim.
The duck wonders how they will cross the stream.
The duck says that there is a plan.
activities.explanation: The group reaches the stream, finds a problem, and then the duck offers a plan.

activities.title: The Crossing Plan
activities.prompt: What do we know about crossing the stream?
options: There is a plan.
There is a bridge.
There is a boat.
They need no help.
activities.explanation: The duck says that there is a plan, but the lesson does not tell us its details.

activities.prompt: The hen is invited to the village fair. She says she will bring her chicks. How does the hen feel about joining?
options: She feels happy about joining.
She feels willing to join.
She feels angry about joining.
She feels afraid to join.

She says she will bring her chicks, so she is willing.
Angry feelings do not fit her willing promise.
Afraid feelings do not fit her willing promise.

activities.explanation: This matches her promise to bring her chicks.

activities.prompt: The duck invites the ducklings to go along. What does this show about the duck?
options: The duck wants the ducklings with the group.
The duck wants the ducklings to stay away.
The duck wants the group to go without them.
The duck wants the ducklings to bring chicks.

why.The duck wants the ducklings to stay awa: Staying away is the opposite of an invitation.
why.The duck wants the group to go without t: Going without them is also the opposite of an invitation.
why.The duck wants the ducklings to bring ch: Bringing chicks is not part of the duck's invitation.

activities.explanation: Inviting the ducklings shows that the duck wants them included.

activities.prompt: The group has reached the stream. The duck cannot swim. The duck wonders how they will cross. What should the group do next?
options: Listen to the duck's plan.
Try to swim across now.
Go back without a plan.
Ask the chicks to go alone.

The duck cannot swim, so swimming is not a good choice.
A plan exists, so going back is not needed.
The facts do not say the chicks should go alone.

activities.explanation: The duck says there is a plan, so the group should listen.

activities.prompt: The duck cannot swim. The duck wonders how they will cross the stream. What does 'wonders' mean here?
options: Thinks about a question
Does a happy dance
Starts a loud fight
Keeps a secret plan

why.Does a happy dance: A dance does not fit the duck's question.
why.Starts a loud fight: A fight is not suggested by the duck's question.
why.Keeps a secret plan: Keeping a secret does not fit the duck's thinking.

activities.explanation: The duck is thinking about how to cross the stream.

activities.prompt: The duck says that there is a plan. What can we understand about the duck?
options: The duck knows a way to continue.
The duck is still helpless and alone.
The duck wants the group to turn back.
The duck has forgotten the stream.

Having a plan does not mean being helpless or alone.
Turning back is not stated in the facts.
The stream is still a problem, so it is not forgotten.

activities.explanation: A plan means the duck knows a way to continue.

lessons.title: Sharing Crayons

activities.prompt: What happens when two friends share their crayons?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sharing Can Help
activities.body: Two children share crayons. One has red, yellow and blue. The other has green, purple and black. One child needs red, and the other needs black. They decide to share, so both children have a full pack. Their poem names six colours and is spoken by two children.
keyPoints: One child has red, yellow and blue.
The other has green, purple and black.
They share, and both have a full pack.
activities.explanation: Sharing helps each child find the crayon they need.

activities.prompt: One child needs a red crayon, and the other needs a black crayon. How can both children get what they need?
steps: One child has red, yellow and blue, while the other has green, purple and black.
Neither child has both needed crayons, so they need each other’s crayons.
Sharing helps because each child can use the crayon the other has.
They decide to share, so both children get what they need.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: The other child has green, purple and black crayons.
activities.explanation: Yes! Those three crayons belong to the other child.

activities.title: Match the Crayons
activities.prompt: Match each crayon set or needed crayon to its clue.
activities.explanation: Great matching! Each child has colours and needs one crayon.

activities.title: A Sharing Choice
activities.prompt: What do the children decide to do?
options: Share their crayons
Hide their crayons
Buy new crayons
Keep crayons apart
activities.explanation: Excellent! Sharing gives both children the crayons they need.

activities.prompt: After sharing, the children say that they have a full pack.
activities.explanation: Yes! Their full pack comes after they share their crayons.

activities.title: The Sharing Sequence
activities.prompt: Put the sharing events in order.
items: After sharing, they have a full pack.
activities.explanation: Perfect order! First they choose to share, and then they share.

activities.prompt: The children share their crayons with each other. How might they feel?
options: They may feel glad that both can use crayons.
They may feel worried because crayons are now mixed.
They may feel bored because sharing takes too long.
They may feel cross because neither child gets crayons.

why.They may feel worried because crayons ar: This mistakes sharing for mixing and losing crayons.
why.They may feel bored because sharing take: This assumes sharing always feels slow and boring.
why.They may feel cross because neither chil: This mistakes sharing for getting no crayons at all.

activities.explanation: Sharing helps both children, so feeling glad makes sense.

activities.prompt: After sharing, the children say, “We have a full pack.” What does this imply?
options: They still have enough crayons to share.
They have no crayons left to use.
They have only one crayon between them.
They have used all their crayons.

This mistakes sharing for using all the crayons.
This mistakes a full pack for having only one.
This assumes crayons disappear when they are shared.

activities.explanation: A full pack shows that many crayons remain.

activities.prompt: One child needs red, and the other needs black. Why might they share?
options: So each child gets the crayon they need.
So one child can keep all the crayons.
So both children lose crayons together.
So the crayons can stay unshared.

This thinks sharing gives one child everything.
This mistakes sharing for losing crayons.
This assumes crayons cannot be shared.

activities.explanation: Sharing gives each child the crayon they need.

activities.prompt: Two friends will say the poem about sharing crayons. Why might two speakers fit it?
options: Because the poem’s children share crayons together.
Because one child must own every crayon.
Because crayons should always stay apart.
Because sharing crayons always causes fights.

This mistakes sharing for one child owning everything.
why.Because crayons should always stay apart: This assumes sharing means keeping crayons apart.
why.Because sharing crayons always causes fi: This wrongly links sharing crayons with fighting.

activities.explanation: The poem is spoken by two children who share crayons.

lessons.title: Finding Colours and Action Words

activities.prompt: Can you find the colours and actions hiding in these tricky words?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Colour groups and action words
activities.body: Letter groups are the letters at the start of a word. The gr group has green, grey, grass and grapes. The cr group has crayon, crab, crane, crow and cradle. The dr group has draw, drum, dress, drop and dragon. The pr group has prince, princess, prize, pray, present and grandmother. Five sets of mixed-up colour letters need rearranging. Action words show actions. Laugh, dance, eat, cry and swim are action words.
keyPoints: Colour word groups include gr, cr, dr and pr.
Action words show actions, such as laugh, dance and swim.
There are five sets of mixed-up colour letters.
activities.explanation: These groups help you spot words that begin in the same way.

activities.prompt: How should I read a YELLOW card in the fun task?
steps: I read a colour because the task forbids reading the written word.
The example confirms this because YELLOW is read as GREEN.
So I should say GREEN when I see YELLOW.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Find the gr word
activities.prompt: Which word begins with gr?
options: green
prize
draw
prince
activities.explanation: Green begins with gr, just like the other gr words.

activities.title: Check the beginning
activities.prompt: The word grapes begins with the gr group.
activities.explanation: Grapes begins with gr, so the statement is true.

activities.title: Match each opening group
activities.prompt: Match each word to its opening letter group.
activities.explanation: The first two letters show each word's group.

activities.title: Find an action word
activities.prompt: Which word is an action word?
options: green
prize
crab
laugh
activities.explanation: Laugh shows an action, so it is an action word.

activities.title: Read the card
activities.prompt: In the fun task, children read the written word.
activities.explanation: Children read the colour, not the written word.

activities.prompt: A card says YELLOW, and the child reads GREEN. Why?
options: The game asks the child to read a colour.
The child changes every letter.
The child reads the written word.
The child does not know colours.

This mistake thinks the child is mixing up all the letters.
This mistake ignores the rule to read the colour instead.
This mistake treats the example as a mistake, not a rule.

activities.explanation: This is right because the example says YELLOW is read as GREEN.

activities.prompt: Green plants cover the ground. Animals eat them. Which gr word fits?
options: green
grey
grass
grapes

why.green: This mistake gives the colour instead of the plant's name.
why.grey: This mistake chooses another colour instead of the ground plant.
why.grapes: This mistake chooses a fruit instead of the ground plant.

activities.explanation: Grass is right because it names the green plants animals eat.

activities.prompt: A sea animal walks sideways with little legs. Which cr word fits?
options: crab
crow
crane
cradle

why.crow: This mistake chooses a bird instead of the sideways sea animal.
why.crane: This mistake chooses a tall bird instead of the sideways animal.
why.cradle: This mistake chooses a bed instead of the walking animal.

activities.explanation: Crab is right because it names the sea animal walking sideways.

activities.prompt: A child uses a pencil to make a picture. Which dr word fits?
options: draw
drum
dress
drop

why.drum: This mistake chooses a musical instrument instead of the picture action.
why.dress: This mistake chooses what someone wears instead of an action.
why.drop: This mistake confuses making a mark with letting something fall.

activities.explanation: Draw is right because it names making a picture with a pencil.

activities.prompt: A royal boy wears a small crown. Which pr word fits?
options: prince
princess
prize
present

why.princess: This mistake chooses the royal word for a girl instead.
why.prize: This mistake chooses an award instead of the royal boy.
why.present: This mistake chooses a gift instead of the royal boy.

activities.explanation: Prince is right because it names a royal boy.

activities.prompt: A child moves through water using their arms. Which action word fits?
options: laugh
dance
cry
swim

why.laugh: This mistake chooses a funny reaction instead of movement in water.
why.dance: This mistake chooses moving to music instead of movement in water.
why.cry: This mistake chooses a sad reaction instead of movement in water.

activities.explanation: Swim is right because it shows moving through water with the arms.

lessons.title: Action Grid and New Alphabet Examples

activities.prompt: Can you find the action words hiding in the grid?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Actions and Letters
activities.body: Find action words hidden in the grid. One answer is already done. The grid includes cough, give, see, open and help. The English alphabet has 26 letters. Anu eats an apple. Basu has a bat and ball. Chandu likes cabbage and carrots.
keyPoints: Find action words in the grid.
One answer is already done.
The English alphabet has 26 letters.
activities.explanation: These clues will help you find actions and letter examples.

activities.prompt: How can Anu use the alphabet to check the action word in her sentence?
steps: Anu eats an apple, so “eats” tells what she does.
That makes “eats” the action word in her sentence.
The alphabet has 26 letters, so each letter can be checked.
Therefore, Anu can check “eats” letter by letter.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Starting Letters
activities.body: The English alphabet has 26 letters. A begins Anu's apple example. B begins Basu's bat and ball example. C begins Chandu's cabbage and carrots example. D begins Dinesh's dancing example. E begins Esha's elephant example. Read each example slowly and listen for its first sound.
keyPoints: Anu's example begins with A.
Chandu's example begins with C.
Esha's example begins with E.
activities.explanation: Starting sounds help you connect each letter with its example.

activities.title: Anu's Example
activities.prompt: What does Anu do in the example?
options: Eats an apple
Has a bat
Likes cabbage
Dances day and night
activities.explanation: Anu eats an apple, just as the example says.

activities.title: Basu's Things
activities.prompt: Basu has a ______ and a ball.
activities.hint: It is the other thing Basu has.
activities.explanation: Basu has both a bat and a ball.

activities.title: Match the Examples
activities.prompt: Match each child to the matching example.
pairs: has a bat and a ball
activities.explanation: Each name has its own matching example in the lesson.

activities.title: Esha's Letter
activities.prompt: Which letter starts Esha's example?
options: A
B
C
E
activities.explanation: Esha enjoys an elephant ride, so E begins that example.

activities.title: Order the Examples
activities.prompt: Put these alphabet examples in the order shown in the lesson.
items: Basu has a bat and a ball
activities.explanation: The examples appear in this order as you read through the lesson.

activities.title: Letters and Examples
activities.prompt: Which statement about the alphabet and Esha is true?
options: The alphabet has 26 letters; Esha's example begins with E.
The alphabet has 26 words; Esha's example begins with E.
The alphabet has 26 letters; Esha's example begins with A.
The alphabet has 26 names; Esha's example begins with E.
activities.explanation: The alphabet has 26 letters, and Esha's example begins with E.

activities.prompt: One grid answer is done. What should the child do next?
options: Find another action word.
Write the same word again.
Look for a different name.
Leave the grid empty.

Writing it again does not find a new answer.
Looking for a name misses the action-word task.
Leaving it empty stops the search too soon.

activities.explanation: Finding another action word follows the grid task.

activities.prompt: A child needs a book. The teacher has one. What should happen?
options: The teacher gives it.
The teacher opens it.
The teacher hides it.
The teacher sees it.

Opening the book does not give it to the child.
Hiding the book leaves the child’s need unmet.
Seeing the book does not give it to the child.

activities.explanation: Giving the book meets the child’s need.

activities.prompt: The poem says, “Dinesh dances day and night.” What does it show?
options: He dances very often.
He hardly ever dances.
He only reads books.
He stays very still.

Hardly ever means dancing is rare, not constant.
Reading is not shown in the poem.
Staying still is the opposite of dancing.

activities.explanation: Day and night means Dinesh dances a lot.

activities.prompt: Esha enjoys an elephant ride. How does she likely feel?
options: pleased
angry
upset
afraid

why.upset: Upset suggests a bad feeling, not enjoyment.
why.afraid: Afraid is possible, but the line points to enjoyment.

activities.explanation: Enjoying the ride supports feeling pleased.

activities.prompt: Chandu likes cabbage and carrots. What kind of food does he like?
options: Vegetables like these.
Fruits like these.
Sweets like these.
Grain foods like these.

Fruits do not match cabbage or carrots.
Sweets do not match cabbage or carrots.
Grain foods do not include cabbage or carrots.

activities.explanation: Cabbage and carrots are vegetables.

activities.prompt: Basu has a bat and a ball. What does this suggest?
options: He may play a game.
He may read a book.
He may cook food.
He may draw a map.

Reading does not need a bat and ball.
Cooking does not need a bat and ball.
Drawing does not need a bat and ball.

activities.explanation: A bat and ball together suggest playing a game.

lessons.title: More Letters and A-to-Z Order

activities.prompt: Ready to discover how letters can help you put words in order?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Spot the Starting Letters
activities.body: Spot each example's first letter. For I, the speaker likes ice-cream. For J, Jack jumps down. Kavita keeps kittens on her knees for K. Lata loves lemonade for L. Madhav mixes milk and mango pulp for M. For N, Navneet writes his name. Om opens a box of oranges for O. Prema puts a pencil in her pocket for P. The Q activity asks children to queue up quietly.
keyPoints: Each example begins with a different letter.
The examples use the letters I, J, K, L, M, N, O, P and Q.
Sorting starts by looking at first letters.
activities.explanation: Look for the starting letter, then use it to sort.

activities.prompt: How can I put the five fruit words in A-to-Z order?
steps: Look at each word's first letter because sorting begins there.
Place apple and banana first because A comes before B.
Place cherry and grapes next because C and G come after B.
Put orange last because O follows G, giving the order apple, banana, cherry, grapes, orange.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Does the Speaker Like?
activities.prompt: In the I example, what does the speaker like?
options: Ice-cream
Lemonade
Mango pulp
A pencil
activities.explanation: Yes! The I example says that the speaker likes ice-cream.

activities.title: Jack's Action
activities.prompt: In the J example, Jack jumps down.
activities.explanation: That is right. Jack jumps down in the J example.

activities.title: Madhav's Mixture
activities.prompt: In the M example, Madhav mixes ______ and mango pulp.
activities.hint: It is one of the two things Madhav mixes.
activities.explanation: Well done! Madhav mixes milk and mango pulp.

activities.title: Who Opens the Oranges?
activities.prompt: Who opens a box of oranges in the O example?
options: Madhav
Navneet
Om
Jack
activities.explanation: Correct! Om opens a box of oranges in the O example.

activities.title: Match Fruits and First Letters
activities.prompt: Match each fruit to its first letter.
activities.explanation: Nice sorting! A comes before B, so apple comes before banana.

activities.title: Order the Fruits
activities.prompt: Put these fruits in A-to-Z order.
activities.explanation: Great work! The A-to-Z order is apple, banana, cherry, grapes and orange.

activities.prompt: The I example says the speaker likes ice-cream. How might the speaker feel when ice-cream is near?
options: Happy and excited
Cross and angry
Sad and lonely
Afraid and worried

why.Cross and angry: This mistake confuses liking ice-cream with being cross with it.
why.Sad and lonely: This mistake thinks a liked treat gives a reason to feel sad.
why.Afraid and worried: This mistake treats a liked treat as something frightening.

activities.explanation: Liking ice-cream makes happiness and excitement likely feelings.

activities.prompt: The K example says Kavita keeps kittens on her knees. How might Kavita feel while doing this?
options: Careful and gentle
Cross and rough
Bored and tired
Scared and worried

why.Cross and rough: This mistake treats gentle care as rough treatment.
why.Bored and tired: This mistake assumes keeping kittens must feel boring.
why.Scared and worried: This mistake assumes close handling makes Kavita afraid.

activities.explanation: Keeping kittens on her knees calls for careful, gentle handling.

activities.prompt: The Q activity tells children to queue up quietly. Why might the teacher ask for quiet?
options: To help children wait calmly
To help children make more noise
To send children far away
To stop children waiting in line

why.To help children make more noise: This mistake reverses the quiet rule into a noisy one.
why.To send children far away: This mistake thinks quiet means sending children away.
why.To stop children waiting in line: This mistake thinks quiet means ending the line.

activities.explanation: Quiet queuing helps the children wait calmly in line.

activities.prompt: Sorting starts with the first letter of each word. These fruits are apple, banana, cherry, grapes, and orange. Which word comes after grapes in A-to-Z order?
options: orange
apple
banana
cherry

why.apple: Apple belongs before grapes because A comes before G.
why.banana: Banana belongs before grapes because B comes before G.
why.cherry: Cherry belongs before grapes because C comes before G.

activities.explanation: Orange follows grapes because O comes after G in A-to-Z order.

lessons.title: The Last Letters and Word Friends

activities.prompt: What makes some letters and words feel like friends?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Words Can Be Friends
activities.body: Words can have friends just as people do. X is the last letter in ox, fox and box. Yasmeen and Yana are word friends. The lesson also shows Radha, Usha, Vishnu and some sparrows. You will look for last letters and match words with their endings. The friend-word task gives one example that is already done.
keyPoints: X comes last in ox, fox and box.
Yasmeen and Yana are word friends.
One friend-word example is already done.
activities.explanation: This lesson helps you find final letters and recognise word friends.

activities.prompt: A child sorts ox, fox, and box together. Why are they word friends?
steps: Their first letters differ, so those letters cannot join the words.
Their last letters match because every word ends with X.
The lesson links matching last letters with word friends.
So ox, fox, and box are word friends because they share X.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which word ends with X?
options: ox
sack
van
activities.explanation: X is the last letter in ox.

activities.prompt: In the word fox, the last letter is ______.
activities.hint: Look at the final letter.
activities.explanation: Well done! X is the final letter in fox.

activities.prompt: Which group has only words ending with X?
options: ox, fox, box
red, van, tale
fox, sack, van
ribbon, wall, box
activities.explanation: The lesson says X ends ox, fox and box.

activities.prompt: Match each word to its last letter.
activities.explanation: Check the final letter of each word.

activities.prompt: Put the X-ending words in the order shown in your book.
activities.explanation: Your book shows ox, fox and box in that order.

activities.prompt: What does the friend-word task include?
options: One finished example
Some colour words
A teacher’s tale
A village visit
activities.explanation: The friend-word task includes one example that is already done.

activities.prompt: Radha rolls a red ribbon. How can we describe the ribbon as she rolls it?
options: Red and moving
White and moving
Red and sitting
White and sitting

why.White and moving: The ribbon is red, not white.
why.Red and sitting: The ribbon is moving because Radha rolls it.
why.White and sitting: The ribbon is neither white nor sitting.

activities.explanation: The ribbon is red, and rolling means that it is moving.

activities.prompt: The last letter of ox and fox is X. Which word starts with b and ends with X?
options: box
six
sack
lamp

why.six: Six starts with s, not b.
why.sack: Sack starts with s and ends with k.
why.lamp: Lamp starts with l and ends with p.

activities.explanation: Box starts with b and ends with X.

activities.prompt: Red and white are colour words. Which word comes first alphabetically?
options: Red
White
Usha
Village

why.Usha: Usha is a name, not a colour word.
why.Village: Village is a place word, not a colour word.

activities.explanation: R comes before W, so Red comes first.

activities.prompt: Words are said to have friends just as people do. What can word friends share?
options: The same last letter
A different last letter
The same first letter
A different first letter

why.A different last letter: Ox, fox, and box all have the same last letter.
why.The same first letter: Their first letters are o, f, and b, so they differ.
why.A different first letter: The matching part is their shared last letter, X.

activities.explanation: Ox, fox, and box show that word friends can share their last letter.

activities.context: When the hen was invited to the village fair, she said that she would bring her chicks. The duck invited her ducklings to go along. When the group reached the stream, the duck could not swim. She wondered how they would cross. Then the duck said that there was a plan.
activities.prompt: If the duck could swim, what change would help her at the stream?
options: She would be able to cross the stream herself.
The whole group could cross together without any other help.
The ducklings could automatically follow her across.
The duck would no longer wonder how to cross.

why.The whole group could cross together wit: One person's ability would not prove that everyone could cross.
why.The ducklings could automatically follow: The ducklings' ability was not established.
why.The duck would no longer wonder how to c: The original problem would disappear for the duck.

activities.explanation: Swimming would directly solve the duck's problem.

activities.context: When the hen was invited to the village fair, she said that she would bring her chicks. The duck invited her ducklings to go along. When the group reached the stream, the duck could not swim. She wondered how they would cross. Then the duck said that there was a plan.
activities.prompt: If the duck had not mentioned a plan, what problem would remain for the group?
options: They would still need to find a way to cross the stream.
They would need to decide whether the hen should bring her chicks.
They would need to explain what a duckling is.
They would need to invite another duck to join them.

why.They would need to decide whether the he: The hen had already said that she would bring her chicks.
why.They would need to explain what a duckli: Explaining the meaning of a duckling would not solve the crossing problem.
why.They would need to invite another duck t: Inviting another duck would not provide a way across.

activities.explanation: The group had reached the stream and still needed to cross.

activities.prompt: Explain why the duck's inability to swim led her to think about a plan.
activities.answer: The group had reached the stream, but the duck could not swim. She wondered how they would cross. That difficulty made her think of a plan, showing that the plan was meant to solve the problem of getting across.
points: The group reached the stream.
The duck could not swim.
The duck wondered how they would cross.
The plan offered a solution to the problem.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Two children talk about crayons. One says that they have a few crayons. One child has red, yellow and blue crayons, while the other has green, purple and black crayons. One child needs the red crayon, and the other needs the black one. The children decide to share their crayons. They say that they have a full pack, and after sharing, they say that they have a full pack. Their poem is spoken by two children and names six crayon colours.
activities.prompt: The children decide to share. Which crayons should change hands so that each child gets the colour they need?
options: The red and black crayons
The green and purple crayons
The yellow and blue crayons
The red and yellow crayons

why.The green and purple crayons: The child needing black would still not get the black crayon.
why.The yellow and blue crayons: The children needing red and black would still not get what they need.
why.The red and yellow crayons: Black would stay with the child who has it, so one need would not be met.

activities.explanation: These are the two colours the children need from each other.

activities.context: Two children talk about crayons. One says that they have a few crayons. One child has red, yellow and blue crayons, while the other has green, purple and black crayons. One child needs the red crayon, and the other needs the black one. The children decide to share their crayons. They say that they have a full pack, and after sharing, they say that they have a full pack. Their poem is spoken by two children and names six crayon colours.
activities.prompt: After the children decide to share, what should they do next?
options: Pass on the crayons that the other child needs.
Keep the crayons apart and continue talking.
Share only the crayons that neither child needs.
Stop speaking the poem and keep the crayons.

why.Keep the crayons apart and continue talk: Keeping them apart would prevent both needs from being met.
why.Share only the crayons that neither chil: The crayons each child needs cannot meet both needs.
why.Stop speaking the poem and keep the cray: Speaking the poem does not replace sharing the crayons.

activities.explanation: This allows each child to receive the colour they need.

activities.prompt: Explain how sharing helps the children in this case.
activities.answer: The child with red, yellow and blue crayons has the black crayon that the other child needs. The other child has the red crayon that the first child needs. Sharing lets both children get the colour they need, and afterwards they say that they have a full pack.
points: Identifies who has the black crayons.
Identifies who has the red crayons.
Explains that sharing meets both children's needs.
Mentions that they say they have a full pack afterwards.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During the lesson "Finding Colours and Action Words," a student works with five sets of mixed-up colour letters. The student rearranges the letters for words beginning with gr, cr, dr and pr. In the fun task, YELLOW is read as GREEN. The student also reads words that show actions: Laugh, dance, eat, cry and swim.
activities.prompt: If the student must explain why "dance" belongs in the action-word part, which explanation is best?
options: It shows an action.
The dr beginning places it in the colour-letter group.
It is read as a colour in the fun task.
It belongs to the pr group.

why.The dr beginning places it in the colour: The dr beginning identifies its colour-letter group, not the action group.
The fun task reads colours instead of written words.
Dance is not in the pr group.

activities.explanation: Dance shows an action, so it belongs in the action-word list.

activities.context: During the lesson "Finding Colours and Action Words," a student works with five sets of mixed-up colour letters. The student rearranges the letters for words beginning with gr, cr, dr and pr. In the fun task, YELLOW is read as GREEN. The student also reads words that show actions: Laugh, dance, eat, cry and swim.
activities.prompt: After the student reads the colour for YELLOW in the fun task, what should happen next with another written colour word?
options: The student should read its colour instead of the written word.
The student should write its colour letters in mixed-up order.
The student should say the written word without reading its colour.
The student should choose an action word instead.

why.The student should write its colour lett: The task starts with letters to rearrange; it does not ask for more mixing.
why.The student should say the written word: That would ignore the special colour-reading rule.
why.The student should choose an action word: Action words are a separate part of the lesson.

activities.explanation: The fun task says to read the colour rather than the written word.

activities.prompt: How does the fun task change the reading, and what happens in the example?
activities.answer: The fun task is different because the student reads the colour instead of the written word. In the example, YELLOW is read as GREEN. The written word stays the same, but the word spoken for it changes to show its colour.
points: Identifies that the colour is read instead of the written word.
Gives YELLOW as the written example.
States that YELLOW is read as GREEN.
Explains that the spoken word changes while the written word stays.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: The teacher gives the children an action grid for a class activity. Cough, give, see, open, and help are hidden in the grid, and one answer is already done. The children use the 26 letters of the English alphabet to check their work. Anu eats an apple. Basu has a bat and a ball. Chandu likes cabbage and carrots. Dinesh dances day and night. Esha enjoys an elephant ride.
activities.prompt: Why can the children use the English alphabet while checking the action grid?
options: The hidden action words are made from the alphabet's letters.
The alphabet shows every example the children will act out.
Only the answer already done belongs in the alphabet.
The children must copy the alphabet before they can read.

why.The alphabet shows every example the chi: The alphabet does not explain the children's examples.
why.Only the answer already done belongs in: The other action words are also made from letters.
why.The children must copy the alphabet befo: Checking the letters does not require copying the alphabet.

activities.explanation: Words in the grid are formed from English letters.

activities.context: The teacher gives the children an action grid for a class activity. Cough, give, see, open, and help are hidden in the grid, and one answer is already done. The children use the 26 letters of the English alphabet to check their work. Anu eats an apple. Basu has a bat and a ball. Chandu likes cabbage and carrots. Dinesh dances day and night. Esha enjoys an elephant ride.
activities.prompt: One answer in the action grid is already done. What should the children do next?
options: Look for the remaining action words.
Copy the completed answer.
Stop because the task is finished.
Use only the alphabet list.

Copying the completed answer would not find another word.
One completed answer does not finish the search.
The alphabet helps with the search, but it is not the answer list.

activities.explanation: The other action words still need to be found.

activities.prompt: Explain how the action grid and the English alphabet can help the children find action words.
activities.answer: The action grid contains action words, while the English alphabet has 26 letters to help check them. The children can use the letters to look for words such as cough, give, see, open, and help. Since one answer is already done, they should continue searching for the remaining action words.
points: Identifies the action grid as containing action words
States that the English alphabet has 26 letters
Explains that the letters help in the search
Notes that one answer is already completed
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During an A-to-Z activity, Jack jumps down. Madhav mixes milk and mango pulp, and Lata loves lemonade. Kavita keeps kittens on her knees, while Prema puts a pencil in her pocket. The children have words to sort. They begin by looking at the first letter of each word. When the Q activity starts, the children queue up quietly. Om opens a box of oranges, and Navneet writes his name on new notebooks.
activities.prompt: The Q activity is about to start, but Jack has just jumped down. What should the other children do?
options: Wait in line and keep the activity quiet.
Leave their places and join Jack.
Keep talking loudly until everyone is ready.
Sort the fruit names before joining the line.

Jack’s action does not change the activity’s instructions.
why.Keep talking loudly until everyone is re: Quiet queueing does not mean talking loudly.
why.Sort the fruit names before joining the: The children are asked to queue, not to sort fruit names.

activities.explanation: The Q activity asks the children to queue up quietly.

activities.context: During an A-to-Z activity, Jack jumps down. Madhav mixes milk and mango pulp, and Lata loves lemonade. Kavita keeps kittens on her knees, while Prema puts a pencil in her pocket. The children have words to sort. They begin by looking at the first letter of each word. When the Q activity starts, the children queue up quietly. Om opens a box of oranges, and Navneet writes his name on new notebooks.
activities.prompt: A sorter looks at the last letter of each word instead of the first. What should they do to correct the activity?
options: Go back to each word’s opening letter and sort again.
Continue with the ending letters and leave the list unchanged.
Place the words in reverse A-to-Z order.
Make no change because any letter order is acceptable.

why.Continue with the ending letters and lea: Ending letters are not the rule for this sorting activity.
A-to-Z order is not the reverse order, since A comes before B.
why.Make no change because any letter order: The words must follow A-to-Z order, not any order.

activities.explanation: Sorting begins by looking at the first letter of each word.

activities.prompt: How do you put apple, banana, cherry, grapes and orange in A-to-Z order?
activities.answer: Put the words in order by their opening letters. Apple begins with A, banana with B, cherry with C, grapes with G, and orange with O. Since A comes before B, the same rule continues through the list. The finished order is apple, banana, cherry, grapes, orange.
points: Looks at the first letter of each word.
Places A before B.
Places C, G and O in the correct positions.
Gives the order apple, banana, cherry, grapes, orange.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Radha rolls a red ribbon. Six sparrows sit on a sack. The teacher tells a tale. Words are said to have friends just as people do. Usha uses an umbrella, and Vishnu visits a village in a van. The children see a watchman near a white wall. X is the last letter in ox, fox and box. Yasmeen and Yana are friends. Zebras graze in the zoo. Colour words are in alphabetical order. One friend-word example is done.
activities.prompt: If the colour words were mixed up, what should Usha do to restore the correct order?
options: Put the colour words back into their A-to-Z sequence.
Keep them in whatever order they were first written.
Sort them by their final letters.
Copy the colours in the order of the friend-word example.

why.Keep them in whatever order they were fi: This leaves them unordered rather than following the alphabet.
Final letters may group words, but they do not give the required colour order.
why.Copy the colours in the order of the fri: The example does not tell Usha to copy the colour order.

activities.explanation: Alphabetic order puts colour words in the correct sequence.

activities.context: Radha rolls a red ribbon. Six sparrows sit on a sack. The teacher tells a tale. Words are said to have friends just as people do. Usha uses an umbrella, and Vishnu visits a village in a van. The children see a watchman near a white wall. X is the last letter in ox, fox and box. Yasmeen and Yana are friends. Zebras graze in the zoo. Colour words are in alphabetical order. One friend-word example is done.
activities.prompt: One friend-word example is already done. What should the children do next so that they understand the idea?
options: Use the example as a model, then make another group with a shared word feature.
Copy the same example and call the second group the same.
Change the words in the example so they no longer belong together.
Replace the example with the colour-word list.

why.Copy the same example and call the secon: Copying does not show that a new group can be made.
why.Change the words in the example so they: Changing the words removes the connection that the example shows.
why.Replace the example with the colour-word: The colour list shows alphabetical order, not the friend-word grouping.

activities.explanation: A completed example shows how to find words with a shared feature.

activities.prompt: Explain why ox, fox and box can be called word friends.
activities.answer: These three words are word friends because each one has X as its last letter. Their shared ending makes a group of word friends. This shows the lesson's main idea: words can be friends just as people can be friends, such as Yasmeen and Yana.
points: Identifies X as the last letter.
Explains that all three words share the same ending.
Connects word friends with people being friends.
Uses Yasmeen and Yana as an example of friends.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

chapters.title: Badal and Moti
chapters.summary: In this chapter: badal finds a puppy; moti grows up; badal falls into the pit; let's think about the story.

lessons.title: Badal Finds a Puppy

activities.prompt: What would happen if Badal opened his heart to a new little friend?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Badal and Moti
activities.body: Badal was a boy who lived with his mother in a village. They were very happy together. One evening, Badal came back from school and saw a little puppy shivering in the cold. He brought the puppy home and asked his mother. She agreed if Badal would care for it. Together, they named the puppy Moti.
keyPoints: Badal lived with his mother in a village.
He brought home a puppy shivering in the cold.
Badal and his mother named the puppy Moti.
activities.explanation: Badal showed kindness by caring for a cold puppy.

activities.prompt: Why did Badal take the shivering puppy home?
steps: The puppy was shivering because it felt cold.
Badal wanted to help, so he brought it home.
He asked his mother because they would live together.
His mother agreed when Badal promised to care for Moti.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Badal's Home
activities.prompt: Who did Badal live with in the village?
options: His puppy
His mother
His teacher
A shopkeeper
activities.explanation: Badal lived with his mother in a village.

activities.title: Match the Story
activities.prompt: Match each person or place to the correct description.
activities.explanation: Badal, Moti, and the village are all part of this story.

activities.title: The Puppy's Name
activities.prompt: Badal and his mother gave the puppy the name ______.
activities.hint: It was the little puppy's new name.
activities.explanation: Badal and his mother named the puppy Moti.

activities.title: Badal's Promise
activities.prompt: What did Badal promise his mother?
options: To take care of the puppy.
To take the puppy to school.
To leave the puppy outside.
To stop caring for the puppy.
activities.explanation: He promised to take care of the puppy.

activities.title: Put the Story in Order
activities.prompt: Put these events in the correct order.
items: Badal and his mother named it Moti.
activities.explanation: Badal found the puppy, cared for it, and named it Moti.

activities.title: Badal's Kind Choice
activities.prompt: Which choice shows what Badal did after seeing the puppy?
options: He brought it home and asked his mother.
He left it outside and went to bed.
He gave it to his schoolteacher.
He asked his mother to leave.
activities.explanation: He brought the puppy home and asked if it could stay.

activities.prompt: A puppy shakes in the cold. How does Badal likely feel?
options: He feels worried because the puppy is cold.
He feels bored because the puppy is still.
He feels angry because the puppy is noisy.
He feels excited because the puppy is moving.

why.He feels bored because the puppy is stil: This mistake ignores the puppy's need for warmth.
why.He feels angry because the puppy is nois: This mistake treats cold shivering as annoying noise.
why.He feels excited because the puppy is mo: This mistake focuses on movement instead of the puppy's cold.

activities.explanation: This is right because shivering shows that the puppy was cold.

activities.prompt: Badal asks about keeping the puppy. What does his question show?
options: He wants to give the puppy a home.
He wants the puppy to leave soon.
He wants his mother to ignore the puppy.
He wants to keep the puppy outside.

This mistake reverses his wish to keep the puppy.
This mistake mistakes his request for permission for indifference.
This mistake confuses taking responsibility with leaving the puppy outside.

activities.explanation: This is right because asking shows that Badal wanted the puppy to stay.

activities.prompt: Badal's mother says yes with a condition. What does her answer show?
options: She trusts Badal to care for the puppy.
She wants Badal to ignore the puppy.
She plans to send the puppy away.
She thinks Badal cannot care for it.

This mistake mistakes a condition of care for neglect.
This mistake reverses her agreement into a plan to send Moti away.
This mistake confuses trust in Badal with doubt about his care.

activities.explanation: This is right because she accepts his promise of responsible care.

activities.prompt: Badal's mother smiles as she speaks. How does she likely feel?
options: She feels pleased that Badal will help.
She feels cross because Badal came late.
She feels bored because Badal asked her.
She feels afraid because the puppy is cold.

This mistake reads a smile as crossness.
This mistake treats a kind answer as boredom.
why.She feels afraid because the puppy is co: This mistake mistakes concern for the puppy as fear.

activities.explanation: This is right because her smile shows that she was pleased.

activities.prompt: Badal's mother smiles while they name Moti. How do they feel?
options: They feel glad that Moti can stay.
They feel sorry that Moti is outside.
They feel cross that Moti is cold.
They feel afraid that Moti will leave.

This mistake treats their happy choice as sadness.
This mistake confuses the puppy's cold with anger at it.
This mistake mistakes a new home for fear of leaving.

activities.explanation: This is right because the smile and shared name show happiness.

lessons.title: Moti Grows Up

activities.prompt: Who did Moti love as he grew up?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Moti and Badal
activities.body: Badal and his mother named the puppy Moti. Badal had promised to take care of the puppy. As the days went by, Moti grew up. Moti loved Badal and followed him everywhere. Badal and Moti became the best of friends. They ate together, played together, and enjoyed their favourite games. His mother called Badal her beta, which means her son.
keyPoints: Badal and his mother named the puppy Moti.
Moti grew up, loved Badal, and followed him everywhere.
Badal and Moti became the best of friends.
activities.explanation: This card introduces Moti's loving friendship with Badal.

activities.prompt: Badal and Moti spend time together. What does this show?
steps: Badal promised to take care of Moti, because he felt responsible.
Moti followed Badal everywhere, because he loved being near him.
They ate and played together, because they enjoyed their time.
Therefore, Badal and Moti became the best of friends.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Badal and his mother named the puppy ______.
activities.hint: Use the puppy's name.
activities.explanation: Well done! Badal and his mother named the puppy Moti.

activities.title: Who Made the Promise?
activities.prompt: Who had promised to take care of the puppy?
options: Badal
Moti
His mother
His friend
activities.explanation: Good thinking! Badal had promised to take care of the puppy.

activities.title: Moti Loves Badal
activities.prompt: What did Moti do when Badal went somewhere?
options: Followed him everywhere.
Ate without him.
Played by himself.
Stayed far away.
activities.explanation: Yes! Moti loved Badal and followed him everywhere he went.

activities.title: Match the Story
activities.prompt: Match each name or group with what happened.
pairs: Grew up as the days went by
activities.explanation: Great matching! Moti grew up and became Badal's best friend.

activities.prompt: Badal and Moti became the ______ of friends.
activities.hint: Choose the word that shows their strong friendship.
activities.explanation: Excellent! Badal and Moti became the best of friends.

activities.title: Moti's Story
activities.prompt: Put these events in their story order.
items: Badal promised to take care of the puppy.
Badal and his mother named the puppy Moti.
As the days went by, Moti grew up.
activities.explanation: You followed the story correctly. Moti grew up as the days went by.

activities.prompt: As the days went by, Moti grew up. What does it show?
options: Moti became older as time passed.
Moti stayed the same as time passed.
Moti became a puppy again.
Moti stopped growing and changing.

Going back to being a puppy means time moved backward.
Staying the same means growing up means no change.
Stopping growth means the change ended.

activities.explanation: Growing up means becoming older as time passes.

activities.prompt: Moti follows Badal everywhere. What does this show about Moti?
options: Moti wants to stay close to Badal.
Moti wants Badal to leave him.
Moti is afraid to be near Badal.
Moti has no wish to follow Badal.

This mistake thinks following means wanting to leave.
This mistake thinks following comes from fear.
This mistake thinks following shows no interest.

activities.explanation: Following everywhere shows Moti wants to stay close.

activities.prompt: Badal and Moti eat and play together. What does this show?
options: They enjoy playing and eating together.
They dislike playing and eating together.
They enjoy such things only when alone.
They prefer to do such things apart.

why.They dislike playing and eating together: Disliking these activities does not match their actions.
Playing alone does not match their shared activities.
Preferring to stay apart does not match their actions.

activities.explanation: Eating and playing together show they enjoy each other.

activities.prompt: Badal promised to take care of Moti. What does he mean?
options: He will look after Moti.
He will give Moti away.
He will leave Moti alone.
He will stop caring for Moti.

Giving him away breaks the promise to care.
Leaving him alone also breaks the promise.
Stopping care is the opposite of the promise.

activities.explanation: Taking care means looking after Moti.

activities.prompt: Badal’s mother calls Badal her beta. What feeling does she show?
options: She shows love for Badal.
She shows anger toward Badal.
She shows no care for Badal.
She shows fear of Badal.

Anger does not match the loving word beta.
No care contradicts the loving word beta.
Fear is not shown by the word beta.

activities.explanation: Calling him beta shows deep love for Badal.

activities.prompt: Badal and Moti play favourite games together. What can we work out?
options: They both enjoy games they like.
They enjoy games only when alone.
They dislike choosing games together.
They want to stop playing together.

Playing alone does not match the shared games.
Disliking choices does not match their happy play.
Stopping play does not match their favourite games.

activities.explanation: Playing favourite games together shows shared enjoyment.

lessons.title: Badal Falls into the Pit

activities.prompt: How did Moti help Badal when he couldn’t get out?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Brave Rescue
activities.body: Badal walked home on a rainy day. He slipped on the muddy lane and fell into a pit. Badal tried, but could not come out. His mother worried because he did not come home. Moti waited at the gate and joined the neighbours. Moti followed Badal's scent to the pit and barked. A scent is a smell. The neighbours pulled Badal out with a rope. Badal hugged and thanked Moti.
keyPoints: Badal slipped on a muddy lane and fell into a pit.
Moti followed Badal's scent and barked at the pit.
The neighbours used a rope to pull Badal out.
activities.explanation: Badal's friends and neighbours worked together to save him.

activities.prompt: How did Moti and the neighbours get Badal out of the deep pit?
steps: Badal slipped because the rainy lane was muddy.
He stayed trapped because he tried hard but could not climb out.
Moti barked because his scent led him to Badal’s pit.
The neighbours pulled Badal out because barking showed them where he was.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Where Did Badal Fall?
activities.prompt: Where did Badal fall?
options: A muddy lane
A deep pit
The school gate
A rope
activities.explanation: Badal slipped on the muddy lane and fell into the deep pit.

activities.title: The Slippery Lane
activities.prompt: Badal slipped on the ______ lane.
activities.hint: The lane was covered with wet mud.
activities.explanation: The muddy lane made Badal slip on his way home.

activities.title: Who Did What?
activities.prompt: Match each person with what they did.
pairs: pulled Badal out with a rope
activities.explanation: Each person played a part in Badal's rescue.

activities.title: Moti Finds the Pit
activities.prompt: What did Moti follow to reach the pit?
options: The rain
The rope
The lane
Badal's scent
activities.explanation: Moti followed Badal's scent to the pit and started barking.

activities.title: The Rescue Sequence
activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: Badal slipped on the muddy lane.
Badal fell into the deep pit.
Moti followed the scent and barked.
activities.explanation: Badal fell into the pit before Moti found him and the neighbours rescued him.

activities.title: Why Did Mother Gather the Neighbours?
activities.prompt: Why did Badal's mother gather the neighbours?
options: Badal did not come home.
Moti was waiting at the gate.
Badal had hugged Moti.
The neighbours needed a rope.
activities.explanation: Badal's mother worried because he had not come home.

activities.prompt: Badal could not leave the deep pit. How did he probably feel?
options: He felt scared because he could not get out.
He felt calm because he thought he was safe.
He felt proud because he came out alone.
He felt bored because the pit was deep.

why.He felt calm because he thought he was s: He may not understand that falling into a deep pit is dangerous.
He may wrongly think escaping alone would make him proud.
He mistakes being trapped for boredom and ignores his danger.

activities.explanation: Badal is trapped in a deep pit, so fear makes sense.

activities.prompt: Moti followed Badal’s scent to the pit. Why did Moti start barking?
options: To show the neighbours where Badal was.
To ask Badal to leave the pit alone.
To frighten the neighbours far away.
To show that Moti was angry.

He may think barking asks Badal to stop trying.
He may think Moti wants to scare people away.
He may think barking only shows anger, not a rescue clue.

activities.explanation: Barking tells the neighbours where Moti found Badal.

activities.prompt: Badal did not come home. Why did his mother gather the neighbours?
options: She wanted neighbours to help search for Badal.
She wanted neighbours to clean the muddy lane.
She wanted to tell neighbours about the rain.
She wanted neighbours to wait at the gate.

why.She wanted neighbours to clean the muddy: She may think neighbours can clean mud instead of search.
why.She wanted to tell neighbours about the: She may think gathering neighbours is only for sharing news.
why.She wanted neighbours to wait at the gat: She may confuse waiting at the gate with searching for Badal.

activities.explanation: She needs many people because Badal is missing.

activities.prompt: Badal came out of the pit. How did everyone probably feel?
options: Relieved because Badal was safe again.
Angry because Moti had barked at him.
Afraid because the rescue rope had broken.
Sad because Badal had to leave Moti.

He may think barking was something to be angry about.
why.Afraid because the rescue rope had broke: He may imagine the rope broke, but Badal was rescued.
He may think leaving Moti was sad, not that everyone was relieved.

activities.explanation: Everyone feels relieved because Badal is safe again.

activities.prompt: Badal thanked Moti after leaving the pit. Why did Badal thank him?
options: Because Moti led the neighbours to him.
Because Moti pulled him from the pit.
Because Moti found and brought the rope.
Because Moti tied and held the rope.

He may think Moti pulled Badal, but neighbours used the rope.
He may think Moti brought the rope, but neighbours used it.
He may think Moti tied the rope, but the neighbours used it.

activities.explanation: Moti’s scent and barking showed where Badal was trapped.

lessons.title: Let's Think about the Story

activities.prompt: Who might help us when we feel lost or lonely?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Story of Badal and Moti
activities.body: Badal found a puppy beside the road and named him Moti. Later, Badal fell into a deep pit. Moti found Badal by following his scent. Badal hugged his puppy and thanked him. Moti grew up and loved Badal. Badal’s mother was worried when he came home late. The lesson also asks children to write T or F and share about a time they fell.
keyPoints: Badal named the puppy Moti.
Moti found Badal by following his scent.
Badal hugged and thanked Moti.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you retell the story and answer its questions.

activities.prompt: What should Badal do after Moti finds him in the deep pit?
steps: Badal fell into a deep pit, so he needed help.
Moti found Badal by following his scent, so Moti helped him.
Badal should hug his puppy because the hug shows love.
He should thank Moti because the words show gratitude.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Who found Badal in the deep pit?
options: Moti
Badal's mother
Badal's grandmother
A stranger
activities.explanation: Moti found Badal by following his scent. Good remembering!

activities.prompt: Moti found Badal by following his scent.
activities.explanation: Yes, Moti followed Badal’s scent to find him.

activities.prompt: Badal hugged his puppy and thanked ______.
activities.hint: Use the puppy's name.
activities.explanation: The puppy's name was Moti. Well done!

activities.prompt: Who did Badal live with?
options: His mother
His grandmother
A neighbour
A stranger
activities.explanation: Badal lived with his mother, not his grandmother.

activities.prompt: Match each person with the correct detail.
activities.explanation: Each detail is connected to the right person or puppy in the story.

activities.prompt: Put these story events in the correct order.
items: Badal fell into a deep pit
activities.explanation: This order shows how the important events in the story happened.

activities.prompt: Badal found a puppy beside a road. The puppy was named Moti. Badal fell into a deep pit. Moti found him by following his scent. How might Badal feel when Moti finds him?
options: He may feel relieved and grateful.
He may feel angry and disappointed.
He may feel bored by the rescue.
He may feel afraid of Moti.

This mistake thinks help would make Badal angry.
This mistake thinks Badal would dislike being found.
This mistake thinks Moti caused the danger.

activities.explanation: Badal was trapped, and Moti found him, so relief and thanks make sense.

activities.prompt: Badal came home late. His mother was worried. Why might Badal tell her that he is safe?
options: So she knows he is safe.
So she knows his name.
So she can find his photo.
So he can show he is late.

Badal's name was already known to his mother.
A photo would not tell his mother that he is safe.
Telling her he is late would not calm her worry.

activities.explanation: A worried mother needs to know that her child is safe.

activities.prompt: Moti followed Badal's smell to a deep pit. What does the word 'scent' mean here?
options: the smell of someone
the color of someone
the voice of someone
the clothes of someone

why.the color of someone: A color cannot help Moti follow Badal's smell.
why.the voice of someone: A voice is not the smell that Moti followed.
why.the clothes of someone: Clothes are not the smell that Moti followed.

activities.explanation: A scent is the smell that someone leaves behind.

activities.prompt: Badal hugged his puppy Moti and thanked him. What did Badal likely feel?
options: He felt grateful for Moti's help.
He felt angry at Moti's help.
He felt bored by Moti's help.
He felt afraid of Moti's help.

Hugging and thanking someone do not show anger.
Badal's actions show care, not boredom.
Badal's actions show gratitude, not fear.

activities.explanation: Badal's hug and thanks show that he felt grateful.

activities.prompt: Moti found Badal by following his scent. Why is saying Moti caught Badal's photo wrong?
options: Following a scent is not taking a photo.
Following a scent means taking a photo.
Finding a photo means finding a scent.
Taking a photo means finding a pit.

This mistake confuses following a smell with taking a photo.
A photo and a scent are two different things.
Taking a photo is not the way Moti found Badal.

activities.explanation: Moti used Badal's scent, not a photo, to find him.

activities.prompt: Can you discover the secret shared by the words in this story?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Words with ed
activities.body: Some words in this lesson end with ed. Words like lived, loved, played, gathered, and thanked talk about actions that have already happened. The lesson asks you to add ed to a verb. It uses lived, loved, and played for Badal and Moti. The teacher reads the story of Badal and Moti once again. Then children number the sentences to put the story in the right order.
keyPoints: The lesson words all end with ed.
These words show actions that have already happened.
Children add ed to a verb and number the story sentences.
activities.explanation: You can spot ed endings, understand their meanings, and help order the story.

activities.prompt: A child sees lived, loved, and played. The child wonders what ed shows.
steps: All three words end in ed because the chapter uses this ending.
They describe earlier actions because those actions have already happened.
Children add ed to verbs because the chapter asks them to do this.
Therefore, ed shows that an action has already happened.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Badal's Home
activities.prompt: Which word tells where Badal was living?
options: lived
loved
played
thanked
activities.explanation: Lived tells where Badal was living. You chose the matching word!

activities.title: Moti's Feelings
activities.prompt: The word loved tells where Badal was living.
activities.explanation: Loved tells how Moti felt about Badal. It does not tell where Badal lived.

activities.title: Match the Words
activities.prompt: Match each word with its meaning in the story.
pairs: what Badal and Moti did together
activities.explanation: Each word matches its meaning in the story. Well done!

activities.title: Why End with ed?
activities.prompt: Why do the lesson words end with ed?
options: They show past actions.
They show future actions.
They name feelings.
They show places.
activities.explanation: These words end with ed and show actions that have already happened. You spotted the pattern!

activities.title: Listen Again
activities.prompt: The teacher reads the story of Badal and Moti once again.
activities.explanation: Yes! The teacher reads the story of Badal and Moti once again.

activities.title: Put the Story in Order
activities.prompt: What do children number to put the story in the right order?
options: The sentences
The lesson words
The page numbers
The verbs
activities.explanation: The first sentence was already marked as number one. Children number the sentences to put the story in the right order.

activities.prompt: Moti helped Badal. Badal thanked Moti. Why did Badal thank Moti?
options: To show that he was thankful.
To show that he was angry.
To show that he was afraid.
To show that he was busy.

This mistakes the reason for thanks for a feeling.

activities.explanation: This is right because thanked shows that Badal showed thanks to Moti.

activities.prompt: The teacher reads the story again. The first sentence is marked one. The next sentence must follow it. How should the children mark the next sentence?
options: With the next number in story order.
With the same number as the first.
With no number on it.
With any number at random.

This overlooks the need to put the sentences in order.
This leaves out the numbering that the task needs.
This ignores the right order of the story.

activities.explanation: This is right because the sentences must be numbered in the right order.

activities.prompt: What do you do before, during, and after school?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Our Day and Our Stories
activities.body: Children talk in pairs about what they do every day. They discuss what happens before school, during school hours, and after going home. In the morning, they brush their teeth and get dressed for school. After breakfast, they go to school. They also learn to tell questions from statements, tell a pigeon and ant story, and begin a conversation with a greeting.
keyPoints: Talk in pairs about every day
Use question marks and full stops
Tell a pigeon and ant story
activities.explanation: This lesson brings together daily routines, punctuation and storytelling.

activities.prompt: How should the mango and shoes sentences be marked?
steps: The mango sentence tells what someone likes, so it is a statement.
A statement ends with a full stop, so the mango sentence needs one.
The shoes sentence asks whose shoes they are, so it is a question.
A question ends with a question mark, so the shoes sentence needs one.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Stories and Sentences
activities.body: Children put a question mark or a full stop in sentences. The sentence about liking mangoes is a statement. The sentence about whose shoes are these is a question. The jumbled pictures tell a story of a pigeon and an ant. The ant is in the stream and cries for help. A conversation between two children begins with a greeting.
keyPoints: Use a question mark for a question
Use a full stop for a statement
Begin a conversation with a greeting
activities.explanation: These clues help you join sentences and tell the story clearly.

activities.title: Before School
activities.prompt: After breakfast, they go to school.
activities.explanation: Yes. The lesson says that they go to school after breakfast.

activities.title: After Breakfast
activities.prompt: Which action happens after breakfast?
options: Brush their teeth
Go to school
Talk in pairs
Tell a story
activities.explanation: The lesson says that they go to school after breakfast.

activities.title: Badal's Question
activities.prompt: Badal asks his ______ a question in the story.
activities.hint: Who gives the answer about caring for the puppy?
activities.explanation: Good work. Badal asks his mother about the puppy.

activities.title: Question or Statement?
activities.prompt: Which sentence is a question?
options: I like mangoes.
Whose shoes are these?
The ant is in the stream.
Badal asks his mother.
activities.explanation: A question asks for an answer. “Whose shoes are these?” is the question.

activities.title: Match the Details
activities.prompt: Match each clue with the correct detail.
pairs: Brush their teeth and get dressed for school
A statement about caring for the puppy
activities.explanation: You matched the daily routine and the details about Badal's question.

activities.title: Ready for School
activities.prompt: Put the school-morning actions in the correct order.
activities.explanation: You placed the actions in the order given in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Badal's mother gives a statement about caring for the puppy. What mark should end her answer?
options: a full stop after it
a question mark after it
a full stop before it
a question mark before it

why.a question mark after it: This mistake thinks that any answer about a puppy asks a question.
why.a full stop before it: This mistake puts the mark before the answer instead of after it.
why.a question mark before it: This mistake puts the question mark before the answer instead of after it.

activities.explanation: This is right because the mother's answer is a statement.

activities.prompt: Badal asks his mother a question. What is his question most likely about?
options: caring for the puppy
talking about school hours
playing after going home
picking some mangoes

why.talking about school hours: This mistake uses the school-hours talk instead of the puppy answer.
why.playing after going home: This mistake uses the after-home talk instead of the puppy answer.
why.picking some mangoes: This mistake uses the mango sentence instead of the puppy answer.

activities.explanation: This is right because the mother's answer is about caring for the puppy.
