lessons.title: Thinking About Meena and the Boy

activities.prompt: What did Meena show the boy, and how did they have fun?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Learning from Meena
activities.body: The boy thought overturning boats was fun. He did not know how to fold paper boats. Meena said making boats was easy. She showed him how to fold paper and fold it again. He watched her carefully, took some paper and made a boat. Several boats were soon ready. Meena and the boy put them in the stream. They enjoyed watching the boats sail.
keyPoints: Meena showed the boy how to fold paper boats.
The boy watched carefully and made a boat.
They put the boats in the stream and watched them sail.
activities.explanation: The boy learns from Meena and then enjoys sailing boats with her.

activities.prompt: A boy cannot fold a paper boat. Meena teaches him. What should he do next?
steps: Meena showed the boy how to fold the paper again.
He watched closely so he could learn each fold.
He took some paper because he wanted to try making boats.
He could now make paper boats too.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did the boy think about overturning the boats?
options: It was hard.
It was boring.
It was fun.
It was scary.
activities.explanation: The boy thought that overturning the boats was fun.

activities.prompt: Meena had coloured paper in different ______.
activities.hint: Choose the word that tells how big or small the papers were.
activities.explanation: Meena had coloured paper in different sizes.

activities.prompt: Match each action with the right person.
pairs: Showed how to fold the paper
activities.explanation: Meena taught the boy, and they both enjoyed watching the boats.

activities.prompt: Put the boat-making events in the correct order.
items: The boy began making a boat.
All the boats sailed down the stream.
activities.explanation: The boy made a boat, more boats became ready, and then they sailed away.

activities.prompt: Which action shows that the boy was learning from Meena?
options: Watched Meena fold the paper.
Overturned the paper boats.
Put his boats in the stream.
Enjoyed watching the boats sail.
activities.explanation: He learned by watching Meena's careful folding demonstration.

activities.prompt: What happened after Meena and the boy put their boats in the stream?
options: Only Meena's boats sailed down the stream.
The boy's boats sailed up the stream.
Meena's boats stayed beside the stream.
All the boats sailed down the stream.
activities.explanation: Both children put boats in the stream, and all the boats sailed down it.

activities.prompt: Meena gently puts her boats into the stream. What does her gentle action show?
options: She cares about her boats and handles them softly.
She is angry with the boats and pushes them hard.
She is afraid of the water and wants to run.
She is bored and wants the boats to stop.

why.She is angry with the boats and pushes t: This wrongly treats gentle handling as anger.
why.She is afraid of the water and wants to: This wrongly treats putting boats in water as fear.
why.She is bored and wants the boats to stop: This wrongly treats a gentle action as boredom.

activities.explanation: Gently shows that she handles her boats with care.

activities.prompt: Meena shows the boy how to fold the paper. Why does he watch her carefully?
options: He wants to learn how to make a boat.
He wants Meena to make every boat.
He thinks he already knows every fold.
He is waiting for Meena to stop showing him.

This mistakes interest in boats for wanting Meena to do them.
This mistakes watching for thinking he already knows.
why.He is waiting for Meena to stop showing: This mistakes careful attention for waiting.

activities.explanation: He watches carefully so he can learn the folding steps.

activities.prompt: Meena says, "Making boats was easy." How should we understand "easy" here?
options: She showed the boy how to fold the boats.
The boats made themselves without any help.
The boy needed no help from Meena.
No paper was needed to make boats.

why.The boats made themselves without any he: This wrongly thinks no one needs to fold the paper.
This wrongly thinks Meena did not help the boy.
This wrongly thinks boats can be made without paper.

activities.explanation: Meena shows him how to fold and fold again.

activities.prompt: After Meena teaches him, the boy takes paper and makes boats. How might he feel?
options: He feels proud because he made boats too.
He feels afraid because his boats might sink.
He feels sorry because Meena made more boats.
He feels bored because his work is finished.

why.He feels afraid because his boats might: Nothing in the story says that he fears his boats.
why.He feels sorry because Meena made more b: Nothing shows that he feels sorry about Meena's boats.
why.He feels bored because his work is finis: Making several boats does not mean he feels bored.

activities.explanation: Making boats himself can make him feel proud.

activities.prompt: Meena has coloured paper in different sizes. What can we work out?
options: She had choices of paper for making boats.
She had one size of paper for making boats.
She had folded all her paper into boats.
She had coloured paper for hiding boats.

why.She had one size of paper for making boa: This wrongly assumes all her paper was one size.
This wrongly assumes every paper was already folded.
This wrongly assumes the coloured paper had another use.

activities.explanation: Different sizes give her choices when making paper boats.

activities.prompt: Meena puts her boats into the stream. The boy does the same. All sail down together. What can we work out?
options: They made boats that can sail together.
They made boats that can stay still.
They made boats that can only overturn.
They made no boats for the stream.

This wrongly assumes their boats cannot move in the stream.
This wrongly assumes sailing in the stream means only overturning.
This wrongly assumes neither child made boats for the stream.

activities.explanation: All the boats sailing together shows they can move together.

lessons.title: Using He and She

activities.prompt: Have you ever wondered which word to use for a boy or a girl?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Words for People
activities.body: She and he are useful when you talk about people. Use “she” instead of “Meena”. Use “he” instead of “boy”. Rani likes playing outside, while Sahil has a top. Durga is five years old. Ranjit goes to school regularly. You can also use prepositions with objects: in, on, and under.
keyPoints: Use she instead of Meena
Use he instead of boy
Use in, on, and under for places
activities.explanation: These examples show how to describe people and objects.

activities.prompt: A story calls Sahil “he.” What does that word mean?
steps: Sahil is the child with the top.
The rule says “he” can be used instead of “boy.”
So “he” points to Sahil because the story talks about that child.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Choose She
activities.prompt: Which word can be used instead of Meena?

lessons.title: Drawing and Writing

activities.prompt: How can a picture help us write a story about fun?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Draw, then Write
activities.body: A rangoli is a drawing you make by following steps. The rangoli activity has six steps. Next, you look at a picture and write a few lines about it. The picture gives you clues. Clues are hints for your writing. They include Park, Children, Playing, See-saw, Swings, Slide, Enjoying and Happy. These clues help you choose what to write.
keyPoints: The rangoli activity has six steps.
The writing task asks for a few lines about a picture.
Writing clues help you choose what to write.
activities.explanation: These ideas will guide both your drawing and your writing.

activities.prompt: A child wants to write about a park picture but feels stuck.
steps: The child looks for clues because the picture gives ideas for writing.
The child notices park, children, playing, and the see-saw, swings, and slide.
The child chooses clues because the task asks for a few lines.
The child writes about fun because clues include enjoying and happy.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does the writing task ask you to do?
options: Write a few lines about a picture
Draw six picture steps
Match words to a playground
Copy all the clues twice
activities.explanation: You look at a picture and write a few lines about it.

activities.prompt: Park is one of the ______ for the picture writing task.
activities.hint: Find the word after “writing” in your book.
activities.explanation: Park can help you write a few lines about the picture.

activities.prompt: Which word is one of the writing clues?
options: Table
Swings
Garden
Pencil
activities.explanation: Swings is a writing clue, so it can help your lines.

activities.prompt: Match each writing clue to its short label.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows one of the writing clues from your book.

activities.prompt: Which word is not a writing clue?
options: Playing
Garden
See-saw
Happy
activities.explanation: Playing, See-saw and Happy are all writing clues.

activities.prompt: Which set contains only writing clues?
options: Park, Garden, Children
Garden, Playing, Happy
Children, Playing, Slide
Pencil, Swings, Enjoying
activities.explanation: Children, Playing and Slide are all listed as writing clues.

activities.prompt: A child smiles in a park. How does the child feel?
options: She feels happy and is enjoying the park.
She feels tired and wants to go home.
She feels bored and wants to leave.
She feels lonely and needs a friend.

This assumes the child has no company.

activities.explanation: This is right because the happy and enjoying clues show fun.

activities.prompt: Children are near the see-saw at the park. Which word fits?
options: playing
play
plays
played

why.play: This uses the base verb where the line needs -ing.
why.plays: This treats children as one child.
why.played: This changes the action to a past action.

activities.explanation: This is right because playing fits children and the line.

activities.prompt: The writing task shows a picture. What should the child do next?
options: Choose a few clues and write some lines.
Copy all the clues again and again today.
Draw more pictures without writing any lines.
Leave the picture and write no lines.

why.Copy all the clues again and again today: This mistakes copying clues for writing about them.
why.Draw more pictures without writing any l: This chooses more drawing instead of doing the writing task.
This avoids the writing task instead of doing it.

activities.explanation: This is right because the task asks for a few lines about a picture.

activities.prompt: A child begins a rangoli. Why follow all six steps?
options: They finish the rangoli in the right order.
They can skip any step they dislike.
They only need to draw one part.
They should copy the steps again later.

This mistakes the steps as optional instead of required.
This mistakes six steps for only one step.
This mistakes repeating steps for following them in order.

activities.explanation: This is right because a rangoli is drawn by following six steps.

activities.prompt: Children enjoy the slide and swings at the park. What does this imply?
options: They enjoy a happy time at the park.
They wait for the park to open.
They leave as the park closes.
They dislike the slide and swings.

This mistakes enjoying play for waiting.
This mistakes enjoying play for leaving.

activities.explanation: This is right because the enjoying and happy clues show a happy time.

lessons.title: Toys, Games and Self-Assessment

activities.prompt: Can you solve the toy and game clues and discover what you can do?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Games and Your Learning
activities.body: The crossword answers are all about toys and games. The clues describe objects that spin, move, or help children play. One clue describes a game played with a ball and a foot. Another describes a seat tied with ropes. You can also talk to your elders about the games they played. Finally, you can check if you can read stories alone and tell stories with your teacher’s help.
keyPoints: The crossword answers are about toys and games.
Your elders can tell you about games they played.
You can assess reading and telling stories.
activities.explanation: This lesson helps you solve the crossword and check your learning.

activities.prompt: A child finds a crossword clue about a round object that spins on a needle. How can the child know it belongs with toys and games?
steps: The clue names a round object that spins on a needle.
This points to a toy because all crossword answers concern toys and games.
It is an object clue, not a story-reading self-check.
Therefore, the child should solve it as a toy-and-game answer.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Read the Clues Carefully
activities.body: Each crossword clue points to something connected with toys and games. One clue describes an object used to hit a ball. Another describes a round object used to play. A further clue describes a round glass ball for playing. One more clue describes a seat tied with ropes that moves back and forth. Keep these clear descriptions in mind as you solve the crossword.
keyPoints: Some clues describe objects used for playing.
A round glass ball is used for playing.
The seat moves back and forth.
activities.explanation: Careful reading will help you match each clue to its answer.

activities.prompt: Which crossword clue describes a round object that spins on a needle?
options: A game played with a ball and a foot
An object used to hit a ball
A round object that spins on a needle
A seat tied with ropes
activities.explanation: This clue clearly says that the round object spins on a needle.

activities.prompt: One crossword clue describes a game played with a ______ and a foot.
activities.hint: Think of the object used in the game.
activities.explanation: The clue says that the game is played with a ball and a foot.

activities.prompt: All the crossword answers are about toys and games.
activities.explanation: Yes, every crossword answer in this lesson is about toys and games.

activities.prompt: Match each crossword clue to its matching detail.
pairs: A round object that spins on a needle
A game played with a ball and a foot
It uses a ball and a foot
An object used to hit a ball
activities.explanation: Each detail tells you what the crossword clue describes.

activities.prompt: Which pair shows two things children can assess?
options: reading stories alone; telling with a teacher’s help
spinning on a needle; moving with ropes
hitting a ball; playing with a glass ball
playing with a foot; sitting on a seat
activities.explanation: Children can assess reading stories by themselves and telling stories with their teacher’s help.

activities.prompt: Put these lesson pages in order from the first page to the last page.
activities.explanation: Page 65 has the crossword, page 66 has the elder discussion, and page 67 has self-assessment.

activities.prompt: A child reads, “A round object spins on a needle.” The child checks the lesson. What kind of answer is this clue?
options: A toy-and-game answer about a spinning object.
A reading check about doing a task alone.
A self-check about telling stories with help.
A talk about games played by elders.

why.A reading check about doing a task alone: This mistake mixes toys with reading-story self-assessment.
why.A self-check about telling stories with: This mistake mixes toys with telling stories with help.
This mistake mixes toys with talking with elders.

activities.explanation: This is right because all crossword answers are about toys and games.

activities.prompt: One clue describes a game played with a ball and a foot. Another describes an object used to hit a ball. What should the child notice?
options: The first clue names a game, while the second names an object.
Both clues name games, so neither names an object.
Both clues describe the same round object used for play.
Neither clue can fit a toys-and-games crossword.

why.Both clues name games, so neither names: This mistake treats the hitting object as another game.
why.Both clues describe the same round objec: This mistake treats different clues as the same round object.
why.Neither clue can fit a toys-and-games cr: This mistake ignores that every answer is about toys and games.

activities.explanation: This is right because one clue describes a game and the other an object.

activities.prompt: A child asks an elder about games the elder played. What is the child learning?
options: The elder’s memories of games from the past.
Whether the elder can read stories alone.
Whether the elder can tell stories with help.
Whether the elder can spin a round toy.

why.Whether the elder can read stories alone: This mistake confuses learning about games with reading self-assessment.
why.Whether the elder can tell stories with: This mistake confuses learning about games with telling stories with help.
This mistake confuses learning about games with testing a spinning toy.

activities.explanation: This is right because children should talk to elders about games they played.

lessons.sceneAlt: An oil painting called “Paper Boats Forever” evokes folded paper boats sailing through childhood memories and imagined seas.
lessons.sceneCaption: An oil painting evokes childhood memories of folded paper boats sailing through puddles, gutters, and imagined seas.

sceneCredit.text: A paper boat made my dream by Erik Pevernagie, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Erik Pevernagie

activities.context: At the stream beside a bamboo bridge, Meena walked towards the water and launched a paper boat. It moved down the stream swiftly, and she felt very happy. She soon placed several paper boats in the stream. A naughty boy kept pushing the boats into the water. Meena gave him an angry look, but he paid no attention. She asked him to stop, yet he carried on. When she questioned him, he explained that overturning the boats was fun.
activities.prompt: If the boy enjoys overturning boats, what should Meena expect after she asks him to stop again?
options: He may keep overturning them because that activity is what he says he enjoys.
He will immediately make his own boats from Meena’s paper.
He will ask Meena to help him overturn every boat.
He will leave the boats alone as soon as she looks angry.

why.He will immediately make his own boats f: Nothing shows that he will change his activity when paper is available.
why.He will ask Meena to help him overturn e: Nothing shows that he wants Meena to join him.
why.He will leave the boats alone as soon as: Her angry look already did not change him.

activities.explanation: He ignored her request and said the activity was fun.

activities.prompt: How should Meena handle the boy without giving up her own paper boats?
activities.answer: Meena should tell the boy clearly that she wants him to stop overturning her boats. If he continues, she can question his reason and offer him enough paper to make his own boats. This gives him another activity while keeping Meena’s request clear and fair.
points: Tell the boy to stop overturning her boats.
Ask him why he is doing it.
Offer him enough paper to make his own boats.
Keep her request to stop clear.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A boy thought overturning boats was fun, but did not know how to fold paper boats. Meena told him making boats was easy. Her coloured paper came in different sizes. She showed him how to fold and fold again. He watched carefully, took some paper, and began making a boat. Soon, several boats were ready. Meena gently put her boats into the stream, and the boy put his boats in too. All boats sailed downstream, and both enjoyed watching them.
activities.prompt: If the boy had not watched Meena carefully, what would probably have happened?
options: He would probably fold the paper incorrectly.
He would probably make boats more quickly than Meena.
He would probably put a folded boat into the stream.
He would probably enjoy watching the boats more.

why.He would probably make boats more quickl: Not watching would not teach him a quicker method.
why.He would probably put a folded boat into: He would need to learn how to fold before making a boat for the stream.
why.He would probably enjoy watching the boa: Not watching would not increase his enjoyment of the boats.

activities.explanation: Without watching the demonstration, he would miss how the paper should be folded.

activities.context: A boy thought overturning boats was fun, but did not know how to fold paper boats. Meena told him making boats was easy. Her coloured paper came in different sizes. She showed him how to fold and fold again. He watched carefully, took some paper, and began making a boat. Soon, several boats were ready. Meena gently put her boats into the stream, and the boy put his boats in too. All boats sailed downstream, and both enjoyed watching them.
activities.prompt: After watching Meena's demonstration, what should the boy do next to make his own boat?
options: He should take some paper and fold it, then fold it again.
He should wait for Meena to make all his boats.
He should put unfolded paper into the stream.
He should ask Meena to overturn the boats for him.

why.He should wait for Meena to make all his: Meena showed him how, so he could make his own boats.
why.He should put unfolded paper into the st: Paper had to be folded before it became a boat for the stream.
why.He should ask Meena to overturn the boat: His task was to make boats, not overturn them.

activities.explanation: Meena showed him how to fold the paper and fold it again.

activities.prompt: Explain how Meena helped the boy learn to make paper boats.
activities.answer: Meena said that making boats was easy. She showed the boy how to fold the paper and fold it again. The boy watched her carefully, then took some paper and began making his own boat. Soon, several boats were ready.
points: Meena said making boats was easy.
She showed the boy how to fold the paper.
The boy watched her carefully.
He took some paper and made boats.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Rani likes playing outside, and Sahil has a top. Meena and a boy are there. Durga is five years old, while Ranjit goes to school regularly. The bat, bag, ball, car, and books each have two possible places. The group must choose the correct word for where each object goes.
activities.prompt: The speaker wants to change the way Meena is mentioned so that her name is not repeated. Which word should replace her name?
options: she
he
it
they

why.he: “He” is the word for the boy, not for Meena.
why.it: “It” is not the stated replacement for Meena.
why.they: “They” would refer to more than one person, but the question is about Meena alone.

activities.explanation: “She” can be used instead of Meena.

activities.context: Rani likes playing outside, and Sahil has a top. Meena and a boy are there. Durga is five years old, while Ranjit goes to school regularly. The bat, bag, ball, car, and books each have two possible places. The group must choose the correct word for where each object goes.
activities.prompt: If the bag is changed from being in the chair, where can it be?
options: on the chair
under the bed
in the box
on the shelves

why.under the bed: Under the bed is one of the bat’s possible places.
why.in the box: In the box is one of the ball’s possible places.
why.on the shelves: On the shelves is one of the books’ possible places.

activities.explanation: The bag can be in or on the chair.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between “he” and “she” in this case?
activities.answer: “She” can be used instead of Meena. “He” can be used instead of boy. The choice depends on whom the speaker is talking about. In the case, Meena is connected with “she,” while the boy is connected with “he.”
points: Uses “she” for Meena.
Uses “he” for boy.
Explains that each word matches a different person.
Shows the two words being used in different situations.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In the Drawing and Writing lesson, a child follows six steps to draw a rangoli. The writing task asks for a few lines about a picture. The picture shows children in a park, playing on a see-saw and swings, and enjoying a slide. The writing clues are park, children, playing, see-saw, swings, slide, enjoying, and happy.
activities.prompt: What should the child do after drawing the rangoli?
options: Use the picture clues to begin the writing task.
Use the rangoli steps to begin the writing task.
Wait until a new picture is provided.
Begin another rangoli instead of writing.

why.Use the rangoli steps to begin the writi: The rangoli steps are for drawing, not writing.
The child can use the given picture.
why.Begin another rangoli instead of writing: The child has already followed the rangoli steps.

activities.explanation: This follows the writing task and uses its clues.

activities.context: In the Drawing and Writing lesson, a child follows six steps to draw a rangoli. The writing task asks for a few lines about a picture. The picture shows children in a park, playing on a see-saw and swings, and enjoying a slide. The writing clues are park, children, playing, see-saw, swings, slide, enjoying, and happy.
activities.prompt: If one activity clue were removed from the list, what should the child do?
options: Choose another clue that the picture still shows.
Add the removed clue to the rangoli steps.
Use the removed clue even if the picture does not show it.
Leave the writing task blank.

why.Add the removed clue to the rangoli step: The rangoli steps guide drawing, not the clue list.
why.Use the removed clue even if the picture: A removed clue should not be used if it is not shown.
Several suitable clues remain for the writing.

activities.explanation: The child can still use the other picture clues.

activities.prompt: How do the writing clues help the child complete the writing task?
activities.answer: The writing task asks for a few lines about a picture. Clues such as park, children, playing, see-saw, swings, slide, enjoying, and happy help the child decide what the lines can describe. The child should use them to write about what the picture shows, not to follow the rangoli steps.
points: The task asks for a few lines.
The clues describe what the picture shows.
The child should use the clues.
The rangoli steps guide drawing.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After finishing a toys-and-games crossword, a learner checked the clues about the spinning object, the ball game, the hitting object, and the round playthings. The learner also thought about reading a story alone and telling one with the teacher’s help. The learner planned to speak with an elder about the games they had played and to assess what they could read and tell.
activities.prompt: The learner finds a clue about a round object that spins on a needle. What kind of entry should they expect in the toys-and-games crossword?
options: A spinning game
A round toy
A game for an elder
A story about a game

why.A spinning game: The clue describes an object, not a game.
why.A game for an elder: An elder is someone to talk to, not the object described.
why.A story about a game: A story is something to read or tell, not the object in the clue.

activities.explanation: The spinning object is a toy, and all the crossword answers are about toys and games.

activities.context: After finishing a toys-and-games crossword, a learner checked the clues about the spinning object, the ball game, the hitting object, and the round playthings. The learner also thought about reading a story alone and telling one with the teacher’s help. The learner planned to speak with an elder about the games they had played and to assess what they could read and tell.
activities.prompt: The learner wants to learn about games that an elder played. What should the learner do next?
options: Ask an elder to describe the games they played.
Use the teacher’s help to tell a story.
Read a story without help.
Use the object for hitting a ball in a game.

This action focuses on storytelling rather than learning about an elder’s games.
This action focuses on independent reading rather than learning about an elder’s games.
why.Use the object for hitting a ball in a g: This action focuses on a game object rather than talking with an elder.

activities.explanation: Children should talk with elders about the games they played.

activities.prompt: Why should the learner expect a toy for the clue about a round object that spins on a needle?
activities.answer: The clue describes an object, and every answer in the crossword is about toys or games. A spinning round object fits the toy group. A person, an elder, or a story would not describe the object in the clue, so the crossword entry should be a round toy.
points: The clue describes an object.
The object spins on a needle.
All crossword answers concern toys and games.
The suitable entry is a round toy.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

he

they

activities.title: Crossword Clue
activities.prompt: Which clue describes a round glass ball used for playing?
options: A round object that spins on a needle.
A game played with a ball and a foot.
An object used to hit a ball.
A round glass ball used for playing.
activities.explanation: All the crossword answers are about toys and games. Children should talk to their elders about games.

chapters.title: Good Food
chapters.summary: In this chapter: let us recite and think.; let us speak and learn about laddoos; let us write and explore; let us learn about khichdi and festivals.

lessons.title: Let us recite and think.

activities.prompt: What might happen if all the laddoos and children became one?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: One Big Poem
activities.body: Imagine that every laddoo in the poem becomes one huge laddoo. Imagine that all the children become one big child, too. The seas also join to make one big sea. The big child picks up the huge laddoo and throws it into the sea. Then the laddoo makes a big splish-splash. The lesson also asks about round things and what happened in the sea.
keyPoints: All the laddoos become one huge laddoo.
All the children become one big child.
The laddoo makes a big splish-splash in the sea.
activities.explanation: These ideas show how the poem turns many things into one.

activities.prompt: The big child throws a huge laddoo into one big sea. Why does it splash?
steps: The laddoo is huge, so the big child picks it up.
Next, the child throws it, because the poem imagines one sea.
The throw causes the splash, so the laddoo makes a big splish-splash.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: One Huge Laddoo
activities.prompt: What do all the laddoos become in the poem?
options: one big sea
one huge laddoo
one big child
one small laddoo
activities.explanation: The poem imagines all the laddoos joining into one huge laddoo.

activities.prompt: All the children become one child in the poem.
activities.explanation: The poem says that all the children become one child.

activities.title: The Big Child
activities.prompt: The big child ______ up the big laddoo.
activities.hint: What does the big child do with the laddoo?
activities.explanation: The poem says that the big child picks up the big laddoo.

activities.title: What They Become
activities.prompt: Match each group with what it becomes in the poem.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows many things becoming one in the poem.

activities.title: Into the Big Sea
activities.prompt: What does the big child do after picking up the laddoo?
options: The big child throws it into the big sea.
The big child throws the sea into the laddoo.
The big laddoo throws the child into the sea.
The big child throws it onto the big laddoo.
activities.explanation: The big child throws the laddoo into the big sea.

activities.title: The Laddoo's Journey
activities.prompt: Put these events in the correct order.
items: The big child picks up the big laddoo.
The big child throws the laddoo into the big sea.
The laddoo makes a big splish-splash.
activities.explanation: The laddoo is picked up, thrown, and then makes a splish-splash.

activities.prompt: The laddoo enters the big sea after the big child's throw. What sound should the child expect?
options: A big splish-splash, because the laddoo hits the sea.
A tiny hush-hush, because the laddoo stays dry.
A dry rustle, because the laddoo never enters water.
A quiet tap, because the big sea is very small.

why.A tiny hush-hush, because the laddoo sta: This mistake thinks a laddoo in water makes a tiny, soft sound.
why.A dry rustle, because the laddoo never e: This mistake thinks the laddoo stays dry after entering the sea.
why.A quiet tap, because the big sea is very: This mistake confuses a big sea with a very small one.

activities.explanation: Right: the laddoo makes a big splish-splash when it hits the sea.

activities.prompt: Many laddoos become one huge laddoo. What happens to the children?
options: They become one child in the same way.
They become one sea in the same way.
They become many children in the same way.
They become round laddoos in the same way.

This mistake swaps the one child for the one sea.
why.They become many children in the same wa: This mistake ignores the poem's joining of all the children.
why.They become round laddoos in the same wa: This mistake mixes the children with the huge laddoo.

activities.explanation: Right: the poem imagines all the children becoming one child.

lessons.title: Let us speak and learn about laddoos

activities.prompt: How can you know a laddoo without seeing it?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meena’s birthday sweets
activities.body: Jithu and Meena are friends. It was Meena’s birthday. Jithu gave her a box of mixed sweets. Meena cannot see properly, so she feels the sweets and picks up the big laddoo. She says she loves laddoos. Jithu is surprised and asks how she knew. A laddoo is a sweet commonly eaten in every house. Children then write words that describe the laddoo.
keyPoints: Meena chose the big laddoo by feeling the sweets.
Meena said that she loved laddoos.
Children write words that describe the laddoo.
activities.explanation: Wonderful listening! You have learnt Meena’s birthday story.

activities.prompt: How can Meena know a laddoo when she cannot see properly?
steps: Meena cannot see properly, so she needs help from another sense.
She felt the mixed sweets and picked the big laddoo.
She could recognise it because she loves laddoos and used touch.
Therefore, Meena knew the sweet by touch, which surprised Jithu.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How Meena knew
activities.body: It was Meena’s birthday. Jithu gave her mixed sweets. Meena could not see properly. She felt the sweets and chose the big laddoo. Then she said she loved laddoos. Jithu was surprised and asked how she knew. Laddoos are sweets commonly eaten in every house. Children write words that describe the laddoo.
keyPoints: Meena used touch to choose the laddoo.
Jithu wanted to know how Meena knew.
Laddoos are commonly eaten in every house.
activities.explanation: Excellent! You can now explain how Meena knew.

activities.prompt: Who gave Meena the box of mixed sweets?
options: Jithu
Meena
Jithu and Meena
activities.explanation: Well done! Jithu gave Meena the box of mixed sweets.

activities.prompt: Meena could not see the sweets properly.
activities.explanation: Good spotting! Meena felt the sweets to choose one.

activities.prompt: Jithu gave Meena a box of ______ sweets.
activities.hint: The box did not contain only one kind of sweet.
activities.explanation: Great work! The box held mixed sweets.

activities.prompt: Match each question with the correct detail.
pairs: Jithu gave a box of mixed sweets.
What did Meena do with the sweets?
Meena felt them and picked up the big laddoo.
She said that she loved laddoos.
How did she know it was a laddoo?
activities.explanation: Perfect matching! You followed the story carefully.

activities.prompt: How did Meena know that the sweet was a laddoo?
options: Meena knew it by touching the sweets.
Meena knew it by looking at the box.
Meena knew it by smelling the sweets.
Meena knew it by tasting every sweet.
activities.explanation: Brilliant thinking! Meena felt the sweets and picked up the big laddoo.

activities.prompt: Put the events in the order they happened.
items: Meena picked up the big laddoo.
activities.explanation: Excellent ordering! You told the story from start to finish.

activities.prompt: Jithu gave Meena mixed sweets. Meena felt them and picked the big laddoo. What does this show?
options: She likes laddoos and can tell one by touch.
She likes every sweet more than a laddoo.
She needs clear sight to choose a sweet.
She remembers the order of sweets in the box.

why.She likes every sweet more than a laddoo: This mistakes liking laddoos for disliking other sweets.
This confuses seeing properly with using touch.
why.She remembers the order of sweets in the: This mistakes feeling a sweet for remembering its place.

activities.explanation: Her choice and words show that she likes laddoos.

activities.prompt: Meena could not see the sweets properly. Jithu gave her mixed sweets. Why was the big laddoo useful to her?
options: She could feel it and choose the sweet she loved.
She could look at it and learn each sweet’s name.
She could use it to show Jithu her best sight.
She could use it to check how well she could see.

why.She could look at it and learn each swee: This depends on clear sight instead of her sense of touch.
why.She could use it to show Jithu her best: This gives the laddoo a job that the facts do not show.
why.She could use it to check how well she c: This turns the laddoo into a test of eyesight.

activities.explanation: She felt the laddoo and knew it was the sweet she loved.

activities.prompt: Laddoos are sweets that are commonly eaten in every house. What does the word “commonly” show?
options: People eat them in many different houses.
People eat them in only one special house.
People eat them only after a birthday.
People eat them less often than other sweets.

why.People eat them in only one special hous: This mistakes many houses for one special house.
This adds a birthday rule that the sentence does not give.
why.People eat them less often than other sw: This compares laddoos with other sweets without support.

activities.explanation: The words “in every house” show that many people eat laddoos.

activities.prompt: Jithu gave Meena mixed sweets for her birthday. What can we best say about his choice?
options: The box included a sweet she loved and could feel.
The box included sweets that she could only enjoy seeing.
The box included only sweets that Jithu did not like.
The box included sweets that Meena had never eaten.

why.The box included sweets that she could o: This depends on clear sight instead of Meena’s sense of touch.
why.The box included only sweets that Jithu: This adds Jithu’s likes, but the facts do not give them.
why.The box included sweets that Meena had n: This adds Meena’s past eating habits, which are not given.

activities.explanation: Meena could feel the sweets and pick the laddoo she loved.

lessons.title: Let us write and explore

activities.prompt: What can we discover when we play with words and objects?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Words to explore
activities.body: Sentence words can be playful. The first word for making sentences is play. Other words include plum, cloud, clock and blue, while blanket is the last word. Notice the blends cl, pl and bl. The matching activity includes a cock and a lioness. Then explore paper, a stone, a green leaf, a pencil, an eraser, a feather and a spoon. Check which objects float and which sink. Think about light and heavy too.
keyPoints: Play is the first sentence word.
Blanket is the last sentence word.
Water objects can float or sink.
activities.explanation: You will play with words and explore objects.

activities.prompt: Why do the teacher and children use words and objects together?
steps: Word choices like play and plum help children make sentences.
The teacher asks children to notice cl, pl, and bl in the words.
Water objects let children check what floats and what sinks.
That check connects with light and heavy ideas, joining words and objects.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: The first word for making sentences is play.
activities.explanation: Play is the first word for making sentences. This helps you remember the beginning.

activities.prompt: Which word is used for making sentences?
options: Stone
Plum
Feather
Green leaf
activities.explanation: Plum is one word used for making sentences. Great choice!

activities.prompt: The last word for making sentences is ______.
activities.hint: It comes after the other sentence words.
activities.explanation: Blanket is the last word for making sentences. You remembered the ending!

activities.prompt: Match each word with its starting blend.
activities.explanation: Plum, cloud and blue begin with the blends pl, cl and bl.

activities.prompt: A child watches a feather in water and waits. What is the child checking?
options: Whether the feather floats or sinks.
Whether the feather starts with pl.
Whether the feather matches a lioness.
Whether the feather is the first word.

This child mixes up word sounds with things in water.
This child thinks the feather belongs in the matching activity.
This child thinks the feather is one of the sentence words.

activities.explanation: The activity checks whether each object floats or sinks.

activities.prompt: The teacher points to cloud and clock. What blend do children notice?
options: The blend cl at the start.
The blend pl at the start.
The blend bl at the start.
The blend cl at the end.

This child hears the taught blend pl instead of cl.
This child hears the taught blend bl instead of cl.
This child knows cl but looks for it at the end.

activities.explanation: Cloud and clock both begin with the blend cl.

activities.prompt: The teacher circles plum and play. Which shared blend should children notice?
options: The shared blend pl.
The shared blend cl.
The shared blend bl.
The words share no blend.

This child chooses the blend cl from another word pair.
This child chooses the blend bl from another word pair.
This child thinks plum and play begin with different sounds.

activities.explanation: Plum and play both begin with the blend pl.

activities.prompt: A child sees blue and blanket together. Which blend can they notice?
options: The shared blend bl.
The shared blend cl.
The shared blend pl.
The words share no blend.

This child chooses cl from cloud and clock.
This child chooses pl from plum and play.
This child thinks blue and blanket begin with different sounds.

activities.explanation: Blue and blanket both begin with the blend bl.

lessons.title: Let us learn about khichdi and festivals

activities.prompt: What makes khichdi a special part of festival celebrations?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Khichdi and festival days
activities.body: Khichdi is a popular, traditional dish. It is usually cooked with rice and lentils together. People prepare it during festivals, especially Sankranti, and eat it as a meal. Different parts of India make khichdi in different ways. Some people add vegetables or use different lentils. Sankranti is celebrated to thank the Sun God for a good harvest. Sankranti is also called the Harvest Festival. Festivals help us stay together.
keyPoints: Khichdi is cooked with rice and lentils together.
Khichdi is eaten as a meal during festivals.
Sankranti is the Harvest Festival.
activities.explanation: This card tells you about khichdi, Sankranti and the joy of festivals.

activities.prompt: A child wonders why khichdi is served during Sankranti.
steps: Khichdi is traditional because it is prepared especially during Sankranti.
Sankranti is the Harvest Festival because it thanks the Sun God.
Khichdi is eaten as a meal because festivals prepare it.
So, khichdi is part of Sankranti's special harvest festival meal.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is khichdi?
options: A harvest festival
A popular dish
A traditional lentil
A festival season
activities.explanation: Khichdi is a popular and traditional dish. It is often prepared during festivals.

activities.prompt: Khichdi is usually cooked with rice and lentils together.
activities.explanation: Yes! Rice and lentils are usually cooked together to make khichdi.

activities.title: Match the festival clues
activities.prompt: Match each festival clue with its matching answer.
activities.explanation: You matched each clue with its correct festival fact. Great work!

activities.prompt: Sankranti is also called the ______ Festival.
activities.hint: This festival thanks the Sun God for a good harvest.
activities.explanation: Sankranti is also called the Harvest Festival.

activities.prompt: Which name is used for Sankranti?
options: Nature Festival
Culture Festival
Food Festival
Harvest Festival
activities.explanation: Sankranti has another name: the Harvest Festival.

activities.prompt: Different parts of India make khichdi in exactly the same way.
activities.explanation: Different parts of India make khichdi in different ways. Some also add vegetables.

activities.prompt: Why do festivals help us?
options: They connect us with nature and culture.
They change every khichdi recipe.
They turn all dishes into sweets.
They stop us staying together.
activities.explanation: Festivals keep us connected with nature and culture. They also help us stay together.

activities.title: Match the clues
activities.prompt: Match each clue with the matching festival fact.
activities.explanation: You matched all the clues with their correct facts. Brilliant!

activities.prompt: Khichdi is served during Sankranti. Everyone smiles. How does the child most likely feel?
options: The child feels happy and excited.
The child feels worried about the food.
The child feels lonely beside everyone.
The child feels bored by the festival.

The child may confuse a special meal with worry.
The child may miss how festivals bring people together.
The child may think smiles mean the festival is boring.

activities.explanation: This matches the joy and smiles that festivals bring.

activities.prompt: Neighbors share a festival meal. They sit together. What does this scene show?
options: Festivals can help people stay together.
Festivals make people lose interest in neighbors.
Festivals can make people eat alone.
Festivals stop people from sharing food.

why.Festivals make people lose interest in n: This mistakes staying together for losing interest in others.
This mistakes sharing a festival meal for eating alone.
This mistakes a shared festival meal for stopping sharing.

activities.explanation: Sharing a meal and sitting together shows festivals bring people together.

lessons.title: Festival names and regional khichdi

activities.prompt: What makes one festival taste so special in different parts of our country?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: One dish, many names
activities.body: Khichdi is known by different names across India. Gujarat calls it Gujarati khichdi, Tamil Nadu calls it Pongal, and Bihar calls it Bihari khichdi. Rajasthan calls it Bajra khichdi. West Bengal calls it Kichuri, Karnataka calls it bisi bele bhat, and Kashmir calls it Moong khetchir. The festival is also called Sankranti, Pongal, Lohri and Bihu. Flying kites during the festival is very popular.
keyPoints: Khichdi has different names in different regions.
The festival is also called Sankranti, Pongal, Lohri and Bihu.
Flying kites during the festival is very popular.
activities.explanation: These names help you recognise the festival and regional khichdi.

activities.prompt: A child hears 'Bajra khichdi' and 'Bisi bele bhat.' Why are these names different?
steps: Khichdi is known by different names across the country, so names vary.
Bajra khichdi is the name used in Rajasthan.
Bisi bele bhat is the name used in Karnataka.
Thus, these are two regional names for the same food.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Find the name
activities.prompt: Which name is used in West Bengal?
options: Pongal
Bajra khichdi
Kichuri
Moong khetchir
activities.explanation: Kichuri is the name used in West Bengal.

activities.title: Match the place and name
activities.prompt: Match each place with the khichdi name used there.
activities.explanation: Each khichdi name belongs with its place in this matching game.

activities.title: Complete the name
activities.prompt: In Bihar, the name is ______ khichdi.
activities.hint: This name tells you the place: Bihar.
activities.explanation: The name used in Bihar is Bihari khichdi.

activities.title: Choose the Kashmir name
activities.prompt: Which name is used in Kashmir?
options: Bisi bele bhat
Bihari khichdi
Kichuri
Moong khetchir
activities.explanation: Moong khetchir is the name used in Kashmir.

activities.title: Festival name order
activities.prompt: Put these festival names in the order listed on your concept card.
activities.explanation: Your concept card lists the festival names in this order.

activities.title: The final task
activities.prompt: What must children list for the final task?
options: kites and boats
sweets and dishes
songs and dances
books and pens
activities.explanation: Children name their favourite festival and list sweets and dishes prepared on that day.

activities.prompt: A child hears 'Bajra khichdi' on a menu. What should the child expect?
options: A regional name for khichdi.
A separate festival with kite flying.
A sweet listed for every festival.
The final task's favourite dish.

This mistake mixes a food name with kite flying.
This mistake thinks every festival meal is a sweet.
This mistake thinks the task chooses one dish for everyone.

activities.explanation: Bajra khichdi is a name used in Rajasthan.

activities.prompt: Friends say 'Bihari khichdi' and 'Bisi bele bhat'. What do the names show?
options: They are regional names for khichdi.
They are names for two separate festivals.
They are sweets served on festival days.
They are places used for kite flying.

why.They are names for two separate festival: This mistake treats regional dish names as festival names.
This mistake thinks both words name foods that are sweets.
This mistake turns food names into places for kites.

activities.explanation: Bihari khichdi is used in Bihar; Bisi bele bhat is used in Karnataka.

activities.prompt: A child hears one festival has many names. Why might the child ask questions?
options: To learn where each name is used.
To check whether the names mean new foods.
To find out which task children must finish.
To learn how to make a flying kite.

why.To check whether the names mean new food: This mistake thinks every name must describe a different food.
why.To find out which task children must fin: This mistake thinks the child asks about school tasks.
This mistake thinks the child wants to build a kite.

activities.explanation: Different names across the country can make a child curious.

activities.prompt: A child's festival page names only the festival. What is still missing?
options: A list of sweets and dishes from that day.
A list of kite shapes and kite flying places.
A list of regional names for one dish.
A list of other children's favourite festivals.

why.A list of kite shapes and kite flying pl: This mistake adds kite details, which are not required.
This mistake adds regional dish names instead of the day's food.
why.A list of other children's favourite fes: This mistake lists other festivals instead of one child's choice.

activities.explanation: Children must list sweets and dishes prepared on the festival day.

activities.prompt: 'Kichuri' appears beside 'khichdi' in a text. What does it mean there?
options: It is another name for khichdi.
It is a festival sweet in every state.
It is a kite used at festivals.
It is a task children must finish.

This mistake treats a regional dish name as a sweet everywhere.
This mistake mixes a food name with a kite.
This mistake mixes a food name with a school task.

activities.explanation: Kichuri is a name used for khichdi in West Bengal.

activities.context: During the lesson, a child imagines that all the laddoos have joined together to become one huge laddoo. The child also imagines that all the children have become one big child and that all the seas have joined together to form one big sea. The big child picks up the huge laddoo and throws it into the big sea. The class must then think about what happens next.
activities.prompt: What would happen next when the huge laddoo enters the big sea?
options: A big splish-splash would occur where the laddoo hits the sea.
The laddoo would stay above the sea.
The sea would turn into a laddoo.
The laddoo would become another big child.

The poem does not say that the laddoo stays above the sea.
The joining happens to the laddoos, children, and seas, not the other way around.
why.The laddoo would become another big chil: The laddoo does not change into a child.

activities.explanation: The poem says that the laddoo makes a big splish-splash.

activities.context: During the lesson, a child imagines that all the laddoos have joined together to become one huge laddoo. The child also imagines that all the children have become one big child and that all the seas have joined together to form one big sea. The big child picks up the huge laddoo and throws it into the big sea. The class must then think about what happens next.
activities.prompt: If the huge laddoo keeps its round shape, what should the child do during the activity about round things that can be eaten?
options: Choose it as a round thing to eat.
Leave it out because it has become huge.
Choose the big sea instead of the laddoo.
Leave it out because it was thrown into the sea.

The activity asks about round shape, not size.
why.Choose the big sea instead of the laddoo: The sea is not something the child can eat.
why.Leave it out because it was thrown into: Being thrown into the sea does not remove the laddoo's round shape.

activities.explanation: A laddoo is a round thing that can be eaten.

activities.prompt: How does the idea of everything joining together make the things in the poem seem bigger?
activities.answer: The poem shows separate things becoming larger when they are imagined as one. All the laddoos become one huge laddoo, all the children become one big child, and all the seas become one big sea. The joining idea makes each group seem enormous and joined together.
points: All the laddoos become one huge laddoo.
All the children become one big child.
All the seas become one big sea.
Each joined group becomes bigger.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: On Meena’s birthday, her friend Jithu gave her a box of mixed sweets. Meena could not see properly, so she felt the sweets and chose the big laddoo. She told Jithu that she loved laddoos. He was surprised and asked how she knew that the sweet was a laddoo.
activities.prompt: After hearing Meena’s answer, what should Jithu do next?
options: Ask Meena how she was able to identify the sweet.
Ask Meena to taste every sweet in the box.
Tell Meena that the sweet cannot be a laddoo.
Ask Meena to choose the sweet again without touching it.

why.Ask Meena to taste every sweet in the bo: Tasting every sweet would not explain her choice.
why.Tell Meena that the sweet cannot be a la: Jithu’s surprise does not mean she was wrong.
why.Ask Meena to choose the sweet again with: Choosing without touch would remove her useful method.

activities.explanation: This question helps Jithu understand her answer.

activities.context: On Meena’s birthday, her friend Jithu gave her a box of mixed sweets. Meena could not see properly, so she felt the sweets and chose the big laddoo. She told Jithu that she loved laddoos. He was surprised and asked how she knew that the sweet was a laddoo.
activities.prompt: If Meena had not been able to feel the sweets, what would she most likely have difficulty doing?
options: Choosing which sweet was the big laddoo.
Saying that she loved laddoos.
Knowing that it was her birthday.
Recognizing that the box held mixed sweets.

Her love of laddoos was not found by touch.
Knowing about the birthday did not depend on touch.
why.Recognizing that the box held mixed swee: She learned about the mixed sweets through Jithu’s gift.

activities.explanation: She used touch to find the big laddoo.

activities.prompt: Explain why Jithu was surprised by Meena’s answer.
activities.answer: Jithu was surprised because Meena could not see properly, yet she chose the big laddoo from the mixed sweets and said that she loved laddoos. Her answer showed that she had been able to identify the sweet without seeing it, so Jithu wanted to know how she knew.
points: Meena could not see properly.
She chose the big laddoo by touch.
She said she loved laddoos.
Jithu wanted to know how she knew.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a lesson, a teacher tells children that making sentences can begin with play. A matching game is ready, while another group is asked to notice the letter blends cl, pl, and bl. In the water activity, children place paper, a stone, and a green leaf in the water. A pencil, an eraser, a feather, and a spoon are ready to test. The teacher uses the results to discuss light and heavy.
activities.prompt: The teacher wants children to practise the blend bl by using two sentence words. Which pair should they choose?
options: blue and blanket
clock and plum
plum and cloud
plum and blue

why.clock and plum: Clock has cl, while plum has pl.
why.plum and cloud: Plum has pl, while cloud has cl.
why.plum and blue: Plum has pl, while blue has bl.

activities.explanation: Blue and blanket both have the blend bl.

activities.prompt: How can the sentence words help children notice the blends cl, pl, and bl?
activities.answer: The teacher can ask children to find the blends in plum, clock, blue, and blanket. Plum has pl, clock has cl, and blue and blanket have bl. This helps children notice how the blends appear in different words used for making sentences.
points: Plum is used to show the blend pl.
Clock is used to show the blend cl.
Blue and blanket are used to show the blend bl.
The words are used for making sentences.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: On festival day, a family in Gujarat calls khichdi “Gujarati khichdi.” The family also flies kites because kite flying is very popular during the festival. Elsewhere, the same festival is called Sankranti, Pongal, Lohri or Bihu. A student wonders why people in different parts of the country use different names. The student also has a final task: name a favourite festival and list the sweets and dishes prepared on that day.
activities.prompt: If the family moved from Gujarat to Bihar, what local name would they use for khichdi?
options: Bihari khichdi
Kichuri
Pongal
Bajra khichdi

why.Kichuri: This name is used in West Bengal.
why.Pongal: This is a festival name used in Tamil Nadu, not a khichdi name.
why.Bajra khichdi: This name is used in Rajasthan.

activities.explanation: This is the name used for khichdi in Bihar.

activities.context: On festival day, a family in Gujarat calls khichdi “Gujarati khichdi.” The family also flies kites because kite flying is very popular during the festival. Elsewhere, the same festival is called Sankranti, Pongal, Lohri or Bihu. A student wonders why people in different parts of the country use different names. The student also has a final task: name a favourite festival and list the sweets and dishes prepared on that day.
activities.prompt: What should the student include to complete the final task?
options: A favourite celebration and the foods served that day.
A regional khichdi name instead of a chosen festival.
Kite flying instead of the festival and its foods.
Festival names only, without listing any dishes.

why.A regional khichdi name instead of a cho: A khichdi name does not complete the favourite-festival task.
why.Kite flying instead of the festival and: Flying kites does not answer either part of the task.
why.Festival names only, without listing any: The task also requires sweets and dishes to be listed.

activities.explanation: The task needs both a chosen festival and its foods.

activities.prompt: Explain why people in different parts of the country use different names for khichdi.
activities.answer: Khichdi is known by different names across the country, so the name used for it changes with the region. Gujarat uses Gujarati khichdi, Bihar uses Bihari khichdi, and West Bengal uses Kichuri. These regional names help people connect the dish with the place where that name is used.
points: Khichdi has different regional names.
Gujarati khichdi is used in Gujarat.
Bihari khichdi is used in Bihar.
Kichuri is used in West Bengal.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: What do all the laddoos become in the poem?
options: Many tiny sweets
One huge laddoo
A box of sweets
A big sea
activities.explanation: The poem imagines all the laddoos joining to make one huge laddoo.

activities.prompt: The poem imagines all the children becoming one child.
activities.explanation: Yes. The poem imagines all the children becoming one child.

activities.prompt: On Meena's birthday, Jithu gave her a box of ______ sweets.
activities.hint: What kind of sweets were in the box?
activities.explanation: Jithu gave Meena a box of mixed sweets on her birthday.

activities.prompt: Match each word with its beginning blend.
activities.explanation: These words contain the blends cl, pl and bl.

activities.prompt: Which name for khichdi is used in West Bengal?
options: Pongal
Bihari khichdi
Kichuri
Bajra khichdi
activities.explanation: Kichuri is the name used in West Bengal.

activities.prompt: Pongal is a name used in Gujarat.
activities.explanation: Pongal is used in Tamil Nadu. Gujarati khichdi is used in Gujarat.

activities.prompt: Put the poem's events in the right order.
items: The big child picks up the big laddoo.
The big child throws the laddoo into the big sea.
The laddoo makes a big splish-splash in the sea.
activities.explanation: The child picks up the laddoo, throws it into the sea, and makes a big splish-splash.

activities.prompt: Khichdi is usually cooked with ______ and lentils together.
activities.hint: What is cooked with lentils?
activities.explanation: Khichdi is usually cooked with rice and lentils together.

activities.prompt: Put these sentence-making words in the order they appear in the lesson.
activities.explanation: These words appear in the lesson in this order.

chapters.title: Thank God!
chapters.summary: In this chapter: the farmer’s gift to the king; thinking about the farmer; learning opposites; using is and are.

lessons.title: The Farmer’s Gift to the King

activities.prompt: Which fruit did the farmer bring, and how did the king react?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Gift for the King
activities.body: The farmer grew many kinds of fruit on his land. His hard work and care helped the trees grow well. He took special care with grapes and watermelons. He chose grapes for the king because watermelons were too heavy. He carried bunches of grapes to the palace in a basket. A guard took him to the royal garden, where the king tasted a grape and played with another one.
keyPoints: The farmer worked hard and cared for his fruit trees.
He chose grapes because watermelons were too heavy.
He carried grapes to the king in a basket.
activities.explanation: The farmer’s hard work led to a gift for the King.

activities.prompt: The farmer has two best fruits for the king. Which fruit should he carry?
steps: His wife says watermelons and grapes are the best fruits.
He chooses grapes because the heavy watermelons are hard to carry.
He puts the grape bunches in a basket for the walk.
So the king will receive grapes as the farmer’s gift.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did the farmer decide to grow on his land?
options: many kinds of fruits
few kinds of flowers
small kinds of stones
young kinds of fish
activities.explanation: He decided to grow fruits, and he worked hard to grow many kinds.

activities.prompt: The farmer chose watermelons because they were light.
activities.explanation: Watermelons were too heavy, so he chose grapes for the king.

activities.prompt: The farmer took special care to grow ______ and watermelons.
activities.hint: This fruit grew in bunches.
activities.explanation: He took special care of both grapes and watermelons.

activities.prompt: Which fruits did his wife call the best?
options: apples and pears
mangoes and lemons
watermelons and grapes
plums and peaches
activities.explanation: His wife said that watermelons and grapes were the best fruits.

activities.prompt: Match each person with what they did.
pairs: said the best fruits were watermelons and grapes
took him to the royal garden
plucked a grape and ate it
activities.explanation: His wife named the best fruits. The guard guided him, and the King ate a grape.

activities.prompt: Put the farmer’s actions in the correct order.
items: Decided to give the best fruit to the king
Put bunches of grapes in a basket
Went with the palace guard to the royal garden
activities.explanation: He chose grapes, put them in a basket, and walked to the palace.

activities.prompt: At a picnic, a friend playfully throws a grape. A guest says, “Thank God!” How does the guest most likely feel?
options: happy about the playful surprise
angry about the thrown grape
afraid of the playing friend
sorry that the picnic ended

why.angry about the thrown grape: This mistakes a playful game for anger.
why.afraid of the playing friend: This mistakes friendly play for fear.
why.sorry that the picnic ended: This assumes the picnic ended, but nothing says that.

activities.explanation: The playful grape and thankful words show happiness.

activities.prompt: Before visiting the king, a farmer fills a basket with grape bunches. What can we work out?
options: He is getting ready to carry a gift
He is getting ready to sell some fruit
He is getting ready to plant new trees
He is getting ready to feed the guard

why.He is getting ready to sell some fruit: This mistakes the royal gift for a sale.
why.He is getting ready to plant new trees: This mistakes carrying ripe grapes for planting.
why.He is getting ready to feed the guard: This mistakes a carried gift for feeding the guard.

activities.explanation: The grape bunches are his gift for the king.

activities.prompt: At the farm, the farmer is choosing a gift. His wife says, “Watermelons and grapes are the best.” What should he think about?
options: which fruit fits the king’s gift
which fruit is easiest to eat
which fruit will earn more money
which fruit will grow the fastest

why.which fruit is easiest to eat: This focuses on eating, not choosing a royal gift.
why.which fruit will earn more money: This assumes money matters, but the gift is for the king.
why.which fruit will grow the fastest: This focuses on growing, not choosing what to give.

activities.explanation: She names the best fruits, so they guide his choice.

activities.prompt: In the royal garden, the King plucks a grape. He puts it in his mouth. What does “plucked” mean?
options: picked it from the plant
threw it through the air
hid it inside a basket
broke it into small bits

why.threw it through the air: This confuses picking with the later playful throw.
why.hid it inside a basket: The King did not hide the grape inside a basket.
why.broke it into small bits: Putting a grape in his mouth does not mean breaking it.

activities.explanation: He picked the grape before putting it in his mouth.

activities.prompt: At a picnic, a child must carry fruit to a friend. The child has grapes and watermelons. Which will the child likely take?
options: grapes, because they are easier to carry
watermelons, because they are easier to carry
grapes, because they need no basket
watermelons, because they are better fruit

why.watermelons, because they are easier to: This reverses the lesson about what was too heavy.
why.grapes, because they need no basket: The grapes were put in a basket, so this is mistaken.
why.watermelons, because they are better fru: Being the best fruit does not remove the problem of weight.

activities.explanation: The farmer chose grapes because watermelons were too heavy.

activities.prompt: A child comes to a school show. A guide takes the child to the head teacher. The teacher looks at the child’s gift. What can we infer?
options: The guide helped the child meet the teacher
The guide wanted to keep the child’s gift
The child came there to clean a room
The teacher sent the child away from class

why.The guide wanted to keep the child’s gif: Nothing shows that the guide wanted to keep the gift.
why.The child came there to clean a room: Taking the child to the teacher does not show cleaning work.
why.The teacher sent the child away from cla: Nothing shows that the teacher sent the child away.

activities.explanation: The guide led the gift carrier to the person receiving it.

lessons.title: Thinking About the Farmer

activities.prompt: What surprising things can a farmer grow and share with others?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Farmer's Choice
activities.body: The farmer grew fruits on his farm. His wife said the best fruits were watermelons and grapes. He chose grapes because watermelons were too heavy. The King threw a grape playfully at him. The farmer thanked God for choosing grapes to give the King. He said God is great and replied with a smile. The lesson asks what else farmers can grow.
keyPoints: The farmer grew the best fruits.
He chose grapes because watermelons were too heavy.
He thanked God and said God is great.
activities.explanation: This helps you follow the farmer's choice and the lesson's questions.

activities.prompt: The farmer must give fruit to the King. Watermelons and grapes are his best fruits. The watermelons are too heavy. Which should he give?
steps: His wife calls both fruits best, so both are good choices.
Watermelons are too heavy, so grapes are easier to carry.
He chooses grapes and gives them to the King.
The King throws one playfully, so he thanks God for his choice.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which fruits did the farmer's wife call the best?
options: Watermelons only
Grapes only
Watermelons and grapes
No fruits at all
activities.explanation: His wife said that watermelons and grapes were the best fruits.

activities.prompt: The farmer chose ______ because watermelons were too heavy.
activities.hint: His wife called grapes one of the best fruits.
activities.explanation: The farmer chose grapes to give to the King.

activities.prompt: The farmer chose watermelons because grapes were too heavy.
activities.explanation: He chose grapes because the watermelons were too heavy.

activities.prompt: Match each person to what they did.
pairs: Said watermelons and grapes were the best fruits
Chose grapes because watermelons were too heavy
Threw a grape playfully at the farmer
activities.explanation: Each action helps you remember the farmer's story.

activities.prompt: How did the wise farmer reply?
options: With a smile
With a shout
With a song
With silence
activities.explanation: The wise farmer replied with a smile.

activities.prompt: Put the farmer's story events in order.
items: The farmer grew the best grapes and watermelons on his farm.
The farmer chose grapes because watermelons were too heavy.
The King threw a grape playfully at the farmer.
The farmer thanked God for choosing grapes to give the King.
activities.explanation: The story moves from growing fruit to choosing, giving, and thanking God.

activities.prompt: The farmer grew fruits. One kind was too heavy to carry. Which kind did he choose for the King?
options: The farmer chooses grapes.
The farmer chooses watermelons.
The farmer chooses both kinds.
The farmer chooses no fruit.

He forgets how heavy the watermelons were.
He misses the choice between the kinds.
He thinks having fruit means he needs none.

activities.explanation: He chose grapes because the watermelons were too heavy.

activities.prompt: The King threw a grape at the farmer. What does “playfully” suggest about the throw?
options: in a joking way
in an angry way
in a scared way
in a rushed way

why.in an angry way: He thinks playful means the King wanted to hurt him.
why.in a scared way: He thinks playful means the King was frightened.
why.in a rushed way: He thinks every quick action must be done in a hurry.

activities.explanation: Playfully suggests the King was joking with the farmer.

activities.prompt: The farmer’s wife says watermelons and grapes are the best fruits. What does “best” show?
options: The fruits had the highest quality.
The fruits had the lowest quality.
The farmer had never grown them.
The King had disliked both fruits.

He reverses the meaning of best and worst.
He thinks best means the farmer did not grow them.
He thinks best describes what the King disliked.

activities.explanation: Best shows that these fruits were better than others.

activities.prompt: The farmer chooses grapes because watermelons are too heavy. Why does he say, “God is great”?
options: He believes his grape choice was good.
He believes his heavy fruit was good.
He believes the King needed more fruit.
He believes his farm grew no fruit.

He thinks heavy watermelons were the better choice.
He thinks the King asked for more fruit.
He thinks the farmer had no fruit to give.

activities.explanation: He thanks God for choosing grapes, so his choice helped.

activities.prompt: The lesson asks whether there are women farmers. Why should children think about this question?
options: It questions who can become a farmer.
It explains which fruit is heaviest.
It teaches how kings throw grapes.
It helps choose the best farm.

It mistakes the lesson’s focus for the question’s purpose.
It mistakes a story event for the question’s purpose.
It thinks the question is mainly about choosing a farm.

activities.explanation: It makes children think about all people who can farm.

lessons.title: Learning Opposites

activities.prompt: What is the opposite of heavy?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What are opposites?
activities.body: This lesson is about learning opposites. Opposite words have opposite meanings. Heavy and light are one pair. The farmer knew that a watermelon was heavy and grapes were light. The lesson asks for the opposite of each underlined word. Its examples include a thick book, a long journey, soft cotton and a slow tortoise. The reading mentions a round ball and brown tables. The teacher asks for more easy examples.
keyPoints: Heavy and light have opposite meanings.
Examples include a thick book and a long journey.
The reading mentions a round ball and brown tables.
activities.explanation: Heavy and light show what opposite meanings mean.

activities.prompt: Why are grapes easier to lift than a watermelon?
steps: Grapes fit because the farmer knows they are light.
Watermelon does not fit because the farmer knows it is heavy.
Light and heavy have opposite meanings because they show opposite weights.
Therefore, grapes are easier to lift because they are lighter than watermelon.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which word has the opposite meaning of heavy?
options: light
soft
long
slow
activities.explanation: Heavy and light have opposite meanings.

activities.prompt: The farmer knew that a watermelon was ______.
activities.hint: This word has the opposite meaning of light.
activities.explanation: The farmer knew that the watermelon was heavy.

activities.prompt: The farmer knew that grapes were light.
activities.explanation: The lesson says that the farmer knew grapes were light.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with the example that describes it.
activities.explanation: Each matching example includes the description from the lesson.

activities.prompt: What does one reading sentence say about the ball?
options: The ball is round.
The book is thick.
The cotton is soft.
The tortoise is slow.
activities.explanation: One reading sentence says that the ball is round.

activities.prompt: Put the examples in the order shown in the lesson.
activities.explanation: These examples appear in this order in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Grapes are light; watermelon is heavy. Why are grapes easier to lift?
options: The grapes are lighter.
The grapes are heavier.
The grapes are darker.
The grapes are rounder.

Heavier is wrong because the farmer knows grapes are light.

activities.explanation: Light is right because the farmer knows grapes are light.

activities.prompt: A thick book is near you. Which word means the opposite of thick?
options: thin
wide
soft
slow
activities.explanation: Thin is right because it means the opposite of thick.

activities.prompt: A long journey is ahead. Which word means the opposite of long?
options: short
straight
soft
light
activities.explanation: Short is right because it means the opposite of long.

activities.prompt: Soft cotton touches your hand. Which word means the opposite of soft?
options: hard
heavy
thick
slow
activities.explanation: Hard is right because it means the opposite of soft.

activities.prompt: A slow tortoise walks by. Which word means the opposite of slow?
options: fast
light
round
short
activities.explanation: Fast is right because it means the opposite of slow.

activities.prompt: The round ball is close. Which word means the opposite of round?
options: square
brown
soft
heavy
activities.explanation: Square is right because it means the opposite of round.
