lessons.title: Using Is and Are

activities.prompt: Which little word fits each sentence: is or are?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Choose Is or Are
activities.body: Use “is” when the sentence names one thing. Use “are” when it names more than one thing. The boy is tall. The toys are on the shelf. The book is on the table. The car is on the road. Always read the whole sentence before you choose.
keyPoints: Use “is” with one thing.
Use “are” with more than one thing.
Read the whole sentence before choosing.
activities.explanation: Look at the subject before the blank. Then choose “is” or “are”.

activities.prompt: A child sees “is” and “are.” Why does the word change?
steps: Toys are on the shelf, so “are” fits because toys is plural.
The book is on the table, so “is” fits for one book.
Plural subjects take “are,” while singular subjects take “is.”
So the word changes because the subject’s number changes.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Raghuram ______ a tall boy.
activities.hint: Think about the subject before the blank.
activities.explanation: Raghuram is one boy, so the sentence needs “is”.

activities.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: The table is made of wood.
The table are made of wood.
The table is made of woods.
The table are made of woods.
activities.explanation: The table is one thing. Its sentence needs “is”.

activities.prompt: The toys is on the shelf.
activities.explanation: No. “The toys” names more than one thing, so it needs “are”.

activities.prompt: Match each subject to its correct sentence.
activities.explanation: Use “is” for one thing. Use “are” for more than one thing.

activities.prompt: Put these words in order to make a correct sentence.
activities.explanation: The sentence says, “The book is on the table.”

activities.prompt: These mangoes ______ sweet.
activities.hint: Look at “these mangoes” before choosing.
activities.explanation: The mangoes are more than one fruit, so the sentence needs “are”.

activities.prompt: The lesson shows animals in the jungle. Which pair fits: “___ animals in the jungle”?
options: is; one animal
are; many animals
am; many animals
be; many animals

why.is; one animal: This wrongly treats the plural word “animals” as one animal.
why.am; many animals: This uses the form for “I,” not for animals.
why.be; many animals: This uses the bare form instead of “is” or “are.”

activities.explanation: This is right because “animals” names more than one animal.

activities.prompt: The table is made of wood. Which pair fits: “The table ___ made of wood”?
options: is; one table
are; many tables
am; one table
be; one table

why.are; many tables: This wrongly treats one table as more than one table.
why.am; one table: This uses the form for “I,” not for the table.
why.be; one table: This leaves the sentence without “is” or “are.”

activities.explanation: This is right because “table” names one thing.

activities.prompt: These mangoes are sweet. What does the word “are” tell us?
options: The mangoes are more than one.
The mangoes are only one.
The mangoes are very tall.
The mangoes are made of wood.

This confuses a plural word with one mango.
This confuses a describing word with the number of mangoes.
This confuses the mangoes with the wooden table.

activities.explanation: This is right because “mangoes” names more than one mango.

activities.prompt: Raghuram is a tall boy. Which pair fits: “Raghuram ___ a tall boy”?
options: is; one boy
are; many boys
am; one boy
be; one boy

why.are; many boys: This wrongly treats one boy as many boys.
why.am; one boy: This uses the form for “I,” not for Raghuram.
why.be; one boy: This leaves the sentence without “is” or “are.”

activities.explanation: This is right because Raghuram is one boy.

activities.prompt: The book is on the table. The toys are on the shelf. Which words fit both blanks?
options: is; are
are; is
am; are
be; are

why.are; is: This reverses the correct word forms for the two subjects.
why.am; are: This uses the form for “I” for the book.
why.be; are: This leaves the book without “is” or “are.”

activities.explanation: This is right because the book is singular and the toys are plural.

activities.prompt: The girls are at the shop. The car is on the road. Which line has a plural subject?
options: The girls are at the shop.
The car is on the road.
Both lines have plural subjects.
Neither line has a plural subject.

This mistakes the one car for a plural subject.
This wrongly treats the one car as plural too.

activities.explanation: This is right because “girls” names more than one girl.

lessons.title: The Elephant’s Cold

activities.prompt: What might an elephant ask a shop for when it feels poorly?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Mighty Elephant Needs a Hanky
activities.body: The poem begins with a mighty elephant who has a very bad cold. The elephant goes to a shop to buy a handkerchief. It asks for a hanky for an elephant, but the shop does not have one of that size. The sales girl is surprised. The elephant sneezes loudly, shakes its mighty head, and asks for a sheet instead.
keyPoints: The elephant has a very bad cold.
The shop has no handkerchief of the needed size.
The elephant asks for a sheet instead.
activities.explanation: This introduces the elephant’s cold and its funny shopping problem.

activities.prompt: Why is the sales girl surprised by the elephant's request?
steps: Because the elephant has a very bad cold, it needs a handkerchief.
It asks for a hanky big enough for an elephant.
That unusual request surprises the sales girl.
No hanky of that size means the elephant asks for a sheet.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Who begins the poem?
options: an elephant
a cold
a shop
a hanky
activities.explanation: Good choice! The poem begins with a mighty elephant.

activities.prompt: The elephant went to buy a ______.
activities.hint: This item is sold at the shop.
activities.explanation: A handkerchief was the item the elephant went to buy.

activities.prompt: Match each part of the story with its detail.
activities.explanation: You matched the hanky request, shop, sneeze, head and sheet correctly.

activities.prompt: What surprised the sales girl?
options: the request
a very bad cold
a loud sneeze
the mighty head
activities.explanation: Good choice! The sales girl was surprised by the elephant’s request.

activities.prompt: What did the elephant ask for first?
options: a hanky for an elephant
a sheet instead
a very bad cold
a handkerchief of that size
activities.explanation: The elephant asked for an elephant hanky before asking for a sheet instead.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happen in the poem.
items: asked for a hanky for an elephant
the shop had no handkerchief of that size
activities.explanation: The elephant asks for a hanky, learns the size is unavailable, then asks for a sheet.

activities.prompt: An elephant asks for a hanky for an elephant. How does the sales girl most likely feel?
options: She feels surprised and unsure
She feels happy and excited
She feels angry and cross
She feels sleepy and calm

why.She feels happy and excited: A happy feeling is not shown by the story.
why.She feels angry and cross: Angry is not shown; the story says she is surprised.
why.She feels sleepy and calm: Sleepy is not shown; the story says she is surprised.

activities.explanation: The unusual request surprises her, as the story says.

activities.prompt: An elephant has a very bad cold. It asks for a hanky for an elephant. What must the hanky be big enough for?
options: The elephant's own body
The sales girl's hand
The shop counter
A small child's face

why.The sales girl's hand: This confuses the shop worker with the elephant.
why.The shop counter: The counter is not the elephant.
why.A small child's face: A small child's face is not the elephant.

activities.explanation: The hanky is for the elephant, so it must fit the elephant.

activities.prompt: The shop sells handkerchiefs, but it has none of the elephant's size. What can you work out about the shop?
options: It cannot meet the elephant's first request.
It has no handkerchiefs at all.
It already has a sheet for sale.
It closes when an elephant arrives.

Having no size does not mean having no handkerchiefs.
The story does not say a sheet is already for sale.
The story does not say the shop closes.

activities.explanation: The missing size means it cannot give the requested hanky.

activities.prompt: The elephant sneezes loudly with an “Achoo!” It shakes its mighty head. What does this show?
options: The bad cold is still affecting the elephant.
The elephant is happy with the shop's answer.
The elephant is trying to become smaller.
The sales girl has forgotten the elephant.

why.The elephant is happy with the shop's an: Nothing shows happiness after the shop's answer.
why.The elephant is trying to become smaller: Shaking the head does not mean trying to become smaller.
why.The sales girl has forgotten the elephan: The elephant's actions do not show the sales girl forgetting it.

activities.explanation: The sneeze and head shake show the elephant's cold is acting on it.

activities.prompt: The shop has no handkerchief of that size. The elephant asks for a sheet instead. Why is this a sensible next step?
options: It is trying another item that might work.
It wants to buy two small handkerchiefs.
It thinks a sheet is smaller than a hanky.
It has decided to leave without buying.

Nothing says it wants two small handkerchiefs.
why.It thinks a sheet is smaller than a hank: Asking for a sheet does not mean it thinks one is smaller.
Asking for a sheet shows it has not simply decided to leave.

activities.explanation: It tries a different item when the first size is unavailable.

lessons.title: Speaking, Writing and Exploring

activities.prompt: What will you say, write, and discover when planning a fruity feast?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Speak, Write and Explore
activities.body: In this lesson, you will practise speaking, writing, and exploring. First, say aloud which food you will take when you visit the Big Elephant. Then, help Chandu put the salad steps in order. Mother cuts the fruit before you add the banana, papaya, apple, and grapes. Mix everything, then finish with lemon and salt. Last, look for fruits in a grid.
keyPoints: Say aloud what food you will take.
Put Chandu's salad steps in order.
Find fruits in the exploring grid.
activities.explanation: You will speak, organise steps, and find fruits.

activities.prompt: You are visiting the Big Elephant and must choose food aloud.
steps: Choose fruit salad, because Chandu wrote the steps for preparing it.
Imagine the visit, because the speaking task asks you to do so.
Say aloud that you will take salad, so others know your choice.
Follow all the written steps, so the salad is prepared correctly.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Speaking Task
activities.prompt: What does the speaking task ask you to say?
options: Read the salad steps silently.
Find fruits in a grid.
Say aloud what food you will take.
Write the fruit names in order.
activities.explanation: Well done! The task asks you to say aloud what food you will take.

activities.title: Imagine a Visit
activities.prompt: Who should you imagine visiting?
options: Mother
Chandu
the fruit grid
the Big Elephant
activities.explanation: Great choice! You should imagine visiting the Big Elephant.

activities.title: Mother's First Job
activities.prompt: Mother ______ some fruits.
activities.hint: Think about what Mother does first.
activities.explanation: Exactly! Mother cuts some fruits first.

activities.title: Match the Fruits
activities.prompt: Match each salad ingredient to its fruit.
activities.explanation: Great matching! These are the fruits added to the salad.

activities.title: The Next Step
activities.prompt: What do you add after putting in papaya cubes?
options: banana slices
apple slices
grapes from a bunch
lemon and salt
activities.explanation: Good job! After the papaya cubes, you add the apple slices.

activities.title: Order the Salad Steps
activities.prompt: Put these salad steps in order.
items: add some grapes from a bunch
activities.explanation: Excellent! After mixing, squeeze a lemon and add a pinch of salt.

activities.prompt: Chandu mixed up the salad steps. Why should children put them in order?
options: So every fruit is added at the right time.
So the salad can be mixed at once.
So the fruit grid is easier to explore.
So the food choice can be spoken.

They think mixing comes before the separate fruit steps.
They confuse the writing task with the exploring task.
They confuse the writing task with the speaking task.

activities.explanation: Correct order tells when each fruit should be added.

activities.prompt: You are visiting the Big Elephant. Why should you say aloud the food you will take?
options: So your food choice is clear to all.
So the salad steps become easier to read.
So the fruit grid can be solved by all.
So Chandu can mix up the salad steps.

why.So the salad steps become easier to read: They think the main need is to read the written steps.
They think the main need is to find fruit pictures.
They think speaking aloud is part of the writing task.

activities.explanation: Speaking aloud tells others which food you choose.

activities.prompt: Chandu wrote, “First take banana slices, then put in papaya cubes.” What does this show?
options: The banana step comes before the papaya step.
The papaya step must come after mixing.
The banana and papaya are mixed together.
The two steps have no clear order.

They move the papaya step past the mixing step.
why.The banana and papaya are mixed together: They think those two fruits are mixed at that point.
They ignore the order words in Chandu's sentence.

activities.explanation: The words “First” and “then” show which step comes first.

activities.prompt: Children see the salad steps all mixed up. Why might they feel excited?
options: There is an order puzzle for them to solve.
There is a fruit grid for them to search.
There is a food choice for them to speak.
There is a salad for Mother to cut.

why.There is a fruit grid for them to search: They mix up the order task with the exploring task.
why.There is a food choice for them to speak: They mix up the order task with the speaking task.
They focus on the first preparation step, not the puzzle.

activities.explanation: The mixed-up steps give the children a puzzle to solve.

activities.prompt: The apple slices are added, but the salad is not mixed yet. Which step comes next?
options: Add grapes from the bunch.
Take banana slices first.
Put in papaya cubes.
Let Mother cut the fruits.

They choose an early fruit step, not the next one.
They move an earlier step forward instead of choosing the next.
They confuse the opening cutting step with the next step.

activities.explanation: Grapes come after apple and before the fruit is mixed.

activities.context: A farmer decided to grow fruits on his land and worked hard to grow fruit trees. His care helped grapes and watermelons grow well. His wife said these were the best fruits for the king. Watermelons were too heavy, so he carried bunches of grapes in a basket to the palace. A guard took him to the royal garden. The King ate one grape and playfully threw another at the farmer, who thanked God when it hit his forehead.
activities.prompt: If the farmer had put less care into his fruit trees, what would be the most likely result?
options: The trees might not have grown as well.
There would be no best fruit for the king.
The farmer would carry watermelons instead of grapes.
The King would eat the same grapes in the royal garden.

why.There would be no best fruit for the kin: Less care might reduce their growth, but it would not necessarily stop all growth.
why.The farmer would carry watermelons inste: The watermelons would not automatically replace the grapes.
why.The King would eat the same grapes in th: The King's actions would depend on whether the farmer brought him any grapes.

activities.explanation: His care helped the fruit trees grow well.

activities.context: A farmer decided to grow fruits on his land and worked hard to grow fruit trees. His care helped grapes and watermelons grow well. His wife said these were the best fruits for the king. Watermelons were too heavy, so he carried bunches of grapes in a basket to the palace. A guard took him to the royal garden. The King ate one grape and playfully threw another at the farmer, who thanked God when it hit his forehead.
activities.prompt: If the farmer had not realized that the King was acting playfully, what might he wrongly think?
options: That the guard should send him away.
That the King was angry with his gift.
That he had chosen the wrong kind of fruit.
That the King wanted watermelons instead.

The guard had taken the farmer to the royal garden, so sending him away was not suggested.
why.That he had chosen the wrong kind of fru: The King ate a grape, so it would be wrong to think he rejected the fruit.
why.That the King wanted watermelons instead: Nothing showed that the King wanted a different kind of fruit.

activities.explanation: The thrown grape was playful, but the farmer might have misread it as anger.

activities.prompt: Explain why the farmer's hard work and care mattered to his fruit trees.
activities.answer: Hard work and care helped the farmer grow many kinds of fruit trees, and the trees grew well because of that effort. He also gave special care to grapes and watermelons. This care mattered because he needed good fruit to choose a gift for the king.
points: He worked hard to grow many kinds of fruit trees.
His care helped the trees grow well.
He took special care with grapes and watermelons.
He needed suitable fruit for the king's gift.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A farmer gave the King grapes from his farm. He had grown the best grapes and watermelons there. His wife had said that the best fruits were watermelons and grapes. He chose grapes because watermelons were too heavy. The King threw a grape playfully at him. The farmer thanked God because he had chosen the fruit to give the King, and he said that God is great. The wise farmer replied with a smile.
activities.prompt: How should the farmer most likely react if the King playfully threw a grape?
options: He would express thanks and remain cheerful.
He would become angry and refuse to answer.
He would blame his wife for suggesting grapes.
He would try to stop the King from playing with the fruit.

why.He would become angry and refuse to answ: He answered the King in a friendly way.
why.He would blame his wife for suggesting g: He did not show anger or blame his wife.
why.He would try to stop the King from playi: He accepted the King's playful action calmly.

activities.explanation: The farmer was grateful for his choice of grapes.

activities.context: A farmer gave the King grapes from his farm. He had grown the best grapes and watermelons there. His wife had said that the best fruits were watermelons and grapes. He chose grapes because watermelons were too heavy. The King threw a grape playfully at him. The farmer thanked God because he had chosen the fruit to give the King, and he said that God is great. The wise farmer replied with a smile.
activities.prompt: If the farmer had chosen watermelons, what would he most likely have needed to do differently?
options: He would have needed a way to move the more difficult load.
He would have needed to grow a different kind of fruit.
He would have needed to ask the King to choose for him.
He would have needed to stop growing grapes on his farm.

why.He would have needed to grow a different: Choosing grapes helped him avoid that difficulty.
why.He would have needed to ask the King to: The farmer had already grown both kinds of fruit.
why.He would have needed to stop growing gra: There was no need to give up growing grapes.

activities.explanation: Watermelons were too heavy for the farmer.

activities.prompt: Explain why the farmer thanked God after the King threw the grape.
activities.answer: The farmer thanked God because he had chosen grapes to give the King. When the King threw one playfully, the farmer was grateful that his choice had made the gift possible. He also said that God is great and replied with a smile.
points: He had chosen grapes to give the King.
He was grateful for his choice.
He believed that God is great.
He replied to the King with a smile.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: The farmer knew that a watermelon was heavy and that grapes were light. Heavy and light have opposite meanings. In the Learning Opposites lesson, the teacher asked pupils for the opposite of each underlined word. The examples included a thick book, a long journey, soft cotton, and a slow tortoise. One reading sentence called the ball round, and another called the tables brown. The teacher also wanted more easy examples of opposites.
activities.prompt: In the farmer's example, if the words heavy and light are underlined, what should a student do?
options: Give the word whose meaning reverses the underlined one.
Give the word with exactly the same meaning.
Give the name of an object instead of an opposite word.
Give a word that describes the object's shape or color.

why.Give the word with exactly the same mean: This repeats rather than reverses the meaning.
why.Give the name of an object instead of an: This names an object instead of answering the question.
why.Give a word that describes the object's: This answers a different question about the object.

activities.explanation: This follows the lesson's task.

activities.context: The farmer knew that a watermelon was heavy and that grapes were light. Heavy and light have opposite meanings. In the Learning Opposites lesson, the teacher asked pupils for the opposite of each underlined word. The examples included a thick book, a long journey, soft cotton, and a slow tortoise. One reading sentence called the ball round, and another called the tables brown. The teacher also wanted more easy examples of opposites.
activities.prompt: What should the teacher do next after asking for more easy examples of opposites?
options: Invite pupils to offer more simple pairs and give each reverse word.
Invite pupils to offer more simple pairs but keep each word unchanged.
Invite pupils to offer fewer examples and give no reverse words.
Invite pupils to offer the same examples and give unrelated words.

why.Invite pupils to offer more simple pairs: This does not practise finding opposite meanings.
why.Invite pupils to offer fewer examples an: This does not provide more examples.
why.Invite pupils to offer the same examples: This repeats the examples without matching the task.

activities.explanation: This follows the teacher's request for more easy examples.

activities.prompt: Explain how heavy and light show opposite meanings.
activities.answer: Heavy describes something with more weight, while light describes something with less weight. The two meanings reverse each other, so they are opposites. The farmer's watermelon and grapes show this difference.
points: Explains what heavy means.
Explains what light means.
Shows that the meanings reverse each other.
Uses the farmer's example.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Raghuram is a tall boy. He is at the shop with the girls. The toys are on the shelf, and the book is on the wooden table. The mangoes are sweet. Their car is on the road, and they are going to the jungle. The jungle contains animals.
activities.prompt: If Raghuram and the girls reach the jungle, which sentence correctly describes what they find?
options: There are animals in the jungle.
There is animals in the jungle.
There are animal in the jungle.
There is animal in the jungle.

“Animals” is plural, so “is” does not agree.
The plural “are” needs a plural noun such as “animals.”
“Animal” does not correctly name the group in the jungle.

activities.explanation: “Animals” is plural, so the sentence needs “are.”

activities.context: Raghuram is a tall boy. He is at the shop with the girls. The toys are on the shelf, and the book is on the wooden table. The mangoes are sweet. Their car is on the road, and they are going to the jungle. The jungle contains animals.
activities.prompt: If the book is moved from the table to the shelf, which sentence correctly describes the change?
options: The book is on the shelf, and the toys are there.
The book are on the shelf, and the toys is there.
The book is on the shelf, and the toys is there.
The book are on the shelf, and the toys are there.

why.The book are on the shelf, and the toys: “Book” is singular, so “are” does not agree.
why.The book is on the shelf, and the toys i: “Toys” is plural, so it needs “are,” not “is.”
why.The book are on the shelf, and the toys: “Book” is singular, so “are” does not agree.

activities.explanation: “Book” is singular, so it takes “is.”

activities.prompt: How does the lesson show when to use “is” instead of “are”?
activities.answer: Use “is” with one boy or one thing. Raghuram is one boy, the book is one thing, and the car is one thing. Use “are” with a plural group, such as the girls, the toys, the mangoes, and the animals.
points: Uses “is” with Raghuram, the book, and the car.
Uses “are” with the girls and the toys.
Explains that singular subjects take “is.”
Explains that plural subjects take “are.”
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a shop, a mighty elephant goes to buy a handkerchief because it has a very bad cold. The elephant asks the sales girl for a hanky for an elephant. She is surprised. The shop does not have a handkerchief of that size. The elephant sneezes loudly with an “Achoo!” and shakes its mighty head. It then asks for a sheet instead.
activities.prompt: In the case, which detail best explains why the sales girl is surprised?
options: The customer wants an elephant-sized hanky.
The elephant has a very bad cold.
The elephant is buying a handkerchief at the shop.
The elephant shakes its mighty head.

A cold explains the purchase, not her surprise.
why.The elephant is buying a handkerchief at: Buying a handkerchief at the shop does not explain her surprise.
The head shake happens later and is not the reason.

activities.explanation: This connects her surprise with the unusual size needed.

activities.context: At a shop, a mighty elephant goes to buy a handkerchief because it has a very bad cold. The elephant asks the sales girl for a hanky for an elephant. She is surprised. The shop does not have a handkerchief of that size. The elephant sneezes loudly with an “Achoo!” and shakes its mighty head. It then asks for a sheet instead.
activities.prompt: If the shop had a handkerchief of the needed size, which action from the case would probably not be needed?
options: Choosing the sheet option.
Buying a handkerchief.
Making the request for a hanky.
Going to the shop to make the purchase.

The elephant would still need to buy a handkerchief.
The elephant would still need to request a hanky.
The elephant would still need to visit the shop.

activities.explanation: With a suitable handkerchief available, the elephant would not need to switch to a sheet.

activities.prompt: Explain why the sales girl was surprised when the elephant asked for a hanky for an elephant.
activities.answer: The sales girl was surprised because the elephant asked for a handkerchief of its own size. The shop did not have a handkerchief of that size, so the request could not be met with the item she had.
points: Identifies the elephant’s special size request.
Explains that the request was unusual.
Notes that the shop lacked the required size.
Connects the missing size to her surprise.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In class, the speaking task is to say aloud what food you will take while imagining that you are visiting the Big Elephant. Chandu has written the steps for preparing a salad, but he mixed up the steps. The children must put them in order. Mother cuts some fruits first. The children then check each step, add the fruit in the right sequence, and mix it before finishing with lemon and salt.
activities.prompt: Chandu's mixed-up list must be corrected. What is the best way for the children to begin?
options: Check the steps and arrange them in the proper order.
Guess the order and mix the fruit immediately.
Use only the last step and begin by squeezing the lemon.
Copy the steps down without deciding their sequence.

why.Guess the order and mix the fruit immedi: Guessing could leave the salad steps mixed up.
why.Use only the last step and begin by sque: Starting with the last step would skip earlier actions.
why.Copy the steps down without deciding the: Copying without ordering would not correct the list.

activities.explanation: Correct: checking and ordering the steps solves the problem.

activities.context: In class, the speaking task is to say aloud what food you will take while imagining that you are visiting the Big Elephant. Chandu has written the steps for preparing a salad, but he mixed up the steps. The children must put them in order. Mother cuts some fruits first. The children then check each step, add the fruit in the right sequence, and mix it before finishing with lemon and salt.
activities.prompt: The children have added the apple slices. What should they do next?
options: Add some grapes from the bunch.
Put in the papaya cubes.
Squeeze the lemon and add a pinch of salt.
Mix all the fruit together.

Papaya cubes belong before the apple slices.
why.Squeeze the lemon and add a pinch of sal: The lemon and salt are added after mixing.
The fruit must be mixed only after the grapes are added.

activities.explanation: Correct: grapes come after the apple slices.

activities.prompt: Explain why the children must put Chandu's salad steps in the correct order.
activities.answer: The steps must be in order so the salad is prepared correctly. Mother cuts the fruit first. Banana slices come first, followed by papaya cubes and apple slices. Grapes are added next, and then everything is mixed. Finally, a lemon is squeezed and a pinch of salt is added.
points: The children correct Chandu's mixed-up order.
Mother cuts the fruits before the salad is assembled.
Banana, papaya, apple, and grapes are added in sequence.
The fruit is mixed before the final lemon and salt.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

options: Toys
Fruits
Tables

activities.prompt: Match each person or action with the correct detail from the story.

took the farmer to the royal garden

King disliked watermelons.

Too heavy.

chapters.title: Madhu’s Wish
chapters.summary: In this chapter: madhu’s lunch and the special wish; madhu’s magical food; hiccups, thirst and water; let us learn.

lessons.title: Madhu’s Lunch and the Special Wish

activities.prompt: What wish did Madhu make after sharing his lunch with an old man?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Madhu’s Kind Lunch
activities.body: Madhu loved food and always wanted to eat different kinds of food and snacks. He never became tired of eating. He ate lunch at noon every day under a banyan tree. An old man came while Madhu was eating. Madhu shared his food and felt sorry. The old man was happy and offered Madhu a wish. Madhu wished for different types of food and nothing else.
keyPoints: Madhu loved different kinds of food and snacks.
Madhu shared his lunch with the old man.
Madhu wished only for different types of food.
activities.explanation: This lesson shows Madhu’s kindness and his special food wish.

activities.prompt: Madhu can make a special wish from the banyan tree. Which wish fits him best?
steps: Madhu loved food and never became tired of eating.
He wanted to try many different kinds of food.
His love of food made the food wish fit him best.
So he wished for different types of food and nothing else.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Did Madhu Love?
activities.prompt: What did Madhu love?
options: Food and snacks
Quiet games
Loud toys
Empty plates
activities.explanation: Madhu loved food and always wanted to eat different kinds of food and snacks.

activities.title: Lunch Time
activities.prompt: Madhu ate his lunch at ______ every day.
activities.hint: This happens in the middle of the day.
activities.explanation: Well done! Madhu ate his lunch at noon every day.

activities.title: A Visitor
activities.prompt: Who came to Madhu while he was eating?
options: An old man
A young boy
A shopkeeper
A teacher
activities.explanation: An old man came to Madhu while Madhu was eating his lunch.

activities.title: Match the Story
activities.prompt: Match each action with what happened next.
activities.explanation: Great matching! Madhu shared his food, and then wished for different food.

activities.title: Madhu’s Special Wish
activities.prompt: What did Madhu wish for?
options: Only one snack
A different banyan tree
A new lunch box
Different types of food
activities.explanation: Madhu wished for different types of food and nothing else.

activities.title: The Lunch Story
activities.prompt: Put these events in the correct order.
items: The old man came while Madhu was eating.
Madhu felt sorry and shared his food.
The old man was happy and offered Madhu a wish.
Madhu wished for different types of food.
activities.explanation: Excellent! The story moves from the old man’s arrival to Madhu’s food wish.

activities.prompt: Madhu shared his food with an old man. The old man became very happy. Why did he offer Madhu a wish?
options: Madhu's kindness made him want to help.
Madhu's lunch made him feel hungry.
Madhu's wish made him leave the tree.
Madhu's food made him feel afraid.

This mistake thinks sharing food made the old man hungry.
This mistake mixes up the wish with Madhu leaving.
This mistake thinks Madhu's food made the old man afraid.

activities.explanation: This is right because Madhu's kindness led to the old man's offer.

activities.prompt: Madhu saw an old man while he was eating. What did his next action show?
options: That he was kind to the old man.
That he was afraid of the old man.
That he wanted to eat alone.
That he disliked sharing food.

This mistake confuses fear with pity for the old man.
This mistake ignores that Madhu shared his food.
This mistake reverses the meaning of dislike.

activities.explanation: This is right because sharing his food showed Madhu's kindness.

activities.prompt: Madhu could wish for anything from the banyan tree. His final wish was only for different foods. What does this tell us?
options: He cared most about different kinds of food.
He cared most about meeting new people.
He cared most about eating at noon.
He cared most about keeping the tree.

This mistake assumes meeting people mattered more than food.
This mistake focuses on noon instead of his final wish.
This mistake assumes keeping the tree was his special wish.

activities.explanation: This is right because Madhu chose food and nothing else.

activities.prompt: Madhu loved trying different foods. He could wish for anything from the tree. What would he most likely wish for?
options: Different types of food for ever.
Food from only one kind of tree.
More lunch only at noon.
A different old man each day.

This mistake limits his love for food to only one kind.
This mistake focuses only on the time of lunch.
This mistake guesses people instead of his love for food.

activities.explanation: This is right because Madhu thought about asking for different food for ever.

lessons.title: Madhu’s Magical Food

activities.prompt: What delicious surprise might Madhu’s magical tree bring him next?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Madhu’s Magical Wishes
activities.body: The tree asked Madhu to think again. Madhu answered that he wanted nothing else without thinking. Madhu first asked the tree for laddoos. A basket full of laddoos appeared at once. Madhu ate them for some time, then became bored. He thought about colourful fruits, and baskets of fruit appeared immediately. He became bored with eating only fruits. The tree gave him savoury snacks, and Madhu happily started eating them.
keyPoints: Madhu first asked for laddoos.
Fruits appeared after he became bored.
Madhu happily started eating savoury snacks.
activities.explanation: Madhu asked for laddoos first and started eating savoury snacks later.

activities.prompt: Madhu ate laddoos and became bored. Why did he wish for colourful fruits?
steps: Madhu first asked for laddoos, so a full basket appeared.
He ate them for some time, so he became bored.
Boredom made him want a change, so he thought about colourful fruits.
Madhu changed his wish because the first food became boring.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did Madhu first ask the tree for?
options: laddoos
colourful fruits
potato chips
savoury snacks
activities.explanation: Madhu first asked the tree for laddoos.

activities.prompt: A basket full of laddoos appeared at once.
activities.explanation: The basket of laddoos appeared at once.

activities.prompt: Match Madhu’s thoughts with the food.
activities.explanation: Madhu first wished for laddoos, then thought about colourful fruits.

activities.prompt: Madhu thought about colourful fruits before he asked for laddoos.
activities.explanation: Madhu asked for laddoos before he thought about colourful fruits.

activities.prompt: Put the events in the correct order.
items: A basket full of laddoos appeared.
Madhu became bored after eating them.
activities.explanation: The laddoos came first, followed by boredom and then the thought of fruits.

activities.prompt: Madhu happily started eating the ______ snacks.
activities.hint: This word describes the kind of snacks the tree gave him.
activities.explanation: Madhu happily started eating the savoury snacks.

activities.prompt: Madhu said he wanted nothing else. Later, he thought about colourful fruits. What did this show?
options: His first answer was not final
He wanted no food after laddoos
He wanted the tree to leave him
He wanted only one basket forever

why.He wanted no food after laddoos: This mistake thinks his first answer must last forever.
why.He wanted the tree to leave him: This mistake confuses his answer with wanting the tree gone.
why.He wanted only one basket forever: This mistake thinks he wanted only one basket forever.

activities.explanation: This is right because his later thoughts changed his first answer.

activities.prompt: A basket of laddoos appeared at once. Baskets of fruit appeared immediately. What kind of tree was this?
options: A tree that gives magical food
A tree that gives only one basket
A tree that gives food very slowly
A tree that gives no food at all

why.A tree that gives only one basket: This mistake ignores the many baskets that appeared.
why.A tree that gives food very slowly: This mistake ignores that the food appeared at once.
why.A tree that gives no food at all: This mistake ignores the food that appeared for Madhu.

activities.explanation: This is right because food appeared immediately when Madhu wished.

activities.prompt: Madhu became bored with eating only fruits. The tree gave him savoury snacks. Why did he seem happier?
options: The savoury snacks gave him a change
The fruit baskets made him happier
The laddoo basket became full again
The tree stopped giving him food

why.The fruit baskets made him happier: This mistake ignores his boredom with the fruit baskets.
why.The laddoo basket became full again: This mistake repeats an earlier basket instead of new snacks.
why.The tree stopped giving him food: This mistake reverses what happened after the snacks arrived.

activities.explanation: This is right because he was bored with eating only fruits.

lessons.sceneAlt: A basket filled with fruits.
lessons.sceneCaption: Madhu received baskets of colourful fruits.

lessons.title: Hiccups, Thirst and Water

activities.prompt: What would you do if your hiccups would not stop?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Madhu's Search for Water
activities.body: Madhu got hiccups while eating. He wanted water, but there was food everywhere and no water. Thirst means wanting water. He thought about drinks called sharbat, kheer and badam milk. They appeared in jugs, but his hiccups did not stop. He wanted water very badly and prayed for it to appear. Later, a jug of water appeared. His hiccups stopped, and he no longer felt thirsty.
keyPoints: Madhu wanted water while food was everywhere.
The other drinks appeared, but his hiccups continued.
After water appeared, his hiccups stopped and thirst ended.
activities.explanation: This shows how Madhu learned that water is important.

activities.prompt: Madhu still has hiccups after drinking the other drinks. What should he ask for, and why?
steps: His hiccups did not stop after the other drinks, so they did not solve his problem.
He became desperate for water, so that was what he truly needed.
He prayed for water, and a jug appeared when he asked.
His hiccups stopped and his thirst ended, so water was important.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Madhu wanted ______ and looked around for it.
activities.hint: He later became desperate for it.
activities.explanation: Madhu wanted water and looked around for it.

activities.prompt: Why did Madhu pray?
options: The food to disappear and water to appear
The drinks to stay in their jugs
His hiccups to continue
More food to appear
activities.explanation: He was desperate for water and prayed for it to appear.

activities.prompt: Match each event with what happened next.
pairs: His hiccups stopped and he was no longer thirsty
activities.explanation: Each pair follows Madhu's story from wanting water to feeling better.

activities.prompt: What did the tree say Madhu had asked for?
options: Food and milk
Only food
Water and kheer
Food and water
activities.explanation: The tree said he had asked only for food, even though he wanted water.

activities.prompt: Put these events in order.
items: Sharbat, kheer and badam milk appeared in jugs
Madhu prayed for water to appear
activities.explanation: You followed the story from hiccups to water appearing and the hiccups stopping.

activities.prompt: What did Madhu say he now knew?
options: Why food was everywhere
Why the drinks appeared
How important water was
Where the jugs were
activities.explanation: Madhu said he now knew how important water was.

activities.prompt: Food was everywhere, but there was no water. Madhu looked around. How did he feel?
options: He felt very thirsty.
He felt very sleepy.
He felt very angry.
He felt very excited.

His search for water does not show sleepiness.
Nothing in his actions shows anger.
Nothing in his actions shows excitement.

activities.explanation: He searched for water, so he was thirsty.

activities.prompt: Madhu drank the other drinks, but his hiccups did not stop. What did he need?
options: plain water
more sharbat
more kheer
badam milk

why.more sharbat: More sharbat did not stop his hiccups or thirst.
why.more kheer: Kheer did not stop his hiccups, so he needed water.
why.badam milk: Badam milk did not stop his hiccups, so he needed water.

activities.explanation: Water appeared, and his hiccups and thirst ended.

activities.prompt: Madhu prayed for all the food to disappear. Why did he make this prayer?
options: He wanted water to appear for his thirst.
He wanted food to appear for his hunger.
He wanted the tree to leave him alone.
He wanted his hiccups to stay longer.

He already had food, and he prayed for it to disappear.
The prayer asked for water, not for the tree to leave.
He prayed to end his hiccups, not to keep them.

activities.explanation: His prayer asked for water to appear because he was thirsty.

activities.prompt: Madhu became desperate for water. What does desperate mean here?
options: He badly needed water.
He easily found water.
He did not need water.
He wanted more food.

Desperate does not mean finding something easily.
Desperate does not mean not needing something.
He was desperate for water, not for more food.

activities.explanation: Desperate means wanting something very badly, so he needed water.

activities.prompt: The tree said Madhu had asked only for food. Why did his search for water fail?
options: He had not asked for water.
He had asked for too much food.
He had asked for another tree.
He had asked for more hiccups.

He had already asked for food, so this is wrong.
The tree said his request was for food, not for another tree.
The tree said his request was for food, not for hiccups.

activities.explanation: He searched for water, but his request had been only for food.

lessons.title: Let Us Learn

activities.prompt: What might Madhu discover when he meets the old man?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: People and Their Actions
activities.body: This lesson shows choices and actions. Madhu enjoys foods, wants to eat everything, and shares his food with an old man. The old man gives Madhu a special gift. Pramod keeps his toys to himself. A woman saves a boy from a robber. Advait lies in bed, while Prerna wishes everyone good morning. Sam and Pratham do the same activity. Sam works in the afternoon, and Pratham works at night.
keyPoints: Madhu shares his food and receives a special gift.
Some people help, share or wish others well.
Sam and Pratham do the same activity at different times.
activities.explanation: These examples help you think about sharing, helping and other actions.

activities.prompt: Madhu wanted to eat everything. Should he still share his food?
steps: Madhu enjoyed the foods, so wanting everything was natural.
He shared his food with the old man, so his choice was sharing.
The old man gave Madhu a special gift, so sharing led to a good result.
Madhu showed that we should share even when we want everything.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Who Shared His Food?
activities.prompt: Who shared his food with the old man?
options: Madhu
Pramod
Advait
Prerna
activities.explanation: Madhu shared his food with the old man. You remembered this action well.

activities.title: Madhu's Wish
activities.prompt: Madhu wanted to eat everything.
activities.explanation: Yes, Madhu wanted to eat everything.

activities.title: Match Each Person
activities.prompt: Match each person with the correct action.
pairs: shared his food with the old man
activities.explanation: Each action in the lesson belongs to the person shown beside it.

activities.title: Prerna's Action
activities.prompt: What does Prerna always do?
options: wishes everyone good morning
always lies in bed
never says good morning
shares food with everyone
activities.explanation: Prerna always wishes everyone good morning.

activities.title: Aman's Things
activities.prompt: Which sentence about Aman is correct?
options: Aman has a pen, a pencil and an eraser.
Aman has a book, a pen and a pencil.
Aman has a bag, a book and a pen.
Aman has a cap, a bag and a book.
activities.explanation: Aman is described as having a pen, a pencil and an eraser.

activities.title: Working at Night
activities.prompt: Sam works in the afternoon, but Pratham works at ______.
activities.hint: The opposite of day.
activities.explanation: Sam works in the afternoon, but Pratham works at night.

activities.title: Compare Two People
activities.prompt: Which statement about Madhu and Pramod is true?
options: Madhu shares food; Pramod keeps toys.
Madhu keeps toys; Pramod shares food.
Madhu gives a gift; Pramod saves a boy.
Madhu saves a boy; Pramod shares toys.
activities.explanation: Madhu shared his food, while Pramod did not share his toys.

activities.prompt: Madhu wanted to eat everything. He shared his food anyway. Why might he do that?
options: He may want the old man to eat.
He may want to hide the food.
He may want to leave the food outside.
He may want to keep every food.

This mistake thinks sharing means hiding food from others.
This mistake thinks sharing means leaving food outside.
This mistake thinks sharing means keeping all the food.

activities.explanation: Sharing gives the old man food, so this reason fits.

activities.prompt: Pramod has toys, but he never shares them. What should he learn?
options: He should share with others.
He should keep all his toys.
He should share only when forced.
He should hide his toys.

This mistake thinks keeping toys helps other children.
This mistake thinks sharing must happen only after pressure.
This mistake thinks keeping toys means hiding them.

activities.explanation: Madhu's sharing shows that sharing is a good choice.

lessons.title: Let Us Listen and Retell

activities.prompt: What might happen if one boy could make his wishes come true?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Follow the Story
activities.body: Listen carefully as you follow Madhu’s story. He wants different kinds of food, and baskets of food appear. While he eats, he gets hiccups. He finds food everywhere, but there is no water. He thinks about drinks and prays. A jug of water appears, and his hiccups stop after he drinks. You will also meet Vijaya, a young girl who lives with her parents and grandparents.
keyPoints: Madhu’s wishes are followed by food and water.
Drinking water stops his hiccups.
Vijaya is young and lives with her family.
activities.explanation: Listen for each change, then retell the story in your own words.

activities.prompt: Madhu has lots of food, but no water. What should he do?
steps: Madhu gets hiccups while eating, so food is not fixing them.
There is no water, so he thinks about drinks such as sharbat.
He prays for the food to disappear because he wants water.
So, water appears, and his hiccups stop after he drinks it.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Spot the Changes
activities.body: For retelling, picture each change. Madhu wants different types of food. A basket full of laddoos appears. Baskets of fruit and savoury snacks appear too. While eating, he gets hiccups. Food is everywhere, but no water appears. He thinks about sharbat, kheer and badam milk, then prays. A jug of water appears, and his hiccups stop.
keyPoints: Food appears after Madhu thinks about it.
Madhu gets hiccups while eating.
A jug of water appears after his prayer.
activities.explanation: Use these changes as clear clues for your retelling.

activities.title: Magic Baskets
activities.prompt: What appears when Madhu thinks about fruit?
options: Baskets of fruit
A plate of laddoos
A jug of water
A basket of pens
activities.explanation: Baskets of fruit appear when Madhu thinks about them.

activities.title: Madhu’s Wish
activities.prompt: Madhu wants different types of food and nothing else.
activities.explanation: Madhu says that he wants different types of food and nothing else.

activities.title: Match the Story
activities.prompt: Match each part of Madhu’s story with its detail.
pairs: different types of food and nothing else
food to disappear and water to appear
activities.explanation: These details connect Madhu’s wishes, thoughts and actions.

activities.title: Put the Events in Order
activities.prompt: Put Madhu’s story events in the correct order.
items: Madhu wants different types of food
A basket full of laddoos appears
Madhu’s hiccups stop after he drinks
activities.explanation: This order follows Madhu’s story from the food to the water.

activities.title: What Stops the Hiccups?
activities.prompt: After Madhu drinks ______, his hiccups stop.
activities.hint: This appears in a jug.
activities.explanation: A jug of water appears, and his hiccups stop after he drinks it.

activities.title: Meet Vijaya
activities.prompt: Which sentence about Vijaya is true?
options: Vijaya is young and lives with her family.
Vijaya is old and lives with her family.
Vijaya is young and lives with her friends.
Vijaya is old and lives with her friends.
activities.explanation: Vijaya is young and lives with her father, mother, grandmother and grandfather.

activities.prompt: Madhu wants different types of food and nothing else. How does he feel about food?
options: He is excited to eat many kinds.
He is bored by every kind of food.
He wants one plain kind of food.
He wants no food for his meal.

This mistake changes Madhu's interest into dislike.
This mistake thinks different means only one kind.
This mistake ignores Madhu's clear wish for food.

activities.explanation: Wanting different foods shows that Madhu is excited to eat.

activities.prompt: Madhu thinks about fruit. Then baskets of fruit appear. What does this show?
options: His thoughts can bring food.
His thoughts can bring water.
His thoughts can stop hiccups.
His thoughts can make him tired.

No basket of water appears when Madhu thinks.
His hiccups stop after he drinks water, not after thinking.
Nothing connects his thoughts with tiredness.

activities.explanation: The fruit appears as soon as Madhu thinks about it.

activities.prompt: Madhu gets hiccups while eating, and no water is around. How can he help himself?
options: He can drink some water.
He can eat more food.
He can hide the baskets.
He can wait alone.

Eating more food does not stop his hiccups.
Hiding baskets does not give him water.
Waiting alone does not bring the water he needs.

activities.explanation: Drinking water is what stops his hiccups.

activities.prompt: Madhu prays for food to disappear and water to appear. A jug appears. What can this show?
options: His wish is answered with water.
His wish is answered with snacks.
His wish brings back all food.
His wish makes the water vanish.

He prayed for water to appear, not snacks.
He prayed for the food to disappear, not return.
The jug appears after his prayer, so it does not vanish.

activities.explanation: A jug of water appears after Madhu prays for water.

activities.prompt: Vijaya is a young girl. Her father, mother, grandmother, and grandfather live with her. How might she feel at home?
options: She may feel happy with her family.
She may feel alone with her family.
She may fear each family member.
She may dislike each family member.

Living with family does not mean she has no family.
Nothing shows that she fears each family member.
Nothing shows that she dislikes each family member.

activities.explanation: Her family is around her, so she may feel happy.

lessons.title: Fun with Words, Writing and Making

activities.prompt: Can you find secret words in your name and make a colorful mat?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Words, Reasons and Table Mats
activities.body: Carrots and Apples examples show how words can make groups. The Carrots words all begin with C, while the Apples words all begin with A. You can make similar groups using your own name. The word because shows a reason. For a table mat, children first draw fruits or vegetables on an A4 sheet. Then they use pictures and coloured paper, and make the mat at the end.
keyPoints: Words with the same beginning can make a group.
Because shows the reason behind something.
Children draw and make a table mat.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you group words, explain reasons, and make a table mat.

activities.prompt: How can I make the table mat and explain Madhu’s choices and feelings?
steps: I draw fruits or vegetables on A4 paper because drawing comes first.
I add needed pictures and coloured paper because the mat needs them.
I make the table mat because children make it at the end.
I use because when explaining Madhu because it shows causes.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Carrots Group
activities.prompt: Which letter begins every word in the Carrots example?
options: A
B
C
D
activities.explanation: Every word in the Carrots example begins with C.

activities.title: Find the Apples Group
activities.prompt: Which example uses words that all begin with A?
options: Carrots
Apples
Madhu
Table mat
activities.explanation: The Apples example uses words that all begin with A.

activities.title: Show the Reason
activities.prompt: Use ______ to show the reason or cause behind something.
activities.hint: This word often appears in answers that begin with a reason.
activities.explanation: Because shows the reason or cause behind something.

activities.title: Match the Lesson Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each example or word with its matching clue.
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an example or word with its matching idea from the lesson.

activities.title: Choose Madhu's Question
activities.prompt: Which question matches Madhu's savoury snacks after the fruits?
options: Why was Madhu happy?
Why did he want savoury snacks?
Why did he ask for water?
Why did he share his food?
activities.explanation: This question is about why Madhu wanted savoury snacks.

activities.title: Madhu's Questions
activities.prompt: Put Madhu's questions in the order they come in the lesson.
items: Why did Madhu share his food?
Why did he want savoury snacks after the fruits?
Why did he ask for water?
activities.explanation: This order follows the questions about Madhu in the lesson.

activities.prompt: The Carrots example has a group of words. Each word begins with C. What rule did the group follow?
options: The words shared the same first letter.
The words shared the same last letter.
The words all named different foods.
The words all had the same length.

The words begin with C, but they need not end with C.
Starting with C does not mean every word names food.
Starting with C does not mean all words have the same length.

activities.explanation: Every word begins with C, so the first letter is the same.

activities.prompt: A child uses their name to make an Apples word group. Their name begins with A. What rule fits the group?
options: Every word begins with the letter A.
Every word ends with the letter A.
Every word has two As inside.
Every word begins with the name.

The rule is about first letters, not last letters.
Two As inside is not the rule for the group.
The words begin with A, not with the child’s whole name.

activities.explanation: An Apples word group uses words beginning with A.

activities.prompt: A child has fruit and vegetable pictures and coloured paper. What can the child make with them?
options: A colourful table mat.
A colourful food book.
A box for food pictures.
A game for playing food.

The lesson does not say that these materials make a book.
A box is not the activity’s final product.
A game is not the activity’s final product.

activities.explanation: These materials are used to make the table mat.

activities.prompt: Explain why Madhu shared his lunch with the old man.
activities.answer: Madhu shared his lunch because he felt sorry for the old man. His kindness made the old man very happy. The old man then offered Madhu a wish from the tree. Madhu was very happy about this offer and chose to wish for different types of food.
points: Madhu felt sorry for the old man.
Madhu shared his food with him.
His kindness made the old man happy.
Madhu received the offer of a wish.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Imagine Madhu has become bored with eating only fruits. Earlier, he had eaten laddoos for some time and had answered without thinking that he wanted nothing else. Baskets of colourful fruit appeared when he thought about them. The tree then gave him samosas, kachori, potato chips and vada, and Madhu happily started eating the savoury snacks. If he now says he wants nothing else, the tree asks him to think about his wish again.
activities.prompt: Madhu is bored with eating only fruits. What should he choose to think about next?
options: The savoury foods that the tree gave him
More of the fruit that has made him bored
Nothing at all, without thinking
The same laddoos he ate earlier

why.More of the fruit that has made him bore: He had already become bored with eating only fruits.
why.Nothing at all, without thinking: He had said this before without thinking, and the tree asked him to reconsider.
why.The same laddoos he ate earlier: He had become bored after eating the laddoos for some time.

activities.explanation: The savoury foods made Madhu happy.

activities.context: Imagine Madhu has become bored with eating only fruits. Earlier, he had eaten laddoos for some time and had answered without thinking that he wanted nothing else. Baskets of colourful fruit appeared when he thought about them. The tree then gave him samosas, kachori, potato chips and vada, and Madhu happily started eating the savoury snacks. If he now says he wants nothing else, the tree asks him to think about his wish again.
activities.prompt: Madhu is still bored with eating only fruits and thinks about colourful fruits again. What should he expect from the magic?
options: He would receive fruit without waiting.
He would have to wait before the fruit appeared.
The tree would give him savoury snacks instead.
Nothing would happen because he already has fruit.

why.He would have to wait before the fruit a: There is no fact suggesting that the fruit took time to appear.
why.The tree would give him savoury snacks i: Thinking about fruit had led to fruit appearing.
why.Nothing would happen because he already: The magic had already appeared when Madhu thought about fruit.

activities.explanation: Baskets of fruit had appeared immediately before.

activities.prompt: Explain why Madhu soon became bored after getting laddoos.
activities.answer: Madhu first asked the tree for laddoos. A basket full of them appeared at once, and he ate them for some time. However, he then became bored. This shows that getting a wish quickly did not mean he would stay interested in it for long.
points: Madhu first asked for laddoos.
A full basket appeared at once.
He ate them for some time.
He later became bored.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Madhu suddenly got hiccups while he was eating. He wanted water and looked around for it, but food was everywhere and there was no water. The tree said that Madhu had asked only for food. Madhu thought about sharbat, kheer and badam milk, and the three drinks appeared in jugs. His hiccups did not stop after he drank them, so he became desperate for water.
activities.prompt: What would happen if Madhu asked for water and a jug of it appeared?
options: The hiccups would end, and Madhu would stop feeling thirsty.
The hiccups would stop, but Madhu would remain thirsty.
The hiccups would continue, but Madhu would stop feeling thirsty.
Both the hiccups and his thirst would continue.

why.The hiccups would stop, but Madhu would: Water stopped the hiccups as well as the thirst.
why.The hiccups would continue, but Madhu wo: The water did not end his continuing hiccups.
why.Both the hiccups and his thirst would co: His hiccups and thirst both ended after water.

activities.explanation: Water ended both his hiccups and his thirst.

activities.context: Madhu suddenly got hiccups while he was eating. He wanted water and looked around for it, but food was everywhere and there was no water. The tree said that Madhu had asked only for food. Madhu thought about sharbat, kheer and badam milk, and the three drinks appeared in jugs. His hiccups did not stop after he drank them, so he became desperate for water.
activities.prompt: What should Madhu ask the tree for next?
options: Water for Madhu to drink
More sharbat
More kheer
More badam milk

why.More sharbat: He had already tried sharbat, and his hiccups continued.
why.More kheer: He had already tried kheer, and his hiccups continued.
why.More badam milk: He had already tried badam milk, and his hiccups continued.

activities.explanation: Drinking water stopped his hiccups and ended his thirst.

activities.prompt: Explain why Madhu came to know how important water was.
activities.answer: Madhu had food and other drinks, yet his hiccups continued and he became desperate for water. He prayed for the food to disappear and water to appear. When water appeared and he drank it, his hiccups stopped and he no longer felt thirsty. This taught him that water was important.
points: Food and other drinks did not stop his hiccups.
Madhu became desperate for water.
He prayed for water to appear.
Drinking water stopped his hiccups and thirst.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Madhu had enjoyed a list of foods and wanted to eat everything. Even so, he shared his food with an old man. The old man then gave Madhu a special gift. Pramod was also mentioned in the lesson, but he did not share his toys with anyone. Madhu’s sharing and Pramod’s refusal made their behaviour clearly different.
activities.prompt: If Madhu had refused to share his food, what would probably have happened?
options: The old man would probably not give Madhu the special gift.
The old man would give Madhu the gift even if Madhu shared nothing.
Madhu would probably keep all the food for himself.
The old man would probably ask Pramod to share his toys.

why.The old man would give Madhu the gift ev: Nothing shows that the old man would give it without sharing.
why.Madhu would probably keep all the food f: Madhu might keep the food, but this does not follow what happened next.
why.The old man would probably ask Pramod to: Pramod’s toys were not connected with the old man’s gift.

activities.explanation: The gift was given after Madhu shared his food.

activities.context: Madhu had enjoyed a list of foods and wanted to eat everything. Even so, he shared his food with an old man. The old man then gave Madhu a special gift. Pramod was also mentioned in the lesson, but he did not share his toys with anyone. Madhu’s sharing and Pramod’s refusal made their behaviour clearly different.
activities.prompt: Why did the old man give Madhu a special gift?
options: Madhu chose generosity rather than keeping everything for himself.
Madhu was upset that the old man had eaten.
Pramod wanted the old man to have his toys.
The old man planned to ask Madhu for more food.

why.Madhu was upset that the old man had eat: Madhu was not angry; he shared willingly.
why.Pramod wanted the old man to have his to: Pramod did not share his toys with anyone.
why.The old man planned to ask Madhu for mor: The lesson does not say that the old man wanted more food.

activities.explanation: Madhu shared his food even though he wanted to eat everything.

activities.prompt: Explain why Madhu’s behaviour was different from Pramod’s behaviour.
activities.answer: Madhu enjoyed a list of foods and wanted to eat everything, yet he shared it with an old man. Pramod did not share his toys with anyone. The difference is that Madhu was willing to share what he had, while Pramod kept his toys to himself.
points: Madhu wanted to eat everything.
Madhu shared his food with the old man.
Pramod did not share his toys.
Madhu shared, while Pramod kept his toys.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Madhu wanted different types of food and nothing else. A basket of laddoos appeared at once. Thinking about fruit brought baskets of fruit, and savoury snacks appeared. Madhu got hiccups while eating. Food was everywhere, but there was no water. He thought about drinks, then prayed for the food to disappear and water to appear. A jug of water appeared, and his hiccups stopped. Vijaya, a young girl, lived with her father, mother, grandmother and grandfather.
activities.prompt: If Madhu thinks about fruit again after the savoury snacks have appeared, what is most likely to happen?
options: He will get more fruit.
A jug of water will appear.
All the food will disappear.
His hiccups will start again.

Thinking about fruit leads to fruit, not water.
The food disappeared after Madhu prayed for water.
His hiccups stopped after he drank water.

activities.explanation: Thinking about fruit has already made fruit baskets appear.

activities.context: Madhu wanted different types of food and nothing else. A basket of laddoos appeared at once. Thinking about fruit brought baskets of fruit, and savoury snacks appeared. Madhu got hiccups while eating. Food was everywhere, but there was no water. He thought about drinks, then prayed for the food to disappear and water to appear. A jug of water appeared, and his hiccups stopped. Vijaya, a young girl, lived with her father, mother, grandmother and grandfather.
activities.prompt: Madhu still has food everywhere, but there is no water. What should he do next, based on what worked in the case?
options: He should ask for the unwanted food to go and for water to come.
He should keep eating until his hiccups stop.
He should think about more savoury snacks.
He should think only about laddoos.

why.He should keep eating until his hiccups: Eating more food does not give him the water he needs.
why.He should think about more savoury snack: Thinking about snacks would bring more food, not water.
Thinking about laddoos would also bring food, not water.

activities.explanation: This repeats the prayer that led to a jug of water appearing.

activities.prompt: How does Madhu get water, and what happens to his hiccups?
activities.answer: Madhu first notices that food is everywhere, but there is no water. He thinks about sharbat, kheer and badam milk. He then prays for the food to disappear and for water to appear. A jug of water appears. Madhu drinks the water, and his hiccups stop.
points: Madhu notices that there is no water.
He thinks about sharbat, kheer and badam milk.
He prays for the food to disappear and water to appear.
He drinks the water, and his hiccups stop.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain how the word “because” can be used to explain Madhu’s actions and feelings.
activities.answer: “Because” joins Madhu’s action to its reason. For example, the class can write, “Madhu shared his food because …” The missing part must give the cause behind sharing. The same pattern can explain why he was happy, wanted savoury snacks, or asked for water.
points: Uses “because” to connect an action with a reason.
Gives the sentence pattern “Madhu … because …”.
Explains that the missing words give the cause.
Shows that the pattern can explain different situations.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Madhu’s Wish

activities.prompt: What did Madhu do when the old man came?
options: Kept all his food for himself.
Shared his food with him.
Asked the old man for food.
Left the banyan tree.
activities.explanation: Madhu felt sorry for the old man and shared his food.

activities.prompt: Madhu ate his lunch at noon under a banyan tree.
activities.explanation: Madhu ate his lunch at noon under the banyan tree.

activities.prompt: Madhu first asked the tree for savoury snacks.
activities.explanation: Madhu first asked for laddoos. Savoury snacks came later.

activities.prompt: Match each choice to what Madhu thought about or received.
pairs: Samosas, kachori, potato chips and vada
activities.explanation: Each choice matches a food, drink or event in Madhu’s story.

activities.prompt: What did Madhu want when he got hiccups?
options: More food
A new basket
Water
Another tree
activities.explanation: Madhu wanted water and looked around for it.

activities.prompt: The old man was unhappy about Madhu’s kindness.
activities.explanation: The old man was very happy because Madhu shared his food.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: The old man offered a wish
activities.explanation: Madhu shared his food before receiving the wish and later asking for water.

activities.prompt: Match each name or example with its description from the lesson.
pairs: Lives with her father, mother, grandmother and grandfather
Has a pen, pencil and eraser
activities.explanation: Each description matches the correct name or word-group example.

activities.prompt: The word ______ shows the reason or cause behind something.
activities.hint: Use this word to explain why something happened.
activities.explanation: The word because introduces the reason or cause behind something.

chapters.title: The Sky
chapters.summary: In this chapter: looking at the picture; the sun and the night poem; thinking about the sun and the sky; playing the i spy game.

lessons.title: Looking at the picture

activities.prompt: What do you notice first in this street picture?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A street picture
activities.body: Take a careful look at the street picture. It shows things on both sides of the street. You can see two dustbins: one is blue, and the other is green. A man wears dark glasses and holds a white stick. Boys play with a toy. The picture also includes some bullock-carts and different animals.
keyPoints: Things appear on both sides of the street.
One dustbin is blue, and the other is green.
The man wears dark glasses and holds a white stick.
activities.explanation: Look closely and notice the colours, people and objects.

activities.prompt: A child wants to check the dustbins in the picture. How can their colours help?
steps: Look at the dustbins because their colours help you count them.
You find one blue dustbin, so one of the bins is blue.
You find one green dustbin, so the other bin is green.
The picture has two dustbins: one blue and one green.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Search the picture
activities.body: Search for the people and objects in the street picture. The man wears dark glasses and holds a white stick. The boys are playing with a toy. Look for the two dustbins. Their colours help you tell them apart: one is blue and one is green. The picture also has bullock-carts and different animals.
keyPoints: The man wears dark glasses.
The boys play with a toy.
The picture includes bullock-carts and different animals.
activities.explanation: Colours and actions help you find important details.

activities.title: Find the green dustbin
activities.prompt: Which dustbin is green?
options: blue
green
white
dark
activities.explanation: Great spotting! One dustbin is blue, and the other is green.

activities.prompt: The man is holding a white stick.
activities.explanation: Yes! The picture shows the man holding a white stick.

activities.title: The other dustbin
activities.prompt: One dustbin is blue. The other dustbin is ______.
activities.hint: Think of the second dustbin's colour.
activities.explanation: Well done! The blue dustbin has a green partner.

activities.title: Picture clues
activities.prompt: Match each group to what the picture shows.
activities.explanation: Excellent! Each clue helps you recognise part of the picture.

activities.title: Find the man's clues
activities.prompt: Which clues describe the man correctly?
options: A toy and bullock-carts
Blue and green dustbins
Different animals and a street
Dark glasses and a white stick
activities.explanation: That's right! The man wears dark glasses and holds a white stick.

activities.prompt: The picture shows only one kind of animal.
activities.explanation: Good try! The picture has different animals, not just one kind.

activities.prompt: The boys are playing with a toy. How do they most likely feel about it?
options: They feel interested and happy.
They feel bored and unhappy.
They feel afraid and nervous.
They feel angry and cross.

Boredom does not fit the boys playing with something.
Fear does not fit the boys playing with something.
Anger does not fit the boys playing with something.

activities.explanation: Playing with the toy supports this feeling.

activities.prompt: The picture shows things on both sides of the street. Why might a child look at both sides?
options: To see all the things shown there.
To find only one person there.
To hear sounds from far away.
To count every window there.

The child is looking for one person, not everything.
The child cannot hear sounds in a picture.
The child is noticing things, not counting windows.

activities.explanation: Looking at both sides shows all the things in the picture.

activities.prompt: A child says, “One bin is blue, and one bin is green.” What does this line imply?
options: The picture has two dustbins.
The picture has one blue cart.
The street has two boys.
The man has two sticks.

The line tells us about bins, not a blue cart.
The line tells us about bins, not two boys.
The line tells us about bins, not two sticks.

activities.explanation: The words “one” and “one” show that there are two bins.

activities.prompt: One child says, “The two dustbins have the same colour.” What can another child check?
options: Whether one is blue and one is green.
Whether one is a bin and one is a cart.
Whether one has a toy and one has a stick.
Whether one is a man and one is a boy.

Both objects are dustbins, not a bin and a cart.
why.Whether one has a toy and one has a stic: The toy and stick belong to others, not both bins.
The man and boy are people, not dustbins.

activities.explanation: The blue and green colours show that the dustbins differ.
