lessons.title: The sun and the night poem

activities.prompt: Where does the sun go after the bright day ends?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The sun and the night
activities.body: The poem says that the sun shines brightly all day. It wonders where the sun goes at night. The sun sinks behind a distant hill, and the world becomes dark and still. The speaker goes to bed and sleeps. Sleep continues until the day begins to peep. In the morning, the speaker opens their eyes and sees the sun shining down on them.
keyPoints: The sun shines brightly all day.
The sun sinks behind a distant hill at night.
The speaker wakes and sees the sun in the morning.
activities.explanation: This card helps you follow the poem from bright day to quiet night and morning.

activities.prompt: Where does the sun go when night comes, and what happens next?
steps: The bright day ends, so the speaker wonders where the sun goes.
The sun sinks behind a distant hill, so darkness and stillness follow.
The world is dark and still, so the speaker goes to bed and sleeps.
Sleep lasts until the day peeps in, when the speaker sees sunlight.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does the poem say the sun does all day?
options: It shines brightly.
It sleeps quietly.
It sinks behind a hill.
It disappears completely.
activities.explanation: The poem says that the sun shines brightly all day. Good listening!

activities.prompt: At night, the sun sinks behind a ______ hill.
activities.hint: This word describes a hill that is far away.
activities.explanation: The poem describes the sun sinking behind a distant hill.

activities.prompt: The sun sinks behind a distant hill.
activities.explanation: Yes, this is one clear picture in the poem.

activities.prompt: What happens after the sun sinks behind the distant hill?
options: The world becomes bright.
The world becomes dark and still.
The speaker starts reading.
The hills begin to sing.
activities.explanation: The world becomes dark and still when night comes.

activities.prompt: Match each part of the poem with its picture.
pairs: the new day starts to appear
activities.explanation: These pairs show the poem's journey from bedtime to a sunny morning.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happen in the poem.
items: The speaker goes to bed and sleeps.
Sleep continues until the day begins to peep.
The speaker opens their eyes in the morning.
The speaker sees the sun shining down on them.
activities.explanation: The order moves from bedtime, through sleep, to waking and seeing the sun.

activities.prompt: A child watches the sun go down and asks a question. What does this show?
options: The child is wondering about it.
The child is counting the hours.
The child is planning a game.
The child is hiding from it.

Asking about the sun does not mean counting time.
The question is about the sun, not a game.
The child asks, so hiding is not suggested.

activities.explanation: Wondering means wanting to know what happened.

activities.prompt: The bright day ends. The world becomes dark and still. What does this suggest?
options: This is a quiet time for sleep.
This is a noisy time for play.
This is when the sun returns.
This is when the speaker wakes.

Noisy play does not fit the still world.
The sun returns in the morning, not at night.
The speaker wakes after sleeping, not when night begins.

activities.explanation: Darkness and stillness lead the speaker to bed.

activities.prompt: The sun sinks behind a far hill. What does “distant” show?
options: The hill is far from us.
The hill is close to us.
The hill is much too small.
The hill is far from the sun.

The child reverses the meaning of distant.
The child thinks distant describes size.
The child attaches distant to the sun, not the hill.

activities.explanation: “Distant” shows that the hill is far away.

activities.prompt: The sleep continues until the day begins to peep. What does “peep” mean here?
options: A little light appears.
A little bird appears.
A person starts speaking.
The wind starts blowing.

Here, peep points to daylight, not an animal.
The child treats the day as a person.
The child links peep to wind, not to daylight.

activities.explanation: “Peep” means a small sign of daylight appears.

activities.prompt: The speaker opens their eyes. Sunlight shines down on them. What do they now know?
options: Morning is here with bright daylight.
Night is here with the sun still gone.
The sun is still behind the hill.
The speaker is still fast asleep.

The child reverses the time because the sun has gone down.
The child ignores the sunlight shining on the speaker.
The speaker has opened their eyes, so they are awake.

activities.explanation: Opening their eyes to sunlight shows that morning has come.

activities.prompt: The sun sinks behind a distant hill. The world becomes dark and still. How might the speaker feel?
options: sleepy and calm
noisy and excited
cross and worried
brave and playful

why.noisy and excited: The world is still, so noisy excitement does not fit.
why.cross and worried: Nothing in the poem shows worry or cross feelings.
why.brave and playful: Play is not suggested when the world becomes dark and still.

activities.explanation: The world is still, and the speaker soon goes to bed.

lessons.title: Thinking about the Sun and the sky

activities.prompt: Where does the sun go after the day ends?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sun and Sky
activities.body: Think about the Sun and the sky as you read this chapter. It asks where the sun goes after the day ends. It also asks which choice needs the sun and why. The poem talks about the sun in the sky. You will think about other sky sights, sunrise and sunset colours, and the night sky.
keyPoints: Where the sun goes after the day ends
Which choice needs the sun and why
Sun, sky, sunrise, sunset and night
activities.explanation: These questions help you explore the sun, the sky and changing light.

activities.prompt: A child wonders what a day without the sun would be like.
steps: The child first imagines a day without the sun, because the chapter asks for this.
The child then thinks about how that day would be, because the chapter asks about it.
The child finally talks about that day, because the chapter asks us to talk.
So we imagine the day first, then talk about how it would be.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does the chapter ask about the sun after the day ends?
options: Which choice needs it
How we feel in the morning
Where the sun goes
What we can see at night
activities.explanation: The chapter asks where the sun goes after the day ends.

activities.prompt: The poem talks about the sun in the ______.
activities.hint: Choose the place named in the poem.
activities.explanation: The poem talks about the sun in the sky.

activities.prompt: What does the chapter ask about a choice?
options: What else we can see in the sky
What we can see in the sky at night
Which choice needs the sun and why
How we feel when we open our eyes
activities.explanation: The chapter asks which choice needs the sun and asks why.

activities.prompt: What does the chapter ask about the sky at night?
options: Where the sun goes after day
How we feel in the morning
Colours at sunrise and sunset
What we can see at night
activities.explanation: The chapter asks what we can see in the sky at night.

activities.prompt: Match each clue to the idea the chapter asks about.
pairs: Which choice needs the sun and why
How we feel when we open our eyes
activities.explanation: Each pair links a clue to an idea in the chapter.

activities.prompt: Which pair contains two ideas about seeing things in the sky?
options: Where the sun goes after day ends; how we feel when we open our eyes
Things we can see in the sky; things we can see at night
Which choice needs the sun and why; the colours during sunrise and sunset
activities.explanation: Both correct ideas ask what we can see in the sky.

activities.prompt: A child opens their eyes in the morning and smiles. How might the child feel?
options: The child feels happy.
The child feels cross.
The child feels afraid.
The child feels bored.

Anger does not fit the child's smiling face.
Fear does not fit the child's smiling face.
Boredom is not the strongest feeling suggested by the smile.

activities.explanation: A smile shows that the child feels happy.

activities.prompt: The poem says, “The sun is in the sky.” A child points up. What does this show?
options: The child links the sun and sky.
The child links the rain and wind.
The child links the night and sleep.
The child links the home and garden.

This choice connects rain and wind, but the clue names neither.
This choice connects night and sleep, but the clue names neither.
This choice connects home and garden, but the clue names neither.

activities.explanation: The poem connects the sun with the sky, and the child points up.

activities.prompt: A child has already noticed the sun in the sky. What should the child explore next?
options: Look for other things in the sky.
Ask where the sun goes after day.
Study the colours seen at sunrise.
Think about how morning feels.

This choice follows the sun-after-day question instead.
This choice focuses on sunrise colours instead of other sky sights.
This choice focuses on morning feelings instead of other sky sights.

activities.explanation: Looking for other things follows the question about what else is in the sky.

activities.prompt: A child pictures a day without the sun. What should the child do next?
options: Discuss what that day would be like.
Ask where the sun goes after day.
Explore what the night sky shows.
Think about how morning feels.

This jumps to a different sun question before the day is discussed.
This focuses on night sights instead of the imagined day.
This focuses on morning feelings instead of the imagined day.

activities.explanation: After imagining the day, the next step is talking about how it would be.

lessons.title: Playing the I Spy game

activities.prompt: How can you make everyone guess what you’re looking at?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How to play I Spy
activities.body: In I Spy, players take turns to be Spies. Each Spy secretly chooses something in the room. The Spy gives everyone a clue, beginning with a special kind of clue. A clue might say something is blue. Everyone looks around for the chosen thing. A tricky guess may need more clues. The child with the correct guess becomes the new Spy.
keyPoints: The Spy chooses something in the room.
Everyone searches using clues.
The child with the correct guess becomes the new Spy.
activities.explanation: Keep the chosen thing secret and use clues to help everyone find it.

activities.prompt: In I Spy, a child sees a blue pen but feels unsure.
steps: The pen may fit, because a clue can say something is blue.
The child looks around, because everyone searches for the chosen thing.
The child asks for another clue, because the guess may be tricky.
The child should guess, because a correct guesser becomes the new Spy.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where does the Spy secretly choose something?
options: Inside a picture
On a cloud
In the room
Under the sea
activities.explanation: The Spy secretly chooses something that is in the room.

activities.prompt: The Spy gives everyone a ______.
activities.hint: It helps everyone find the chosen thing.
activities.explanation: The Spy gives a clue so that everyone can look for the chosen thing.

activities.prompt: Match each word to the correct part of I Spy.
pairs: Players take turns to be Spies
The child becomes the new Spy
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an important rule or clue in I Spy.

activities.prompt: A guess is tricky. What may it need?
options: More clues
A new room
A secret hiding place
A different game
activities.explanation: A tricky guess may need more clues from the Spy.

activities.prompt: Put the I Spy steps in order.
items: The Spy gives everyone a clue
The child with the correct guess becomes the new Spy
activities.explanation: First, the Spy chooses something and gives a clue. Then everyone looks and guesses.

activities.prompt: Who becomes the new Spy after a correct guess?
options: The player who gave no clues
The child with the correct guess
The player who looked away
The first player in the game
activities.explanation: Great work! The child with the correct guess becomes the new Spy.

activities.prompt: A child says, “I need another clue.” What does this most likely mean?
options: The guess may be tricky and need more help.
The child wants everyone to take a turn.
The child wants to change the chosen thing.
The child wants the game to end now.

This mistake confuses asking for help with taking a turn.
why.The child wants to change the chosen thi: This mistake confuses asking for help with changing the chosen thing.
This mistake confuses asking for help with ending the game.

activities.explanation: This is right because a tricky guess may need more clues.

activities.prompt: A child guesses the shirt. What happens to that child next?
options: The child becomes the Spy and chooses something.
The child becomes a helper and gives clues.
The child becomes a watcher and looks around.
The child becomes a player and leaves the game.

why.The child becomes a helper and gives clu: This mistake confuses becoming the Spy with becoming a helper.
why.The child becomes a watcher and looks ar: This mistake confuses choosing a new thing with only searching.
why.The child becomes a player and leaves th: This mistake confuses changing players with leaving the game.

activities.explanation: This is right because the child with the correct guess becomes the new Spy.

activities.prompt: After a blue clue, a child feels unsure. Why?
options: The chosen thing may still be hard to find.
The child may want a new room.
The child may expect the game to end.
The child may think the clue is wrong.

This mistake confuses feeling unsure with wanting a new place.
This mistake confuses needing more clues with ending the game.
This mistake confuses a hard search with thinking the clue is wrong.

activities.explanation: This is right because the blue clue may not make the chosen thing easy to find.

activities.prompt: After a correct guess, another child gives clues. What does this show?
options: The children are taking turns as Spies.
The children are sharing the same Spy role.
The children are looking for different things.
The children are giving clues outside the room.

why.The children are sharing the same Spy ro: This mistake confuses taking turns with sharing one Spy role.
why.The children are looking for different t: This mistake confuses changing players with searching for different things.
why.The children are giving clues outside th: This mistake confuses giving clues with leaving the room.

activities.explanation: This is right because the players take turns to be Spies.

lessons.title: Practising new sounds

activities.prompt: Can you spot the secret sounds hiding in words about the sky?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: New sounds in the sky
activities.body: Read the sentence about spying on stars in the sky. Say all twelve sky and sound words aloud. The word spy begins with sp, stars begins with st, and sky begins with sk. These three sounds are called blends. Practise the sounds sp, st and sk, and take time to get used to them.
keyPoints: spy begins with sp
stars begins with st
sky begins with sk
activities.explanation: These words help you practise three new sounds.

activities.prompt: A child mixes up new sounds. How can the child practise better?
steps: Say spy first, because its first sound is sp.
Say stars next, because its first sound is st.
Say sky last, because its first sound is sk.
Take time to say all three aloud, because practice helps with blends.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which sound do you hear at the start of spy?
options: sp
st
sk
activities.explanation: The word spy begins with the sound sp.

activities.prompt: The word stars begins with the sound st.
activities.explanation: Yes, stars begins with the sound st.

activities.prompt: The word stars begins with the sound ______.
activities.hint: Say the first sound in stars.
activities.explanation: The first sound in stars is st.

activities.prompt: Which sound begins the word sky?
options: sp
st
sk
activities.explanation: The word sky begins with the sound sk.

activities.prompt: Match each word with its beginning sound.
activities.explanation: Spy begins with sp, stars begins with st, and sky begins with sk.

activities.prompt: Put these learning steps in order.
items: Read the sentence about spying on stars in the sky.
Say all the listed words aloud.
Practise the sounds sp, st and sk.
Take time to get used to the sounds.
activities.explanation: Read, say the words, practise the sounds, and take time to get used to them.

activities.prompt: The word spy begins with the sound sk.
activities.explanation: No, spy begins with sp. The sound sk begins the word sky.

activities.prompt: Which activity helps you get used to the new sounds?
options: Take time to practise them.
Practise only one sound.
Say only one word aloud.
Practise no sounds.
activities.explanation: Take time to practise the sounds sp, st and sk.

activities.prompt: A child watches stars. Which sound starts the action word?
options: sp
st
sk
sl

why.st: Stars names what is watched, not the action.
why.sk: Sky names the place, not the action.
why.sl: Sl is not one of the listed blend sounds.

activities.explanation: Spy means watching and begins with sp.

activities.prompt: The child says, “The ___ are in the sky.” Which word fits?
options: stars
spy
sky
blends

why.spy: Spy names the one watching, not what is in the sky.
why.sky: Sky names the place, not what is inside it.
why.blends: Blends names the sounds, not what is in the sky.

activities.explanation: Stars fits because stars are in the sky.

lessons.title: Finding sky words and making new words

activities.prompt: What words can we find in the sky and turn into new words?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sky words and new words
activities.body: Circle words found in the sky. The word list starts with Stars and Storm. Store, Stain and Sun are also in the first group. Bicycle and Moon appear in the next group, with Rain and Clouds. The last group has Flowers, Rainbow, Monkeys, Computer and Shoes. Next, add Sun to words to make new words. Write the new words in the given spaces. Sunlight is a completed example.
keyPoints: Words are grouped in a word list.
The first activity circles words found in the sky.
Adding Sun makes new words for the given spaces.
activities.explanation: Great start—look for where each word sits in the list.

activities.prompt: A child has a page of word groups and wonders which words to circle and how to make new words.
steps: First, check every group carefully, because the activity asks for words found in the sky.
Judge each word by meaning, because Store and Stain share a group with Stars and Storm.
Next, add Sun to the base words, because this activity aims to make new words.
Then, write each new word in its given space, using Sunlight as the completed example.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which word begins the word list?
options: Stars
Bicycle
Flowers
Computer
activities.explanation: Good choice! The word list begins with Stars and Storm.

activities.prompt: Store and Stain are in the first group.
activities.explanation: Yes! Store and Stain are also in the first group.

activities.prompt: Match each word to its group in the list.
activities.explanation: Excellent matching! Stars starts the list, Bicycle comes next, and Flowers is in the last group.

activities.prompt: The last group has Bicycle and Moon.
activities.explanation: Not quite. Bicycle and Moon appear in the next group.

activities.prompt: What is the aim of adding Sun to words?
options: make new words
find the sky
count the groups
circle shoes
activities.explanation: Yes! Adding Sun to words helps us make new words.

activities.prompt: We must write the new words in the given ______.
activities.hint: Think about where each new word should go.
activities.explanation: You got it! Each new word must be written in the given spaces.

activities.prompt: A child sees Stars and Store in the same group. Why should the child circle only Stars?
options: Stars is found in the sky.
Store is found in the sky.
Both words are found in the sky.
Grouping makes both words sky words.

This reverses which word fits the sky.
This assumes every word in the group belongs in the sky.
This assumes the group decides which words are sky words.

activities.explanation: Stars is found in the sky, so it matches the activity.

activities.prompt: The sky is dark. I can see many bright dots. Which word fits the line?
options: Stars
Store
Storm
Stain

why.Store: Store is a place rather than something seen in the sky.
why.Storm: Storm is sky weather, but it does not mean the bright dots.
why.Stain: Stain means a mark rather than the bright dots.

activities.explanation: Bright dots in a dark sky point to Stars.

activities.prompt: A child wants to make new words from base words. What should happen next?
options: Add Sun to the base word.
Add Stars to the base word.
Add Moon to the base word.
Add Rain to the base word.

This uses another sky word instead of the required Sun.
This uses another sky word instead of the required Sun.
This uses another sky word instead of the required Sun.

activities.explanation: The activity says to add Sun to the base words.

activities.prompt: The example Sunlight appears after several base words. How was it made?
options: Sun was added to light.
Sun was added to stars.
Sun was added to rain.
Sun was added to shoes.

Stars is not the part that joins Sun in Sunlight.
Rain is not the part that joins Sun in Sunlight.
Shoes is not the part that joins Sun in Sunlight.

activities.explanation: Sunlight is made by adding Sun to light.

activities.prompt: Why does the page give spaces for the new words?
options: To show each completed new word.
To hide all the base words.
To mark words found in the sky.
To hold the last word group.

This mistakes the answer spaces for places to hide words.
This mixes up two different activities.
This mistakes the answer spaces for a place for word groups.

activities.explanation: The spaces show where each completed new word belongs.

activities.prompt: One example, Sunlight, is already completed. How can the child fill the other spaces?
options: Use the same add-Sun rule.
Choose from the last word group.
Choose from the first word group.
Follow the order of the groups.

This confuses the word groups with the new-word task.
This confuses the word groups with the new-word task.
This assumes the group order explains how to fill the spaces.

activities.explanation: The completed example shows how to make the other new words.

activities.context: The picture shows a street with things on both sides of it. Two dustbins are visible, one blue and the other green. A man is wearing dark glasses and holding a white stick. The boys are playing with a toy. The picture also includes some bullock-carts and different animals.
activities.prompt: If one of the two dustbins is taken away, which statement would be true?
options: One dustbin would still be on the street.
Both dustbins would still be on the street.
No dustbin would be on the street.
Three dustbins would be on the street.

why.Both dustbins would still be on the stre: Taking away one does not leave both.
At least one dustbin would remain.
Removing a dustbin does not create another.

activities.explanation: Taking away one leaves one behind.

activities.context: The picture shows a street with things on both sides of it. Two dustbins are visible, one blue and the other green. A man is wearing dark glasses and holding a white stick. The boys are playing with a toy. The picture also includes some bullock-carts and different animals.
activities.prompt: If the boys' toy is exchanged for a different toy, what would remain true?
options: The boys' play would still involve a toy.
The boys' play would involve a dustbin.
The boys' play would involve a bullock-cart.
The boys' play would involve an animal.

A dustbin is not the boys' toy.
why.The boys' play would involve a bullock-c: A bullock-cart is separate from their play.
An animal is separate from their toy.

activities.explanation: They are still playing with a toy.

activities.prompt: Explain how the picture shows that it contains more than just people.
activities.answer: The picture does not show only people. It also includes some bullock-carts and different animals. The boys are playing with a toy, while a man wears dark glasses and holds a white stick.
points: Mentions the bullock-carts.
Mentions the different animals.
Explains that the boys are playing with a toy.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: The sun shines brightly all day. The speaker wonders where it goes at night. It sinks behind a distant hill, and the world becomes dark and still. The speaker goes to bed and sleeps. The sleep continues until the day begins to peep. In the morning, the speaker opens their eyes and sees the sun shining down on them.
activities.prompt: In the case, what would happen if the sun did not sink behind the distant hill?
options: The world might stay bright instead of becoming dark.
The speaker would sleep all through the morning.
The day would never begin to peep.
The sun would shine down on the speaker at night.

why.The speaker would sleep all through the: Incorrect: sleeping through the morning is not supported by the poem.
Incorrect: the day still begins after the speaker sleeps.
why.The sun would shine down on the speaker: Incorrect: the sun does not shine down at night in the poem.

activities.explanation: Correct: without the sun sinking behind the hill, darkness might not follow.

activities.context: The sun shines brightly all day. The speaker wonders where it goes at night. It sinks behind a distant hill, and the world becomes dark and still. The speaker goes to bed and sleeps. The sleep continues until the day begins to peep. In the morning, the speaker opens their eyes and sees the sun shining down on them.
activities.prompt: If the speaker woke before the day began to peep, what would they most likely see?
options: A dark world without sunlight.
The sun shining down on them.
A bright morning with sunlight.
The distant hill in bright light.

Incorrect: the sun shines down after morning begins.
Incorrect: bright sunlight belongs to the daytime.
Incorrect: bright light would not be present before morning.

activities.explanation: Correct: the world is still dark before day begins to peep.

activities.prompt: How does the poem show the difference between day and night?
activities.answer: During the day, the sun shines brightly. At night, the speaker wonders where the sun goes, and it sinks behind a distant hill. The world becomes dark and still, and the speaker sleeps until the day begins to peep and sunlight returns.
points: The sun shines brightly during the day.
The sun sinks behind a distant hill at night.
The world becomes dark and still.
The speaker sleeps until day begins.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain how the poem helps the child think about the sun and the sky.
activities.answer: The poem connects the sun with the sky, so it gives the child an idea to think about. This supports the question about where the sun goes after the day ends. It also makes the child think about the sky during the day and gives ideas for the talk.
points: Connects the sun with the sky.
Supports the question about the sun after the day ends.
Links the poem to thinking about the sky.
Gives ideas for the discussion.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At the fun game called “I Spy”, the players take turns to be Spies. A Spy secretly chooses something in the room. The Spy begins with a special clue and tells everyone that something is blue. Everyone looks around for the thing, which might be a pen, a chair or a shirt. A tricky guess may need more clues. The child with the correct guess becomes the new Spy, and the game continues until everyone has had a turn.
activities.prompt: What should a child do after hearing the clue that something is blue?
options: Look around for a blue thing and make a guess.
Look around for a thing that is not blue and guess it.
Secretly choose a different thing in the room.
Guess that the thing must be a chair.

why.Look around for a thing that is not blue: Option 2: This guess goes against the clue.
why.Secretly choose a different thing in the: Option 3: Only the Spy secretly chooses the thing.
Option 4: The clue does not name a chair.

activities.explanation: Option 1: The blue clue guides the child's search.

activities.context: At the fun game called “I Spy”, the players take turns to be Spies. A Spy secretly chooses something in the room. The Spy begins with a special clue and tells everyone that something is blue. Everyone looks around for the thing, which might be a pen, a chair or a shirt. A tricky guess may need more clues. The child with the correct guess becomes the new Spy, and the game continues until everyone has had a turn.
activities.prompt: What should a player do if a guess is tricky and more help is needed?
options: Ask the Spy for more clues.
Secretly choose a different thing in the room.
Give everyone a blue clue without being the Spy.
Stop the game until the next turn.

why.Secretly choose a different thing in the: Option 2: The player is not the one choosing secretly.
why.Give everyone a blue clue without being: Option 3: The Spy gives the clues.
Option 4: A tricky guess does not stop the game.

activities.explanation: Option 1: More clues can help with a tricky guess.

activities.prompt: Explain how the Spy starts and guides the I Spy game.
activities.answer: The Spy secretly chooses something in the room, then begins with a special clue. A clue might tell everyone that the thing is blue. The players look around and make guesses. If a guess is tricky, the Spy can give more clues until someone makes the correct guess.
points: The Spy chooses something secretly.
The first clue is special.
Players search and make guesses.
More clues may be needed.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain why saying the listed words aloud helps the learner get used to the sounds.
activities.answer: Saying spy, stars and sky aloud helps the learner hear the sounds sp, st and sk. Repeating all the listed words and taking time helps the learner become more used to these blends. The words all give practice with the three sounds.
points: Names spy, stars and sky.
Identifies the sounds sp, st and sk.
Explains the purpose of saying the words aloud.
Mentions taking time to get used to the blends.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A learner began the “Finding sky words and making new words” lesson. In the first activity, the learner had to circle words found in the sky. One group began with Stars and Storm and also included Store, Stain and Sun. Another group showed Bicycle, Moon, Rain and Clouds. The learner then moved to the next activity, which added Sun to words to make new words. The completed example, Sunlight, appeared after several base words.
activities.prompt: When the learner reaches the first group, what should guide which words to circle?
options: Check the meaning and circle only words connected with the sky.
Circle every word because all the words belong to one group.
Choose words that begin with the same letters as the first two words.
Add Sun to every word and write the results in the spaces.

why.Circle every word because all the words: Words can belong to the same group without all being sky words.
why.Choose words that begin with the same le: Matching beginning letters does not decide whether a word is found in the sky.
why.Add Sun to every word and write the resu: Adding Sun belongs to the next activity, not the circling activity.

activities.explanation: This follows the rule that the words found in the sky must be circled.

activities.context: A learner began the “Finding sky words and making new words” lesson. In the first activity, the learner had to circle words found in the sky. One group began with Stars and Storm and also included Store, Stain and Sun. Another group showed Bicycle, Moon, Rain and Clouds. The learner then moved to the next activity, which added Sun to words to make new words. The completed example, Sunlight, appeared after several base words.
activities.prompt: After studying the completed example, what should the learner do with the remaining base words?
options: Join Sun to each base word in the same way, then record each new word in its space.
Write only the unchanged base words in the given spaces.
Add Sun to the first base word and leave the rest unchanged.
Write the base words in reverse order without adding anything.

why.Write only the unchanged base words in t: The task requires new words, not unchanged base words.
why.Add Sun to the first base word and leave: Every base word must be used to make a new word.
why.Write the base words in reverse order wi: The new words must follow the pattern shown by the example.

activities.explanation: This follows the completed example and makes new words.

activities.context: A learner began the “Finding sky words and making new words” lesson. In the first activity, the learner had to circle words found in the sky. One group began with Stars and Storm and also included Store, Stain and Sun. Another group showed Bicycle, Moon, Rain and Clouds. The learner then moved to the next activity, which added Sun to words to make new words. The completed example, Sunlight, appeared after several base words.
activities.prompt: Why should the learner accept a word formed by joining Sun to a base word?
options: Because it follows the activity's rule of adding Sun to make a new word, just as the completed model does.
Because every word in the first group must be changed.
Because the new word belongs in the first group's circle.
Because joining letters always creates another word found in the sky.

why.Because every word in the first group mu: The first group is used for the sky-word activity, not for adding Sun.
why.Because the new word belongs in the firs: A word made with Sun belongs in the next activity's spaces.
why.Because joining letters always creates a: Making a new word does not automatically make it a sky word.

activities.explanation: This gives the required reason under the word-making rule.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between the two activities and what the learner must do with the answers.
activities.answer: The circling task checks which words can be found in the sky. The next task uses Sun with base words to make new words. When a new word is made, it must be written in the given space. The completed Sunlight example shows the pattern the learner should follow.
points: Explains that the first task is about circling sky words
Explains that the second task adds Sun to make new words
Mentions writing each new word in the given space
Uses Sunlight as the completed model
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

chapters.title: Chanda Mama Counts the Stars
chapters.summary: In this chapter: chanda mama begins to count; chanda mama gets help; here and there; sorting things we can count.

lessons.title: Chanda Mama Begins to Count

activities.prompt: What will Chanda Mama count when the morning sun peeks out?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Chanda Mama Counts the Stars
activities.body: Chanda Mama is sometimes round, like a circle. He starts counting the stars and counts from one to ten. He counts bigger numbers too. Later, he yawns and counts up to nine hundred and ninety-nine. While counting, he falls asleep. The Sun peeks out from behind the clouds, and it is morning. Chanda Mama begins counting again but cannot remember where he stopped.
keyPoints: Chanda Mama sometimes looks round.
He counts stars from one to ten.
He falls asleep and forgets his stopping point.
activities.explanation: You followed Chanda Mama's counting from stars to morning.

activities.prompt: Why does Chanda Mama forget where he stopped counting?
steps: He counts from one to ten and then much higher.
He yawns and falls asleep while he is still counting.
The Sun comes out, and he begins counting again.
Because his sleep broke the count, he forgets his old place.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does Chanda Mama start counting?
options: the stars
the Sun
the clouds
activities.explanation: Chanda Mama starts counting the stars.

activities.prompt: Chanda Mama counts from one to ______.
activities.hint: This is the last number in his first count.
activities.explanation: Well done! He counts from one to ten.

activities.prompt: What does Chanda Mama do just after he yawns?
options: He counts up to nine hundred and ninety-nine.
He begins counting the stars again.
He falls asleep while counting.
The Sun peeks out from behind the clouds.
activities.explanation: After yawning, he counts up to nine hundred and ninety-nine.

activities.prompt: Match each action with what happens.
pairs: counts up to nine hundred and ninety-nine
activities.explanation: Each action matches the event in Chanda Mama's story.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happen.
items: Chanda Mama starts counting the stars.
He counts from one to ten.
He yawns and counts up to nine hundred and ninety-nine.
The Sun peeks out from behind the clouds.
activities.explanation: The story moves from counting to sleep and then the Sun peeking out.

activities.prompt: Chanda Mama begins counting the stars again. What happens next?
options: He forgets his stopping point.
He remembers each number.
He starts counting the Sun.
He counts only one cloud.
activities.explanation: He cannot remember where he stopped counting.

activities.prompt: Chanda Mama is round like a circle at some times. Can we always draw him that way?
options: No, because his round shape fits only at some times.
Yes, because his round shape never changes.
No, because he changes shape while counting.
Yes, because all the stars look the same.

why.Yes, because his round shape never chang: This mistake treats “at some times” as “at all times”.
why.No, because he changes shape while count: Nothing in the facts says counting changes his shape.
why.Yes, because all the stars look the same: This mistake uses the stars he counts to explain his shape.

activities.explanation: “At some times” limits the circle shape to certain times.

activities.prompt: The Sun peeps out from behind the clouds. It is morning. Why does Chanda Mama begin counting again?
options: A new morning has begun, so he starts counting again.
He has finished counting every star in the sky.
He wants to count clouds instead of stars.
He must wait for another night to begin.

why.He has finished counting every star in t: This mistake thinks he completes every star before morning.
why.He wants to count clouds instead of star: This mistake changes his task from stars to clouds.
This mistake makes memory a condition for starting again.

activities.explanation: The Sun comes out in the morning, and he starts again.

activities.prompt: Chanda Mama yawns before counting up to nine hundred and ninety-nine. What does the word “yawns” show?
options: He is feeling sleepy.
He is feeling hungry.
He is feeling angry.
He wants to run away.

A yawn shows tiredness, not hunger.
A yawn shows tiredness, not anger.
A yawn shows tiredness, not a wish to run.

activities.explanation: He later falls asleep, so the yawn shows sleepiness.

activities.prompt: Chanda Mama counts from one to ten. Then he counts much larger numbers. What does this show?
options: He keeps counting toward larger numbers.
He starts counting down from ten.
He stops after the number ten.
He counts only the same small numbers.

This mistake treats larger numbers as smaller ones.
This mistake thinks ten ends his counting.
This mistake ignores the larger numbers he says.

activities.explanation: The numbers keep growing, from one to ten and beyond.

activities.prompt: Chanda Mama counts three hundred and eleven. He also counts five hundred and sixteen and eight hundred and ninety. Why might he yawn next?
options: His counting has gone on for a long time.
He has already reached the very last number.
The Sun has made him feel sleepy.
He wants to count the clouds next.

why.He has already reached the very last num: The facts never say he reaches the last number.
The Sun comes out later, so it does not cause this yawn.
He counts stars, so choosing clouds is a mistake.

activities.explanation: He counts many large numbers, then yawns, which suggests tiredness.

activities.prompt: Chanda Mama begins counting the stars again. He cannot remember where he stopped. What does this show about starting again?
options: He can start again even after forgetting his place.
He must count the same stars in the same way.
He can count only when he remembers every number.
He will always stop at nine hundred and ninety-nine.

why.He must count the same stars in the same: This mistake assumes every new round is exactly the same.
why.He can count only when he remembers ever: This mistake says he cannot start without remembering.
why.He will always stop at nine hundred and: This mistake treats nine hundred and ninety-nine as his fixed limit.

activities.explanation: He starts again even though he cannot remember his place.

lessons.title: Chanda Mama Gets Help

activities.prompt: How does the Sun help Chanda Mama count the stars?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Chanda Mama Counts the Stars
activities.body: Chanda Mama counts the stars on many nights. He often forgets how many he has counted. One night, he becomes upset and begins to cry. He thinks he will never finish. The Sun smiles and says it can tell him how many stars there are. Chanda Mama becomes surprised and then happy.
keyPoints: He counts stars on many nights.
He becomes upset and begins to cry.
The Sun says it can tell him how many stars there are.
activities.explanation: This card explains Chanda Mama's feelings and what the Sun says.

activities.prompt: Why does Chanda Mama cry, and how does the Sun help him?
steps: The night ends before he remembers his count, so he counts on many nights.
He often forgets the number he reached, so he thinks he will never finish.
One night, this worry makes him very upset, so he begins to cry.
The Sun sees his tears and tells him the star number, so he becomes happy.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does Chanda Mama often forget?
options: the number he has reached
the names of the stars
the colour of the sky
the way to his home
activities.explanation: Chanda Mama often forgets the number he has counted.

activities.prompt: Chanda Mama keeps counting the stars on many ______.
activities.hint: He does this again and again.
activities.explanation: The lesson says he counts the stars on many nights.

activities.prompt: Match each beginning with what happens next.
pairs: When the Sun sees his tears
After the Sun gives his answer
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a moment and what happens next.

activities.prompt: What does the Sun say it can tell Chanda Mama?
options: how many stars fill the sky
how many clouds fill the sky
how many lights shine at home
how many children need his help
activities.explanation: The Sun says it can tell him how many stars are in the sky.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happen.
items: He forgets the number he has reached
He becomes upset and begins to cry
The Sun says it can tell him the stars' number
activities.explanation: He counts the stars, forgets his count, and cries. Then the Sun speaks.

activities.prompt: Why was Chanda Mama surprised by the Sun's answer?
options: The Sun said it could count the stars.
The Moon had counted all the stars.
The stars began to speak very loudly.
The lovely children began to cry loudly.
activities.explanation: He was surprised because the Sun said it could tell him the stars' number.

activities.prompt: Chanda Mama counts stars on many nights. He often forgets his number. How does he feel?
options: He thinks he may never finish counting.
He knows that every count is perfect.
He believes that stars stop appearing.
He feels sure that he has finished.

This wrongly thinks forgetting means every count was perfect.
This wrongly thinks forgetting makes the stars disappear.
This wrongly thinks forgetting means the counting is already done.

activities.explanation: Forgetting his number makes him fear that the count will never end.

activities.prompt: The Sun sees Chanda Mama crying and smiles. What does this show?
options: The Sun wants to help him.
The Sun thinks his tears are funny.
The Sun is angry about his tears.
The Sun wants the counting to stop.

It mistakes kindness for laughing at his tears.
It mistakes a happy smile for anger.
It mistakes help for a wish to stop counting.

activities.explanation: The Sun wants to help by offering the star number.

activities.prompt: The Sun says, "I can tell him how many stars there are." What does "tell" mean?
options: Give him the number
Count them beside him
Hide them from him
Ask him to guess

why.Count them beside him: This wrongly makes telling sound like counting together.
why.Hide them from him: This wrongly makes telling sound like hiding stars.
why.Ask him to guess: This wrongly makes telling sound like asking a question.

activities.explanation: That is what the Sun says it can do.

activities.prompt: Lovely children and stars have equal numbers. How does this help Chanda Mama?
options: It gives him the number of stars.
It tells him when the night ends.
It makes the Moon count the children.
It shows that children cannot count.

This wrongly makes the answer end the night early.
This wrongly gives the Moon the Sun's counting power.
This wrongly says that children cannot count.

activities.explanation: The equal number answers the count he wanted.

activities.prompt: Chanda Mama counts stars on many nights. Why does the Moon matter?
options: It comes out every night while he counts.
It knows the number of stars better.
It stops the Sun from helping him.
It makes the children count the stars.

This wrongly gives the Moon the Sun's counting power.
This wrongly makes the Moon work against the Sun.
This wrongly makes the children do his counting.

activities.explanation: Its nightly appearance belongs with his many counting nights.

lessons.title: Here and There

activities.prompt: How do we know when to say here or there?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Here or There?
activities.body: We use "here" for things near us. We use "there" for things far from us. The distance from the speaker helps us choose the right word. The chapter shows a sharpener and some crayons. It also shows students playing kabaddi there.
keyPoints: Here means near us.
There means far from us.
The speaker's distance helps us choose.
activities.explanation: Here points to a near place, while there points to a far place.

activities.prompt: The speaker sits on a bench with friends. The sharpener is in the pencil box. The crayons are in a big box far away. Which word points to the crayons?
steps: The sharpener is near because the speaker has it.
The crayons are far because their big box is far away.
Therefore, we use there because the crayons are far.
So the speaker should say, “The crayons are there.”
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Places in the Chapter
activities.body: The chapter shows objects in different places. The speaker is on the Earth, and the Moon is in the sky. A sharpener is in the pencil box, while crayons are in the big box. The speaker sits on a bench with friends. Students are playing kabaddi there.
keyPoints: The speaker is on the Earth.
The Moon is in the sky.
Different objects are shown in different places.
activities.explanation: Looking carefully helps us remember where each thing is.

activities.prompt: Which word do we use for something near us?
options: Here
There
Cab
Bench
activities.explanation: We use "here" for things that are near us.

activities.prompt: The crayons are in the big box.
activities.explanation: Yes, the crayons are in the big box.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with its place or activity.
activities.explanation: Each thing has the matching place or activity shown in the chapter.

activities.prompt: Which word tells us that the kabaddi game is far from us?
options: Here
There
Pencil
Crayons
activities.explanation: We use "there" for things far from us.

activities.prompt: The speaker visited Chandigarh this year.
activities.explanation: The speaker visited Chandigarh last year.

activities.prompt: The students are playing ______ there.
activities.hint: It is a game played by two teams.
activities.explanation: The students are playing kabaddi there.

activities.prompt: A child holds a sharpener close by. The crayons are far away. Which word points to the crayons?
options: The child should say here, because the crayons are close.
The child should say there, because the crayons are far.
The child should say here, because the crayons are far.
The child should say there, because the crayons are close.

why.The child should say here, because the c: This uses here for something far.
why.The child should say there, because the: This uses there for something close.

activities.explanation: There is right because the crayons are far.

activities.prompt: A child walks to a big box across the room. The crayons are inside. Why might the child walk there?
options: The child wants the crayons that are far away.
The child wants the crayons that are close by.
The child wants the sharpener in the pencil box.
The child wants the bench where friends sit.

why.The child wants the crayons that are clo: Near does not fit the box across the room.
why.The child wants the sharpener in the pen: This confuses the sharpener with the crayons.
why.The child wants the bench where friends: This confuses the bench with the crayons.

activities.explanation: The crayons are in the far big box.

activities.prompt: A poem says, “Near things are here. Far things are there.” What does this poem teach us?
options: It teaches us to choose words by distance.
It teaches us which things are inside boxes.
It teaches us where the speaker sits with friends.
It teaches us that the Moon is in the sky.

why.It teaches us which things are inside bo: It mistakes a poem about distance for a list of things.
why.It teaches us where the speaker sits wit: It confuses the poem's lesson with the speaker's seat.
why.It teaches us that the Moon is in the sk: It confuses the poem's lesson with the Moon's place.

activities.explanation: It is right because near uses here and far uses there.

activities.prompt: A big box is far from a child. It holds crayons. Read this: “The crayons are there.” What does “there” show?
options: It shows the far place where the crayons are.
It shows the near place where the crayons are.
It shows the place of the sharpener instead.
It shows the place of the Moon instead.

why.It shows the near place where the crayon: Near is wrong because the box is far.
why.It shows the place of the sharpener inst: This confuses the sharpener with the crayons.
This confuses the Moon with the crayons.

activities.explanation: It is right because the crayons are in a far box.

activities.prompt: Students are playing kabaddi. A child says, “They are playing there.” What does “there” tell us?
options: It tells us the students are far away.
It tells us the students are very near.
It tells us the students are holding crayons.
It tells us the students are sitting down.

Near is wrong because there does not mean near.
why.It tells us the students are holding cra: This confuses playing with holding school things.
why.It tells us the students are sitting dow: This confuses playing kabaddi with sitting down.

activities.explanation: Far is right because there means far from the speaker.

activities.prompt: The speaker stands on Earth. The Moon is in the sky, far from Earth. Which sentence fits the Moon's place?
options: The Moon is there because it is far from Earth.
The Moon is here because it is far from Earth.
The Moon is there because it is near Earth.
The Moon is here because it is near Earth.

why.The Moon is here because it is far from: Here is wrong because the Moon is not near Earth.
why.The Moon is there because it is near Ear: There is wrong because near should use here.
why.The Moon is here because it is near Eart: Here is wrong because far should use there.

activities.explanation: There is right because the Moon is far from Earth.

lessons.title: Sorting Things We Can Count

activities.prompt: Which things can we count, and which are too many to count?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Will You Sort the Items?
activities.body: Your teacher will read out a list of items. You will put each item into the correct column of a table. One column is for things that can be counted easily. The other column is for things that are too many to be counted. The stars are too many to be counted. The list includes children, flowers, books, pencils, fingers, people in a town or city, and notebook pages.
keyPoints: The teacher reads out a list of items.
Each item goes into the correct table column.
One column holds things that are easy to count.
activities.explanation: Listen carefully, then sort each item into its correct column.

activities.prompt: A child must sort stars and pencils into the table's two columns. Which column should each one go in?
steps: The table has two columns because one is for easy counts and one is for things that are too many.
The stars are too many to count, so they belong in the too-many column.
Pencils in a pencil box can be counted easily, so they belong in the easy column.
Therefore, the child should sort the stars and pencils into different columns.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Will the Teacher Do First?
activities.prompt: What will the teacher do before sorting the items?
options: Read out items.
Count out stars.
Hide the table.
Thank the teacher.
activities.explanation: The teacher will read out the list so you know which items to sort.

activities.title: The Teacher's List
activities.prompt: The teacher will read out a list of ______.
activities.hint: What will be placed in the table?
activities.explanation: Yes! The teacher reads out items for you to sort.

activities.title: Choose the Column
activities.prompt: Which phrase describes one column?
options: Counted easily.
Counted twice.
Left outside.
Named only.
activities.explanation: One column is for things that can be counted easily.

activities.title: Match Each Part
activities.prompt: Match each part of the lesson to its meaning.
activities.explanation: Great matching! Each part has a clear job in the sorting activity.

activities.title: Too Many to Count
activities.prompt: Which item is too many to be counted?
options: Stars
Pencils in a pencil box
Books in the library
Pages in a notebook
activities.explanation: Correct! The lesson says that the stars are too many to be counted.

activities.title: Find the List Items
activities.prompt: Which pair has both items in the teacher's list?
options: Books in the library and stars
Children in the classroom and fingers on the right hand
Pages in an English notebook and stars
Flowers in a garden and stars
activities.explanation: Well done! Classroom children and right-hand fingers are both list items.

activities.prompt: The teacher reads a list. It has classroom children and children in a city or town. Which choice sorts them correctly?
options: Classroom children go easily; city or town children go in the too-many column.
Classroom children go in the too-many column; city or town children go easily.
Both classroom children and city or town children go in the easy column.
Both classroom children and city or town children go in the too-many column.

why.Classroom children go in the too-many co: This swaps the columns by treating classroom children as too many.
why.Both classroom children and city or town: This wrongly treats the many children in a city or town as easy to count.
This wrongly treats the classroom children as too many to count.

activities.explanation: This is right because classroom children are easy to count, but city or town children are too many.

activities.prompt: The teacher explains the table's two columns. Where should stars and right-hand fingers go?
options: Stars go in the too-many column; right-hand fingers go in the easy column.
Stars go in the easy column; right-hand fingers go in the too-many column.
Both stars and right-hand fingers go in the too-many column of the table.
Both stars and right-hand fingers go in the easy column of the table.

why.Stars go in the easy column; right-hand: This swaps the columns by treating stars as easy and fingers as too many.
why.Both stars and right-hand fingers go in: This wrongly treats easily counted fingers as too many to count.
This wrongly treats the too many stars as easy to count.

activities.explanation: This is right because stars are too many, while right-hand fingers are easy to count.

activities.prompt: The teacher says the stars cannot all be counted. A child counts right-hand fingers and smiles. Why does the child smile?
options: The child is happy because counting fingers is possible, but counting stars is not.
The child is happy because counting stars is possible, but counting fingers is not.
The child is happy because counting fingers is impossible, but counting stars is possible.
The child is happy because both items belong in the same table column.

why.The child is happy because counting star: This reverses what is possible because fingers can be counted, but stars cannot all be counted.
why.The child is happy because counting fing: This reverses what is possible because fingers can be counted, but stars cannot all be counted.
why.The child is happy because both items be: This wrongly assumes that stars and fingers belong in the same column.

activities.explanation: This is right because the child can finish counting fingers, unlike the stars.

activities.prompt:
A poem says:
“The stars are too many to count.
Right-hand fingers can be counted.”
What does the poem show?
options: Some things are easy to count, while others are too many to count.
Everything in the poem is easy to count, including the stars.
Everything in the poem is too many to count, including the fingers.
Only stars can be placed in the table, because fingers cannot be counted.

why.Everything in the poem is easy to count,: This mistake ignores that the poem says the stars are too many.
why.Everything in the poem is too many to co: This mistake ignores that the poem says fingers can be counted.
why.Only stars can be placed in the table, b: This mistake says fingers cannot be counted, but the poem says they can.

activities.explanation: This is right because the poem contrasts easy counting with counting too many things.

activities.prompt: The chapter says the stars are “too many to be counted.” What does “too many” mean here?
options: There are more stars than a person is able to count.
The stars are hard to count because they stay very close together.
The stars are easy to count because they make one small group.
The stars do not belong in any column of the teacher's table.

why.The stars are hard to count because they: This mistake reads “too many” as meaning close together.
why.The stars are easy to count because they: This mistake reads “too many” as meaning easy to count.
why.The stars do not belong in any column of: This mistake thinks the phrase is about table columns, not the number of stars.

activities.explanation: This is right because “too many” means more than a person can count.

activities.prompt: The teacher reads items for sorting. Which pair belongs in the easy-to-count column?
options: Pencils in a pencil box and pages in an English notebook.
Pencils in a pencil box and flowers in a garden.
Pages in an English notebook and books in the library.
Fingers on the right hand and books in the library.

why.Pencils in a pencil box and flowers in a: This mistake includes garden flowers, which are too many to count.
why.Pages in an English notebook and books i: This mistake includes library books, which are too many to count.
why.Fingers on the right hand and books in t: This mistake includes library books, which are too many to count.

activities.explanation: This is right because pencils and notebook pages can both be counted easily.

lessons.title: Writing About the Full Moon

activities.prompt: What might the children see and do on the moonlit night?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Full Moon Night
activities.body: On a full moon night, the children come out to see the Moon. Safura says the Moon looks big and bright. Govind also says it is so bright and big. Ramani says the children should take a picture. Safura’s mother has a camera, which is for taking the picture. Dhruv asks everyone to stand there and take a picture. The help box gives words for taking a picture.
keyPoints: The children come out to see the full Moon.
Safura and Govind say the Moon is big and bright.
The camera is for taking the picture.
activities.explanation: These details will help you write about the full moon night.

activities.prompt: How can they describe the full moon night and take a picture?
steps: Children come out on the full moon night to see the Moon.
Safura and Govind say the Moon looks big and bright.
Ramani suggests a picture, so Safura's mother can use her camera.
Dhruv gathers everyone, and the help box gives words for their writing.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Who says that the children should take a picture?
options: Safura
Govind
Ramani
Dhruv
activities.explanation: Ramani says that the children should take a picture. Good listening!

activities.prompt: Safura’s mother has a ______ for the picture.
activities.hint: You use it to take a picture.
activities.explanation: The camera is for taking the picture. You found the right word.

activities.prompt: Match each child with the correct detail.
pairs: says the Moon looks big and bright
says the children should take a picture
asks everyone to stand here and take a picture
says the Moon is so bright and big
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a child with the correct words. Excellent work!

activities.prompt: What does the help box give?
options: The names of the children
The words for taking a picture
The place for the picture
The words for writing about the Moon
activities.explanation: The help box gives words for taking a picture. Nice job!

activities.prompt: Which two details are both true?
options: Govind says the Moon is small. Safura has the camera.
Ramani says the Moon is bright. Dhruv has the camera.
Dhruv says the Moon is dim. Safura’s mother has a help box.
Safura says the Moon is big. Ramani says to take a picture.
activities.explanation: Safura says the Moon is big, and Ramani says to take a picture. Great work!

activities.prompt: Safura says the Moon looks big and bright. How does she likely feel?
options: She feels excited and amazed.
She feels bored and tired.
She feels afraid and alone.
She feels cross and upset.

Her words show interest, not boredom or tiredness.
She is looking at the Moon, not hiding from it.
Her positive words do not show anger or upset.

activities.explanation: Big and bright sights can make a person feel amazed.

activities.prompt: Ramani says the children should take a picture. Why might she say this?
options: To remember the full moon night.
To make the Moon shine far brighter.
To give Safura's mother the camera.
To send all the children away.

This choice cannot make the Moon shine brighter.
The camera is already with Safura's mother.
Seeing the Moon does not mean sending children away.

activities.explanation: Taking a picture can keep the memory of that night.

activities.prompt: Dhruv asks everyone to stand there and take a picture. What is he preparing?
options: He is preparing one picture for everyone.
He is preparing to hide the camera.
He is preparing to leave the night.
He is preparing to read a poem.

Hiding the camera would stop the picture.
Standing together does not mean leaving the night.
No poem is mentioned when Dhruv asks for a picture.

activities.explanation: Getting everyone ready points to taking one picture.

activities.prompt: Dhruv says, “Everyone, stand here and take a picture.” What does he want?
options: He wants the children in the photo.
He wants the camera left alone.
He wants the Moon moved away.
He wants the help box closed.

Leaving the camera alone would not take a picture.
Moving the Moon is not what he asks for.
Closing the help box would not help the picture.

activities.explanation: His instruction helps everyone appear in the picture.

activities.prompt: Govind says the Moon is so bright and big. What does “so” show?
options: It shows a very strong feeling.
It shows the Moon is moving.
It shows the Moon is hidden.
It shows the Moon is empty.

It does not show that the Moon is moving.
It does not show that the Moon is hidden.
It does not show that the Moon is empty.

activities.explanation: The strong word shows a deep impression.

lessons.title: Making Wind Chimes

activities.prompt: What will our handmade wind chimes look like when the breeze moves them?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How we make wind chimes
activities.body: We make wind chimes with moon and star shapes. We begin by taking a cardboard sheet. We use a pair of scissors to cut a crescent-shaped moon. We draw stars on cardboard and cut them out. Thread is one material used for the shapes. Glue attaches the shapes. We use paper to decorate the sun. At the end, the beautiful wind chimes are ready.
keyPoints: We begin with a cardboard sheet.
We cut and attach moon and star shapes.
The beautiful wind chimes are ready at the end.
activities.explanation: These are the materials and steps for making wind chimes.

activities.prompt: How can I make wind chimes with moon and stars?
steps: Take a cardboard sheet first, because this is where we begin.
Cut the moon and stars from cardboard, because both shapes are needed.
Decorate the sun with paper, because paper is used for decoration.
Attach shapes with glue and thread, so the wind chimes are ready.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Sun decoration
activities.prompt: We use paper to decorate the sun.
activities.explanation: Yes! Paper helps us decorate the sun.

activities.title: Complete the sentence
activities.prompt: We use a pair of ______ to cut the moon.
activities.hint: This tool helps us cut cardboard.
activities.explanation: A pair of scissors helps us cut the crescent-shaped moon.

activities.title: Match the shapes and actions
activities.prompt: Match each shape with how we make or use it.
activities.explanation: We cut the moon, draw the stars, decorate the sun, and attach the shapes.

activities.title: Put the steps in order
activities.prompt: Put these making steps in the correct order.
activities.explanation: We start with cardboard, cut the shapes, attach them, and finish the wind chimes.

activities.title: Choose what we make
activities.prompt: What do we make by attaching the moon and star shapes?
options: Wind chimes
A cardboard sheet
A pair of scissors
A sheet of paper
activities.explanation: Attaching the moon and star shapes helps us make wind chimes.

activities.title: The finishing step
activities.prompt: The beautiful wind chimes are ready before all the shapes are attached.
activities.explanation: We attach all the shapes first. The beautiful wind chimes are ready at the end.

activities.prompt: The shapes are attached. The wind chimes look beautiful. How does the child most likely feel?
options: happy and proud
sad and bored
angry and afraid
tired and cross

why.sad and bored: Sadness and boredom do not fit a beautiful result.
why.angry and afraid: Anger and fear do not fit this happy result.
why.tired and cross: Tiredness and crossness do not fit this happy result.

activities.explanation: The beautiful, finished wind chimes fit pride and joy.

activities.prompt: A child says, “I will draw stars on paper.” Then the child cuts them out. Why is this plan wrong?
options: Stars belong on cardboard, not paper.
Stars need thread before they are cut.
The sun needs cardboard, not paper.
Stars are attached before they are drawn.

Thread is used with finished shapes, not before cutting.
Paper decorates the sun, not the cardboard stars.
why.Stars are attached before they are drawn: Stars are drawn and cut before they are attached.

activities.explanation: The stars are drawn on cardboard, not paper.
